title: Best Coves Near Mandelieu Cannes by Boat: Snorkel Spots
excerpt: Discover the best coves near Mandelieu Cannes by boat, from snorkel spots to secluded beaches. Your guide to anchorages, depths, and local tips for a day on the water.
metaDescription: Find the best coves near Mandelieu Cannes by boat with our guide. Snorkel spots, anchor depths, and local tips for your day on the French Riviera. Book now.
author: Mardo Soo
content:
The 30-second answer

The best coves near Mandelieu Cannes by boat are the Îles de Lérins (especially Sainte-Marguerite for snorkelling), the calanques of the Esterel massif (like Calanque d'Anthéor), and the sandy stretch of Plage de la Rague. You can reach them in under 30 minutes from Mandelieu's port. Most anchor in 3-10 metres of clear water, and you'll want a licensed skipper if you're hiring a boat through BoatHire24. Bring your mask and fins, because these coves offer some of the best snorkelling on the Côte d'Azur.

Why Mandelieu Cannes Works for a Boat Day

Mandelieu sits at the western edge of the Cannes bay, just a few nautical miles from the open sea. You get the glamour of Cannes without the crowds, and the Esterel mountains provide a red-rock backdrop that makes every photo look like a postcard. The local marina, Port de Mandelieu, is a departure point for many boat rentals, including motor yachts and RIBs. You can also launch from Cannes Vieux Port if you prefer. Either way, the coves are close. The water temperature hits 22-26 degrees C in summer, so snorkelling is comfortable from June to October. Visibility often exceeds 15 metres, especially in the calmer bays. For a full selection of boats, check our boat search.

Top 5 Coves and Snorkel Spots

Cove nameDistance from MandelieuAnchor depthBest for
Île Sainte-Marguerite (Plage de la Batterie)4 NM5-12 mSnorkelling, marine life
Calanque d'Anthéor8 NM6-10 mCliff jumping, clear water
Plage de la Rague2 NM3-6 mFamily swimming, sand
Calanque du Petit Caneiret9 NM4-8 mSeclusion, rocky coves
Anse de la Figueirette6 NM5-9 mDolphin sightings, calm water

Each spot has its own character. Île Sainte-Marguerite is the most popular, with a protected bay and a small beach. Calanque d'Anthéor offers dramatic red cliffs and deeper water for snorkelling. Plage de la Rague is a sandy option for less confident swimmers. Calanque du Petit Caneiret is quieter, with fewer boats. Anse de la Figueirette is known for occasional dolphin pods passing through the Golfe de la Napoule.

What to Expect at Each Cove

Île Sainte-Marguerite (Plage de la Batterie)

This is the closest island to Cannes, about 20 minutes from Mandelieu. The bay is sheltered, so the water is usually calm. You anchor in sand or seagrass, and the depth ranges from 5 to 12 metres. The snorkelling is excellent around the rocky edges of the island, where you can see bream, wrasse, and sometimes octopus. There is a restaurant on the island, but it's worth packing a picnic. The beach itself is pebbly, so bring water shoes. The island also has a fort and a small museum, but you are here for the water.

Calanque d'Anthéor

This calanque is further east, about 8 nautical miles from Mandelieu. It is part of the Esterel massif, and the red porphyry cliffs create a stunning contrast with the turquoise water. The anchor depth is 6-10 metres, and the bottom is mostly sand. The calanque is narrow, so it can get busy in July and August. Arrive early, before 10 am, to secure a spot. The snorkelling is best near the cliff faces, where the water is deeper and the fish are larger. You can also climb the rocks for a jump, but check the depth first.

Plage de la Rague

This is a small sandy beach between Mandelieu and Théoule-sur-Mer, only 2 nautical miles from the port. It is popular with families because the water is shallow and the bottom is sandy. Anchor in 3-6 metres, and you can swim to the beach easily. The snorkelling is moderate, with some seagrass beds and small fish. It is a good option if you have children or if the sea is choppy elsewhere. There is a beachside restaurant, but it can be pricey.

Calanque du Petit Caneiret

This is a quieter spot, about 9 nautical miles from Mandelieu, near the village of Théoule-sur-Mer. The cove is small and surrounded by red rocks. The anchor depth is 4-8 metres, and the bottom is rocky in places, so use a buoy if available. The water is very clear, with visibility often exceeding 20 metres. You can snorkel along the rock walls and see small caves. It is less crowded than Anthéor, but still worth a visit.

Anse de la Figueirette

This bay is about 6 nautical miles west of Mandelieu, near the town of La Napoule. It is more open than the calanques, but it offers calm water and occasional dolphin sightings. The anchor depth is 5-9 metres, and the bottom is sandy. The snorkelling is good around the rocky headlands. It is a good spot for a lunch stop, with a few beachside cafes. The bay also has a small port, but you are better off anchoring.

Snorkelling Tips for the Côte d'Azur

The Mediterranean here is clear but can be cold in spring and autumn. A 3mm wetsuit is recommended from April to June and again in September and October. In July and August, you can get away with just a rash vest. The best snorkelling is along rocky shorelines, where fish hide in crevices. Seagrass beds are also good for spotting cuttlefish and sea horses, but avoid disturbing the grass. Bring a dive flag if you are snorkelling away from the boat, as there can be jet skis and other boats. The water is generally calm in the mornings, with a light sea breeze picking up in the afternoon. Plan your snorkelling for before 1 pm for the best visibility.

Packing List for a Boat Day

  • Mask, snorkel, and fins (rental options available, but bring your own for fit)
  • Wetsuit or rash vest
  • Water shoes for pebble beaches
  • Sunblock (reef-safe, SPF 50)
  • Hat and sunglasses
  • Towels and dry bags
  • Picnic and plenty of water (no glass bottles on boats)
  • Underwater camera or GoPro
  • First aid kit (including for jellyfish stings)
  • Extra fuel for the boat if you are heading to Anthéor or further

Most boat rentals through BoatHire24 include a skipper who knows the local anchorages. They can advise on the best spots based on the weather and wind. If you are self-driving a licence-free boat, stick to the closer coves like Plage de la Rague or Île Sainte-Marguerite.

Weather and Wind Considerations

The Mistral wind can blow hard from the north-west, making the sea choppy in the open bay. The Esterel coves are more sheltered, but the Mistral can still create swell. Check the forecast before you go. The best conditions are with a light southerly or easterly breeze, which keeps the water flat. In summer, thermal winds often pick up in the afternoon, so plan your return to port before 4 pm. The water temperature is around 22-24 degrees C in June and September, and 25-26 degrees C in July and August. Visibility is best after a calm spell, as wind stirs up sediment.

How to Book a Boat for the Day

You can rent a boat from Mandelieu or Cannes. Options include motor yachts from around EUR 400 per day, RIBs from EUR 250, and catamarans from EUR 800. All rentals through BoatHire24 include a licensed skipper, so you can relax and enjoy the scenery. The skipper will handle navigation, anchoring, and safety. You just bring your swimwear and a sense of adventure. Book in advance during July and August, as boats sell out quickly. For more tips, read our blog on Mediterranean boating.

Common Questions

Do I need a licence to rent a boat in Mandelieu?

No, if you rent through a company that provides a skipper. Licence-free day boats are available for self-drive, but they are limited to smaller RIBs and require a short briefing. Most visitors prefer the skipper option for convenience and local knowledge.

What is the best time of year for snorkelling?

June to October is the best window. July and August have the warmest water, but also the most crowds. September offers good visibility and fewer boats. April and May are cooler, but you can still snorkel with a wetsuit.

Are there any dangerous animals in the water?

Jellyfish can appear in summer, especially after storms. Weever fish are buried in the sand, so wear water shoes. Sharks are extremely rare in this part of the Mediterranean. Moray eels hide in crevices, so don't put your hands in holes.

Can I anchor anywhere?

No, some areas are protected seagrass meadows (Posidonia) where anchoring is prohibited. Look for sandy patches or use a mooring buoy if available. Your skipper will know the rules. Fines can be high for damaging seagrass.

How far are the coves from Mandelieu port?

Plage de la Rague is 2 NM (10 minutes). Île Sainte-Marguerite is 4 NM (20 minutes). Anse de la Figueirette is 6 NM (30 minutes). Calanque d'Anthéor is 8 NM (40 minutes). Calanque du Petit Caneiret is 9 NM (45 minutes). Times are at cruising speed.

Is there food and drink available at the coves?

Some coves have beachside restaurants, like Plage de la Rague and Anse de la Figueirette. Île Sainte-Marguerite has a restaurant near the fort. Calanque d'Anthéor and Petit Caneiret have no facilities, so bring your own supplies.

What should I do if I see dolphins?

Reduce speed, maintain a distance of at least 100 metres, and do not chase them. Turn off the engine if they approach. Do not feed or touch them. Enjoy the sighting from the boat.

Navigating the Esterel Massif: A Closer Look at the Red Rocks

The Esterel massif is a geological oddity on the Côte d'Azur, made of red porphyry that glows in the late afternoon sun. The coves here are not just scenic; they are sheltered from the prevailing westerly winds, making them reliable snorkelling spots even when the bay outside is choppy. Calanque d'Anthéor and Calanque du Petit Caneiret are the two main ones, but there is also Calanque de la Mauboussière, a smaller cove just west of Anthéor, which is often overlooked. You anchor in 5-8 metres of water, and the rock formations create natural pools and shallow caves. The water clarity here is exceptional because there is no river runoff. If you are renting a RIB from Mandelieu, you can reach these coves in 30-40 minutes. For a full list of available boats, check our boat search.

Port de Mandelieu: Your Departure Point

Port de Mandelieu is a modern marina with 700 berths, located at the mouth of the Siagne river. It is less flashy than Cannes Vieux Port, but that is a good thing. Parking is easier, the fuel dock is open from 8 am to 8 pm, and there are several boat rental companies on site. You can rent a motor yacht from around EUR 400 per day, a RIB from EUR 250, or a catamaran from EUR 800. All rentals through BoatHire24 include a licensed skipper, so you do not need to worry about docking or anchoring. The marina has a few restaurants and a supermarket for provisioning. If you are arriving by car, the A8 motorway exit is 5 minutes away. The port is also a short walk from the Mandelieu train station, which connects to Cannes and Nice.

Costs and Budgeting for a Boat Day

A full-day boat rental from Mandelieu typically costs between EUR 250 and EUR 1,500, depending on the boat type and season. A RIB with a 115hp engine is around EUR 250-350 per day, a 30-foot motor yacht is EUR 400-600, and a 40-foot catamaran is EUR 800-1,200. Fuel is extra, and a day trip to the Esterel coves will use about 30-50 litres, costing EUR 50-80. You should also budget for lunch at a beach restaurant (EUR 20-40 per person) or bring your own. Mooring fees are rare in these coves, but if you use a buoy at Île Sainte-Marguerite, it might cost EUR 10-20. The total cost for two people is around EUR 200-400, which is cheaper than a similar day trip from Cannes. For more detailed pricing, visit our blog on Mediterranean boating costs.

Seasonal Variations: When to Go for the Best Snorkelling

The snorkelling season runs from June to October, but the conditions change month by month. In June, the water is around 22 degrees C, and the visibility is often 15-20 metres because the spring plankton bloom has settled. July and August are the warmest (25-26 degrees C), but the water can be hazier due to sunscreen and boat traffic. September is the sweet spot: water still warm (24 degrees C), fewer boats, and the marine life is active after the summer feeding. October is cooler (20-22 degrees C), but you can still snorkel with a 3mm wetsuit, and the crowds are gone. Avoid July and August weekends if you want a quiet cove. The Mistral wind can blow in spring and autumn, so check the forecast 48 hours ahead. A light easterly wind is ideal for the Esterel coves, as it pushes the surface water away, improving visibility.

Safety and Regulations: What You Need to Know

French maritime regulations are strict. You must carry life jackets for everyone on board, a first aid kit, and a VHF radio if you are going more than 2 NM from shore. The speed limit in the bay is 5 knots within 300 metres of the shore. Anchoring is prohibited in Posidonia seagrass meadows, which are protected by law. Fines start at EUR 750. Your skipper will know where to anchor, but if you are self-driving, look for sandy patches or use a mooring buoy. The coves are patrolled by the maritime police in summer, especially around the Îles de Lérins. Also, be aware of the no-wake zones near the beaches. If you see a jellyfish, do not touch it; the common mauve stinger can cause a painful rash. A vinegar solution is the best first aid.

Combining Coves: A Sample Itinerary

A good day itinerary from Mandelieu starts at 9 am. Head to Plage de la Rague first (10 minutes), anchor for a quick swim and coffee. Then motor to Île Sainte-Marguerite (20 minutes), spend an hour snorkelling around the rocky points. By 11:30 am, head east to Calanque d'Anthéor (30 minutes), anchor for lunch and a longer snorkel. In the afternoon, move to Calanque du Petit Caneiret (15 minutes) for a quieter swim. Start heading back to Mandelieu by 4 pm (45 minutes). This itinerary covers four coves, with plenty of time for snorkelling and lunch. Adjust based on wind and crowds. If you want a shorter day, skip Anthéor and stay around the Îles de Lérins. Your skipper can tailor the route to your preferences.

Local Wildlife: What You Might See Underwater

The Mediterranean is not the tropics, but it has a surprising diversity of marine life. In the coves near Mandelieu, you can see ornate wrasse, damselfish, and bream in the shallows. In the seagrass beds, look for cuttlefish, sea horses, and sometimes octopus. The rocky areas are home to moray eels (keep your hands out of crevices) and conger eels. If you are lucky, you might spot a stingray buried in the sand. In the open water, you can see jellyfish, mostly the mauve stinger in summer. Dolphins are common in the Golfe de la Napoule, especially in the morning. The best way to see them is to keep a lookout from the bow. Do not chase them; they will often approach the boat out of curiosity. The Strait of Gibraltar is a major migration route, but you are unlikely to see whales this close to shore.

faqs.a: June to October is the best window. July and August have the warmest water, but also the most crowds. September offers good visibility and fewer boats. April and May are cooler, but you can still snorkel with a wetsuit.

title: Best Beaches Near Alanya by Boat: Hidden Coves Guide
excerpt: Discover the best beaches near Alanya by boat, from Cleopatra Beach to hidden coves like Fosforlu Cave. Your guide to boating in Alanya, Turkey.
metaDescription: Find the best beaches near Alanya by boat, including Cleopatra Beach and hidden coves. Book your boat hire with BoatHire24 for a day on the water.
author: Mardo Soo
content:
The 30-second answer

The best beaches near Alanya by boat are Cleopatra Beach, Keykubat Beach, Damlataş Beach, and the hidden coves around Fosforlu Cave and Mahmutlar. You can reach them all from Alanya Marina in under 30 minutes. A private boat charter gives you access to quieter spots that the tourist ferries skip. Start your search on BoatHire24 for options with a local skipper who knows the coastline.

Why take a boat to Alanya's beaches

Alanya's coast is a mix of golden sand, pebble coves and dramatic cliffs. The main beaches get busy in summer, with temperatures hitting 30 degrees C and crowds stacking up by midday. A boat lets you dodge the queues and find your own stretch of sea. You can anchor off Cleopatra Beach and swim in water that stays around 26 degrees C in August. Or you can head east to the coves near Mahmutlar, where the water is clearer and the only sound is the waves.

Motor yachts and RIBs are the common choices here. A motor yacht from around EUR 400 a day gives you shade, a sun deck and a cooler for drinks. A RIB is faster and cheaper, from about EUR 200, and can get into the rocky inlets that bigger boats can't. Every charter on BoatHire24 includes a licensed skipper, so you don't need a licence or local knowledge. The skipper knows the spots where the water is calmest and the snorkelling is best.

The departure point is Alanya Marina, which is 15 minutes from the town centre. You can also launch from the small harbour at Mahmutlar if you are staying on that side. The typical route goes west along the coast towards the Dim Çayı river mouth, then east past the castle to the Fosforlu area. You cover about 10-15 nautical miles in a half-day trip, with stops at two or three beaches.

Cleopatra Beach

Cleopatra Beach is the famous one. It stretches for 2 kilometres west of the castle, with fine sand and shallow water that shelves gently. The story goes that Cleopatra herself swam here. The beach is free to walk onto, but it gets packed by 11 am. A boat solves that: you anchor 50 metres off the sand and swim in, or you stay on board and use the ladder. The water is clear enough to see the bottom at 5 metres depth.

The beach has cafes and sunbeds, but from the boat you have your own setup. You can moor for a couple of hours, then move on. The sea breeze keeps it cooler than on land. The depth at anchor is 4-6 metres, good for snorkelling around the rocks at the eastern end. You can see small fish and the occasional sea turtle if you are lucky.

If you want a quieter version, head to the western end of the beach, near the Dim River. The water gets a bit murky after rain, but the crowds thin out. A skipper can drop you at the river mouth where the fresh and saltwater mix. It is a strange feeling, floating in two temperatures at once. The boat can stay for as long as you like, then take you to the next spot.

Keykubat Beach

Keykubat Beach is east of the castle, in front of the Alanya Gardens district. It is narrower than Cleopatra, about 800 metres long, with a mix of sand and small pebbles. The water is deeper here, 2-3 metres at the shore, so it drops off faster. That makes it better for jumping off the boat. The current is mild, but the skipper will check before you dive.

The beach is backed by pine trees, which give some shade if you want to go ashore. But the real advantage from the boat is the view of the castle on the hill. You can anchor about 100 metres out and look up at the Seljuk walls. It is a photo spot that the land-based tourists miss because they are too close to the walls to see them properly.

Keykubat is also the launch point for paragliders from the castle. You see them floating down while you are anchored. It adds a surreal backdrop to your swim. The beach has a few restaurants, but you can eat on the boat with food you brought or order from a nearby spot that delivers to the water. The skipper can arrange that.

Damlataş Beach

Damlataş Beach is a small cove right under the castle, next to the Damlataş Cave. The cave is famous for its stalactites and humid air, which is supposed to help asthma. The beach itself is only 100 metres long, with coarse sand and rocks at the edges. It is popular with locals because it is sheltered from the wind.

From a boat, you can approach the cove and anchor just outside the swimming zone. The water is 3-5 metres deep and very clear. The cave entrance is visible from the water, and you can swim to the small platform at the base. The beach gets crowded in the afternoon, but the boat gives you a front-row seat without the noise.

The best time to go is early morning or late afternoon. The sun hits the cliff face and lights up the cave. You can also combine it with a stop at the castle itself. The skipper can drop you at the small jetty near the cable car station, and you can go up to the castle for an hour. Then back to the boat for lunch.

Hidden coves around Fosforlu Cave

Fosforlu Cave is the hidden gem. It is a sea cave about 3 nautical miles east of Alanya Marina, near the Mahmutlar area. The name means 'phosphorescent cave' because of the bioluminescent plankton that glow in the dark. You can only reach it by boat. The cave is about 20 metres deep and 5 metres high at the entrance. Inside, the water is turquoise and the light filters through a hole in the roof.

Around the cave are several small coves with pebble beaches and no facilities. These are the spots for a private swim. The water is 5-10 metres deep, and the snorkelling is excellent. You can see groupers, bream and sometimes moray eels in the rocks. The coves are sheltered from the west wind, so the water stays calm.

No cafes, no sunbeds, no crowds. You bring your own supplies. The skipper can anchor or tie to a mooring buoy if one is available. You can spend a couple of hours here, then move on to the next cove. The total area covers about 1 nautical mile of coastline, with 5 or 6 coves to choose from. The water temperature is a degree or two cooler than the main beaches, but still pleasant.

Bioluminescence is best seen at dusk. If you book a sunset charter, the skipper can stay until the light fades and the water starts to glow. It is a surreal experience, swimming in water that lights up with every stroke. You can only do it from a private boat because the public ferries are back by 5 pm.

Mahmutlar beaches and the eastern coast

Mahmutlar is a resort town 10 kilometres east of Alanya. Its main beach is long and sandy, with a promenade and cafes. But the real draw for boaters is the coast between Mahmutlar and the Fosforlu area. There are several undeveloped coves with no road access. You can only reach them by boat or a long hike.

One of these is Çıplak Koyu, or 'Naked Cove', a nudist beach that is quiet and secluded. The beach is pebbly, and the water is deep right from the shore. You can anchor 20 metres out and swim in. The cove is surrounded by pine forest, and the only sounds are the birds and the waves. It is a good spot for a peaceful afternoon.

Further east, near the town of Gazipaşa, there are more coves, but they are a longer trip. A full-day charter from Alanya can reach them, but most people stick to the Mahmutlar area. The water here is generally clearer than around Alanya town because there is less river runoff. Visibility can be 15-20 metres on a calm day.

The eastern coast is also good for fishing. You can troll for bonito and mackerel on the way. The skipper can set up a line if you want. It adds another dimension to the trip. You catch your lunch, and the skipper cleans and grills it on the boat. That is a proper day out.

Practical tips for your boat trip

Book in advance, especially in July and August. The best boats go fast. On BoatHire24, you can filter by boat type, capacity and price. Most charters are half-day (4 hours) or full-day (8 hours). Half-day is enough for three beaches. Full-day lets you explore the caves and have a long lunch.

Bring sunscreen, a hat and a towel. The sun is strong, and there is no shade on a RIB. Motor yachts have a bimini or a cabin. The skipper will provide water and soft drinks on most boats, but check. You can bring your own food and alcohol. Some skippers can arrange a barbecue on a deserted beach if you ask.

Wear shoes that can get wet. The beaches are pebbly in places, and the rocks are sharp. Flip-flops are fine on the boat, but water shoes are better for the coves. A dry bag is useful for your phone and wallet.

The sea can get choppy in the afternoon when the wind picks up. The skipper will adjust the route. Morning trips are usually calmer. If you are prone to seasickness, take a pill an hour before departure. The RIBs can be bumpy in a chop.

Check the weather forecast. The Meltemi wind can blow from the north-west in summer, making the sea rough on the western side of the castle. The eastern side is more sheltered. The skipper knows the local conditions and will choose the best route.

Boat options and costs

You can hire a RIB for 4-6 people from around EUR 200 for a half-day. These are fast, open boats with a small console and bench seats. They are good for reaching the coves quickly but have no shade. A motor yacht for 8-12 people costs from around EUR 400 for a half-day. These have a cabin, toilet, sun deck and sometimes a small galley. They are more comfortable for a family or group.

Sailing yachts are available but less common in Alanya. The wind is light in summer, so you motor most of the way. A catamaran is a good option for stability, from around EUR 600 for a half-day. It has a wide deck and plenty of space for lounging.

All charters on BoatHire24 include a licensed skipper. Fuel is usually included in the price, but check. Some boats charge extra for fuel if you go far. The standard route to the coves and back is about 15-20 nautical miles, which is covered by the base price.

You pay a deposit at booking, and the balance on the day. Cash is common, but some skippers take card. Tipping is not mandatory, but 10-15% is appreciated if the service is good.

Other things to do on the water

Alanya is not just about beaches. You can combine your boat trip with a visit to the Dim River. The river flows into the sea west of Cleopatra Beach. You can motor up the river for a few hundred metres, where the water is fresh and cold. It is a popular spot for a swim and a meal at one of the riverside restaurants. The restaurants have jetties where you can tie up the boat.

Snorkelling is good at the rocks near the castle and around Fosforlu Cave. You can bring your own gear, or the skipper may have masks and fins on board. The best snorkelling is in the morning when the water is calm.

If you are interested in history, the boat can stop at the castle jetty. You can walk up to the Seljuk castle and the Red Tower. It takes about an hour to see the main sights. The view from the top is worth the climb.

For a longer trip, you can go west to the Incekum area, where the beach is long and the water is shallow. The beach is 15 nautical miles from Alanya Marina, so you need a full-day charter. The water is very clear, and there are fewer boats.

Common questions

Do I need a boat licence in Alanya? No. All boats on BoatHire24 include a skipper who holds the required Turkish licence. You just relax and enjoy the trip.

What is the best time of year for a boat trip to Alanya beaches? May to October is the season. June and September are best for fewer crowds and comfortable temperatures around 28 degrees C. July and August are hot and busy, but the sea is warmest.

Can I swim in the Fosforlu Cave? Yes, you can swim inside the cave. The water is deep, and the entrance is wide. The skipper will advise on currents.

How long does it take to reach the hidden coves from Alanya Marina? Fosforlu Cave is about 20 minutes by RIB, 30 minutes by motor yacht. Mahmutlar coves are 15-20 minutes.

Are there toilets on the boats? Most motor yachts and catamarans have a toilet. RIBs and small speedboats do not. Check the boat details before booking.

Can I bring my own food and drink? Yes. Most boats have a cooler. Some skippers provide soft drinks and water. You can also order a lunch box from local restaurants.

What happens if the weather is bad? The skipper will decide if it is safe to go. If the trip is cancelled, you get a full refund or a reschedule. Rough seas are rare in summer, but the afternoon wind can be strong.

How many people can a boat take? RIBs carry 4-6 people. Motor yachts carry 8-12. Catamarans can take up to 20. Check the capacity on the listing.

Is it worth hiring a boat for just two people? Yes. A small RIB is affordable and gives you the freedom to explore. You can share the cost with another couple if you want.

Can I book a sunset trip? Yes. Many skippers offer sunset charters. You can watch the sun go down from the water and see the bioluminescence at Fosforlu Cave. Prices are similar to half-day rates.

title: Snorkeling Spots Near Kemer by Boat: Top Coves
excerpt: Discover the best snorkeling spots near Kemer by boat, from secluded coves to vibrant reefs, with tips on boat hire and local conditions.
metaDescription: Explore top snorkeling spots near Kemer by boat. Find hidden coves, crystal-clear waters, and boat rental tips for an unforgettable day on the coast.
author: Mardo Soo
content:
The 30-second answer

If you are looking for snorkeling spots near Kemer by boat, you are in the right place. The Turkish Riviera offers clear, calm waters and a coastline dotted with hidden coves and rocky reefs. The best way to reach them is by hiring a private boat from Kemer Marina or nearby ports. You can expect water temperatures around 25-28°C in summer, visibility often exceeding 15 metres, and a mix of sandy bottoms and seagrass meadows teeming with fish. A typical half-day trip from Kemer can cover three or four spots, including Paradise Bay, Phaselis Bay, and the quieter coves near Çıralı.

Why Kemer is a top choice for snorkeling

Kemer sits on the Mediterranean coast of Turkey, about 40 kilometres southwest of Antalya. The region benefits from a long snorkeling season from May to October, with July and August offering the warmest water and calmest seas. The coastline is a mix of pebble beaches, rocky headlands, and pine-clad mountains that drop straight into the sea. This geology creates a variety of underwater habitats: seagrass beds, rocky crevices, and sandy patches. You can spot bream, wrasse, parrotfish, and occasionally octopus or sea turtles. The water clarity is helped by the lack of large rivers dumping sediment into this part of the coast. For a full list of boats available in the area, check boat hire options in Kemer.

Top snorkeling spots you can reach by boat

Here are the standout spots within a short cruise from Kemer. Each offers something different, from sheltered bays to open-water reefs.

  • Paradise Bay (Cennet Koyu): A small, sheltered cove about 15 minutes by boat from Kemer Marina. The water is shallow and clear, with a sandy bottom and scattered rocks. It is good for beginners and families.
  • Phaselis Bay: Part of the ancient city of Phaselis, this bay has three separate coves with a mix of sand and seagrass. The underwater ruins and stone blocks attract a variety of fish. It is 20 minutes from Kemer.
  • Çıralı Beach: A long, open beach backed by dunes and forest. The snorkeling is best near the rocky headlands at either end. You can sometimes see sea turtles here.
  • Olympos Bay: Adjacent to the ancient city of Olympos, this bay has a pebble beach and clear water over a rocky bottom. It is less crowded than Phaselis.
  • Moonlight Bay: A narrow, deep bay with steep sides. The water is deep close to shore, so you can see bigger fish. It is about 30 minutes from Kemer.
  • Adrasan Bay: A longer trip, around 45 minutes, but worth it for the remote feel and clear water. The bay has a sandy beach and rocky reefs at the edges.

How to hire a boat for snorkeling in Kemer

You have a few options for getting to these spots. The most straightforward is to charter a private motor yacht or a RIB with a skipper. Prices for a half-day charter start from around EUR 300 for a small RIB, and go up to EUR 800 or more for a larger motor yacht with a cabin and sun deck. Most charters include fuel, the skipper, and basic snorkeling gear. You can also join a group tour on a gulet, which is a traditional wooden sailing boat, but that gives you less flexibility on timing and locations. If you want to explore at your own pace, a private boat is better. You can find a range of options on BoatHire24, which lists boats in Kemer and the surrounding area. Remember that all charters include a licensed skipper, so you do not need a boating licence yourself.

What to expect underwater: marine life and visibility

The Mediterranean is not as colourful as tropical reefs, but it has its own charm. In the coves near Kemer, you will see schools of two-banded bream, saddled seabream, and ornate wrasse. If you look under overhangs, you might find moray eels or scorpionfish. Octopus are common but well-camouflaged. In seagrass meadows, you can spot pipefish and seahorses, though they are harder to find. Visibility varies with weather and season. In summer, after a few calm days, it can reach 20 metres. After a storm or in spring, it might drop to 5-8 metres. The water temperature in August is around 28°C, so a thin wetsuit is optional. In May or October, the water is cooler, 20-22°C, and a 3mm wetsuit is comfortable.

Best time of year for snorkeling near Kemer

The snorkeling season in Kemer runs from late April to early November. The peak months are July and August, when the sea is warm and the weather is stable. However, these months also bring more boat traffic and crowds at popular spots like Phaselis. If you prefer quieter coves, aim for June or September. The water is still warm, 24-26°C, and the beaches are less crowded. May and October are cooler but still pleasant, especially if you wear a wetsuit. The sea can be choppier in spring due to the meltemi wind, but the morning hours are usually calm. For more seasonal advice, read our blog on the best times for boat trips in Turkey.

Tips for a successful snorkeling trip by boat

Plan your route in advance. Most boat charters from Kemer can cover two or three spots in a half-day trip. Start early, around 9am, to beat the heat and the crowds. Bring your own mask and snorkel if you have them, as the provided gear might not fit well. A rash guard or thin wetsuit protects against sunburn and jellyfish stings. Sunscreen is essential, but use reef-safe brands to protect the marine environment. Pack plenty of water and snacks, as some coves have no facilities. If you are prone to seasickness, take a motion sickness pill before boarding. The boat will anchor in most spots, so you can swim directly from the boat. Some coves have a ladder or steps for easy entry.

Combining snorkeling with other activities

A boat trip to these coves does not have to be just about snorkeling. Many charters offer a lunch stop at a beachfront restaurant, especially in Phaselis or Çıralı. You can also combine snorkeling with a visit to the ancient ruins at Phaselis or Olympos. Some boats have a slide or a swimming platform for kids. If you are interested in fishing, you can bring a handline or ask the skipper to stop at a reef. For a full-day trip, you can head further south to Adrasan or even to the island of Üç Adalar, which has a few snorkeling spots. Just let the skipper know your preferences when booking.

Common questions

Do I need a boat licence to charter a boat in Kemer? No. All boats on BoatHire24 include a licensed skipper, so you do not need any licence. Just relax and enjoy the ride.

How much does a private boat charter cost in Kemer? Prices vary by boat type and duration. A small RIB for a half day starts from around EUR 300. A larger motor yacht for a full day can be EUR 800 or more. Check the listings for exact prices.

Can I bring my own snorkeling gear? Yes, you can. Most boats provide basic masks and snorkels, but your own gear will fit better and be more comfortable.

Are there any dangerous animals in the water? The Mediterranean is generally safe. You might see jellyfish in late summer, but they are usually not dangerous. Scorpionfish and moray eels are venomous but not aggressive. Do not touch anything you do not recognise.

What is the best time of day for snorkeling? Morning, between 9am and 12pm, when the water is calmest and the light is good for visibility. Afternoon winds can stir up the sea.

Can I book a boat trip on the same day? It depends on availability. In peak season, it is better to book a day or two in advance. Use the search on BoatHire24 to check last-minute options.

Is it possible to see sea turtles while snorkeling? Yes, especially around Çıralı Beach and Olympos Bay. Loggerhead turtles (Caretta caretta) nest on the beach at Çıralı. They are most common from May to August.

Departure ports and their advantages for snorkeling trips

Kemer Marina is your main launch point, but it is not the only option. Kemer Marina has full facilities: fuel, water, restaurants, and parking. A boat from here can reach Paradise Bay in 15 minutes and Phaselis in 20. If you are staying in a resort between Kemer and Antalya, you might prefer departing from Çamyuva, a smaller jetty about 8 kilometres south of Kemer. Çamyuva cuts 10 minutes off the trip to Çıralı and Olympos. For the southern spots like Adrasan, you can also depart from Kumluca, though the boat selection there is smaller. Each port has its own character. Kemer Marina is busier but offers more boat choices, from small RIBs to 15-metre motor yachts. Çamyuva is quieter and feels more local. If you are booking through BoatHire24, you can filter by departure port to find the closest option to your accommodation.

Boat types best suited for snorkeling in Kemer waters

Not every boat is ideal for snorkeling. RIBs and speedboats are the most practical choice for a group of up to six people. They are fast, so you can cover more spots in a half day, and they have a low freeboard, making it easy to get in and out of the water. A 6-7 metre RIB with a 150-200hp engine costs from around EUR 300 for a half day. For larger groups, a motor yacht between 10 and 14 metres gives you more deck space, a sun pad, and a cabin for changing. These cost from EUR 600 for a half day. Catamarans are stable and have a wide platform at the stern, ideal for families with children. Sailing yachts are slower and less convenient for multiple snorkel stops, but they offer a more relaxed experience. Whatever you choose, make sure the boat has a swim ladder or platform. Most boats in Kemer do, but it is worth confirming when you book through the search page.

How to read the sea conditions for a snorkeling day

Wind direction is the main factor. The prevailing wind in summer is the meltemi, which blows from the north-west in the afternoon. It picks up around 11am and can make the sea choppy, especially in exposed bays. Morning is almost always calm. Check the forecast on Windy or a local marine app. If the wind is forecast to be over 15 knots, avoid open spots like Adrasan Bay and stick to sheltered coves like Paradise Bay or the inner part of Phaselis. Swell direction matters too. A south-westerly swell affects the whole coast, but the coves with a north-facing entrance, like Moonlight Bay, stay flat. Your skipper will know the local conditions, but it helps to have a backup plan. If the sea is rough, ask to head to the lee side of the peninsula near Phaselis. The water clarity drops after a windy day, so aim for a calm spell of at least 24 hours for the best visibility.

Cost breakdown: what you actually pay for a snorkeling charter

The advertised price often excludes a few items. Fuel is usually included for a half-day trip within a 10-nautical-mile radius, but for longer trips to Adrasan or beyond, there may be a fuel surcharge of around EUR 50-100. Snorkeling gear is provided free on most boats, but it is basic: a mask, snorkel, and fins. If you want a wetsuit, expect to pay EUR 10-15 extra or bring your own. Lunch is not included in the standard charter price. Many skippers will stop at a waterfront restaurant in Phaselis or Çıralı, where a set menu costs EUR 20-30 per person. Alternatively, you can bring your own picnic. Dock fees and taxes are usually included in the charter price for trips under 8 hours. For a full-day charter, the total cost for a family of four on a motor yacht can be around EUR 700-900, including fuel, skipper, and basic gear. Always confirm what is included when you enquire through BoatHire24.

Lesser-known coves worth the extra cruising time

Beyond the main spots, there are a few hidden gems that require a bit more travel time. Sazak Koyu is a small cove about 35 minutes south of Kemer, near the village of Ulupınar. It has a pebble beach and a rocky reef on the left side where you can find groupers and red mullet. The water is deep close to shore, so it is not for absolute beginners. Another is Boncuk Koyu, 40 minutes south, which is a narrow inlet with steep cliffs. The snorkeling is along the cliff face, where you can see damselfish and wrasses in the crevices. For the adventurous, the island of Üç Adalar (Three Islands) is 50 minutes from Kemer. The islands have underwater caves and a drop-off that attracts larger pelagic fish like amberjack. These spots are less crowded than Phaselis, especially in July and August. Ask your skipper if they are willing to go the extra distance. It might add EUR 50-100 to the fuel cost, but the solitude is worth it.

What to pack for a day of snorkeling from a boat in Kemer

You will spend most of the day in and out of the water, so pack light but smart. A dry bag is essential for keeping your phone, wallet, and towel dry. Bring a microfibre towel because it dries fast and takes up little space. Sun protection is non-negotiable. Use a reef-safe sunscreen with SPF 50, and reapply after each snorkel. A rash guard or a light wetsuit top protects your back from sunburn and your skin from jellyfish stings. Water shoes are useful if you plan to walk on pebble beaches. A hat and sunglasses with a strap are good for the boat ride. Bring a reusable water bottle with at least 1.5 litres per person. Some boats have a cooler with water, but do not rely on it. Snacks like nuts, fruit, and crackers are better than heavy food before snorkeling. If you take medication, bring it in your dry bag. Motion sickness pills are worth taking even if you are not usually prone, as the boat can rock at anchor.

How to combine snorkeling with a visit to ancient ruins

Phaselis and Olympos are the two main archaeological sites reachable by boat. Phaselis has three coves, and the ruins of the ancient city are scattered along the shoreline. You can anchor in the middle cove, swim to the beach, and walk to the theatre and the aqueduct. The entrance fee for Phaselis is around EUR 5-10 per person. Olympos is more extensive, with ruins hidden in the forest behind the beach. A boat trip to Olympos Bay lets you snorkel in the morning, then go ashore for a few hours to explore the Lycian tombs and the temple. Combine the two for a full-day trip: snorkel at Phaselis in the morning, have lunch on the boat, then head to Olympos in the afternoon. The distance between them is 12 nautical miles, about 30 minutes by motor yacht. Your skipper can drop you at the beach and pick you up later. Check our blog for a detailed itinerary for a full-day ruins and snorkeling trip.

Safety tips specific to snorkeling from a boat in Turkey

Always tell the skipper where you are going before you enter the water. In open coves, the boat may drift on the anchor, so stay aware of your position. Use a dive flag or a brightly coloured buoy if you are snorkeling away from the boat. In Turkey, boats are required to display an alpha flag when divers are in the water, but not all do. Take a whistle in case you need to signal. Be cautious of boat traffic in busy bays like Phaselis. Stay within the marked swimming area if there is one. Jellyfish are common in late summer. The most frequent species is the mauve stinger, which has a mild sting. Vinegar or baking soda paste helps. If you see a lionfish, do not touch it; they are invasive and venomous. In rocky areas, watch for sea urchins. They hide in crevices and their spines can break off in your skin. Wear water shoes or fins to protect your feet. If you are not a strong swimmer, wear a life jacket or a snorkel vest. Most boats have them on board.

title: Marmaris vs Antalya Boat Rental: Which is Better?
excerpt: Marmaris vs Antalya boat rental: which Turkish coast is better for your charter? We compare costs, routes, boat types, and local quirks to help you decide.
metaDescription: Marmaris vs Antalya boat rental: compare costs, routes, and boat types for your Turkey charter. Find out which coast suits your trip with our honest guide.
author: Andra Kiirkivi
content:
The 30-second answer

If you want lively nightlife, easy access to Greek islands, and a huge choice of motor yachts under EUR 1,500 a day, pick Marmaris. If you prefer Roman ruins, quieter coves, and longer sailing routes along the Lycian coast, go with Antalya. Both have reliable skippers and modern fleets, but your vibe dictates the choice. For a similar setup in Spain, check out BoatHire24 in Marbella.

Location and atmosphere: two different worlds

Marmaris sits on the southwest coast, wrapped around a natural bay with a massive marina that can hold over 700 yachts. The town is a tourist machine: bars, clubs, and souvenir shops line the waterfront. You step off your charter and you are in the middle of it. Antalya, further east, is older and more spread out. The old town, Kaleici, has Ottoman houses and a harbour that feels like a postcard. The vibe is more relaxed, with a mix of history and beach clubs. If you are after a party, Marmaris wins. If you want culture and calm, Antalya edges ahead. For a similar contrast in Spain, you can compare Marbella's glitz with Estepona's old-town charm when you search for boats near Puerto Banus versus Estepona.

Boat types and fleet availability

Marmaris has the larger fleet, especially for motor yachts, catamarans, and RIBs. You will find everything from budget day boats at around EUR 300 to superyachts over EUR 5,000. Antalya also has a solid selection but leans more towards gulet-style sailing yachts and traditional wooden boats. If you want a fast RIB for a day trip to the Greek islands, Marmaris is better. For a week-long gulet charter along the Lycian coast, Antalya offers more authentic options. Both ports have licensed skippers included in the rental, so no need for a licence. The fleets in both are well-maintained, though Marmaris gets more turnover due to higher tourist volume.

Typical routes and distances

From Marmaris, the classic route is to Icmeler Bay, then across to the Greek island of Symi. That is about 10 nautical miles each way. You can also head to Dalyan for the mud baths and turtle beach, about 25 NM. Antalya routes are longer and more varied. You can sail to Olympos and the Chimera flames, 40 NM west, or to Phaselis and the ancient ruins, 20 NM south. The Lycian coast has more secluded bays and fewer crowds. If you have a week, Antalya gives you more to explore. For a day trip, Marmaris is more efficient. In both cases, fuel costs are separate and typically run from EUR 100 to EUR 300 for a day, depending on the boat and distance.

Cost comparison: what you actually pay

Marmaris is generally cheaper for day charters. A 10-metre motor yacht with skipper costs from around EUR 600 in Marmaris, compared to EUR 750 in Antalya. Catamarans start at EUR 1,200 in Marmaris and EUR 1,500 in Antalya. For week-long gulet charters, Antalya can be more expensive, from EUR 3,000, while Marmaris offers similar boats from EUR 2,500. Fuel, food, and marina fees are extra in both places. Marmaris has more competition, which keeps prices down. Antalya has higher demand for longer charters, so prices are firmer. For a budget-friendly option, Marmaris wins. For a more exclusive long charter, Antalya is worth the extra. For a comparable experience in Spain, you can read our blog on costs in Marbella versus Sotogrande.

Best season and weather

Both coasts have long seasons from April to October. July and August are hot, 35 degrees C, and crowded. Marmaris gets the meltemi wind in July and August, which can make the sea choppy, especially in the afternoon. Antalya is more sheltered and has lighter winds, making it better for sailing yachts. The water temperature in both is 24 to 28 degrees C in summer. May, June, and September are the sweet spots: warm, less wind, and fewer tourists. If you are prone to seasickness, Antalya is safer. If you want wind for sailing, Marmaris is better. Both have clear water and sunny days, but Marmaris has more sudden gusts.

Local attractions and extras

In Marmaris, the big draw is the Greek island of Symi, with its pastel-coloured houses and harbour. You can also visit the Dalyan mud baths and see the rock tombs. In Antalya, the ancient cities of Olympos, Phaselis, and Aspendos are all within a short sail. The Chimera flames, natural gas vents that burn on the mountainside, are a unique night excursion. Both have dolphin-watching opportunities, but Antalya is closer to the open sea where dolphins are more common. For food, Marmaris has more international restaurants, while Antalya has better traditional Turkish meyhane. If you want a mix of history and nature, Antalya is richer. If you want nightlife and island hopping, Marmaris is better.

Which one should you choose?

Choose Marmaris if you want a short day trip with party options, easy access to Greece, and lower costs. Choose Antalya if you want a longer charter with historical sites, quieter bays, and more sailing wind. If you are still unsure, consider your group: Marmaris suits groups of friends looking for fun, Antalya suits couples or families wanting culture and relaxation. Both have excellent infrastructure, English-speaking skippers, and reliable booking platforms. For a completely different experience, you could also consider the Costa del Sol in Spain, where BoatHire24 offers similar options from Puerto Banus to Estepona. But for Turkey, the choice is clear once you know your priority.

Common questions

Do I need a boating licence to rent a boat in Marmaris or Antalya?

No, you do not. Every charter includes a licensed skipper who handles the boat. You just relax and enjoy the trip.

Which is cheaper for a day charter, Marmaris or Antalya?

Marmaris is generally cheaper. A 10-metre motor yacht with skipper starts from around EUR 600, while Antalya starts from EUR 750.

Can I visit Greek islands from both Marmaris and Antalya?

From Marmaris, yes, Symi is a short 10 NM trip. From Antalya, Greek islands are much further, over 50 NM, so not practical for a day trip.

What is the best month for boat rental in these areas?

May, June, and September are best. The weather is warm, water is 24-28 degrees C, and crowds are smaller. July and August are hot and busy.

Are there any age restrictions for renting a boat?

You must be at least 18 to book. There is no upper age limit, but the skipper must be fit to handle the boat. Children are welcome on board.

Which has better nightlife after a boat trip, Marmaris or Antalya?

Marmaris has much more nightlife. Bars and clubs are right on the marina. Antalya has a quieter scene, with a few bars in Kaleici.

How far in advance should I book a charter?

In peak season (July-August), book at least 2-4 weeks ahead. In shoulder months, 1-2 weeks is enough. Last-minute bookings are possible but have less choice.

Port infrastructure and embarkation points

Marmaris has one main marina, Netsel Marina, with 700 berths and full services: fuel, restaurants, chandlery. You will board most charters from there or from the town jetty. Antalya has Kaleici Marina in the old town, smaller with about 100 berths, plus a newer marina at Kemer, 40 km south. Kemer is better for longer charters heading west along the Lycian coast. Marmaris is more convenient for walk-on day charters because the marina is central. Antalya requires a taxi to Kemer if you want a wider boat selection, adding 30 minutes and around EUR 30. If you are staying in the old town, Kaleici is charming but limited for large yachts. For a similar setup in Spain, Puerto Banus is like Marmaris in terms of central marina access, while Cabopino is quieter like Kemer.

Typical day charter itinerary: Marmaris

A standard day charter from Marmaris leaves at 10 am. You head to Icmeler Bay first, 3 NM away, for a swim stop. Then you cross to Symi, 10 NM, arriving around 12.30. You dock at Symi harbour for lunch and a walk through the pastel-coloured streets. Depart at 2.30 pm back to Marmaris, with a second swim stop at Turunc Bay. You dock back at Netsel Marina by 5 pm. Total distance: 26 NM. Fuel cost: around EUR 120 for a 30-foot motor yacht. Lunch at Symi costs extra, about EUR 25 per person. This itinerary is efficient and popular. You can also skip Symi and go to Dalyan instead, but that takes 25 NM each way, so you need a faster boat or a longer day. For a similar day trip in Spain, you could go from Marbella to Cala del Faro.

Typical day charter itinerary: Antalya

From Antalya, a day charter often heads west to Phaselis, 20 NM. You leave at 9 am, arrive at Phaselis at 11 am, swim and explore the ancient ruins for an hour. Then you sail to Olympos, another 20 NM, arriving at 1 pm. You have lunch at a beachside restaurant near the Chimera flames. After lunch, you sail back to Antalya, arriving at 6 pm. Total distance: 80 NM. Fuel cost: around EUR 200 for a 35-foot motor yacht. This is a longer day with more sailing time. If you want a shorter trip, you can just go to Phaselis and back, 40 NM total. The ruins at Phaselis are right on the beach, so you can swim and see history in one stop. For a cultural boat trip in Spain, you could sail from Estepona to the Roman ruins at Baelo Claudia.

Week-long charter routes compared

For a week-long charter, Marmaris offers a loop: Marmaris to Datca (20 NM), then to Knidos (10 NM), then to Bodrum (35 NM), and back via Gulf of Gokova. This covers ancient ruins, quiet bays, and a lively stop in Bodrum. Total distance: about 150 NM. Antalya offers a longer route: Antalya to Kemer (20 NM), to Olympos (30 NM), to Kas (50 NM), to Kalkan (20 NM), and back. Total distance: about 240 NM. The Antalya route has more sailing time and fewer party stops. Marmaris has more nightlife options in Bodrum and Datca. For a week in Spain, you could do Marbella to Sotogrande to Gibraltar and back, about 100 NM. Both Turkish routes require a skipper, which is included. Food and fuel for a week add around EUR 800 to EUR 1,500.

Boat size and suitability for groups

In Marmaris, you can rent a 10-metre motor yacht for up to 10 people. For groups of 6 to 8, that is comfortable. For larger groups, 12-metre catamarans are available from EUR 1,200 a day. In Antalya, the same size boats cost more, but you get more space because the boats are often wider. Gulet charters in Antalya are ideal for 8 to 12 people, with cabins and a crew. For a day trip, a RIB or speedboat in Marmaris can fit 6 people and costs from EUR 300. In Antalya, RIBs are less common; you usually get a motor yacht. If your group has children, both ports have boats with safety rails and shaded areas. Marmaris has more boats with water slides and toys. Antalya has more traditional boats with wooden decks and less modern equipment.

Hidden costs and booking tips

Both ports have hidden costs you should know. Fuel is always extra and varies by boat speed and distance. In Marmaris, fuel for a day is EUR 100 to EUR 200. In Antalya, EUR 150 to EUR 300 because routes are longer. Marina fees are sometimes included, but some charters charge EUR 20 to EUR 50 for docking. Food and drink on board can be provided by the skipper, but you pay extra, around EUR 30 per person for lunch. Tips for the skipper are customary, 10 to 15 per cent of the charter fee. Booking directly with a local operator can save 10 per cent compared to online agencies. Always confirm what is included in the price: some charters include snorkel gear, others charge extra. For a transparent booking experience in Spain, BoatHire24 shows all costs upfront.

Weather patterns and sea conditions by month

In Marmaris, the meltemi wind blows from July to September, strongest in the afternoon, 15 to 25 knots. This can make the sea choppy in open water. Morning trips are calmer. In Antalya, the wind is lighter, 5 to 15 knots, and the sea is flatter because the coast is more sheltered by mountains. April and May have cooler water, 18 to 22 degrees C, and occasional rain. June and September are ideal: water 24 to 26 degrees C, wind 10 to 15 knots. October is still warm, 22 degrees C water, but shorter days. For sailing yachts, Marmaris has better wind in summer. For motor yachts, Antalya is more comfortable. If you are prone to seasickness, choose Antalya or take a morning charter in Marmaris when the sea is flat. For similar conditions in Spain, the Costa del Sol has light winds in summer, like Antalya.

Wildlife and marine life encounters

Both areas have dolphin sightings, but Antalya is better because it is closer to the open Mediterranean. You often see common dolphins and bottle-nose dolphins near Olympos and Kas. Marmaris has dolphins too, but more in the Gulf of Gokova, 20 NM away. Sea turtles are common in both, especially near Dalyan in Marmaris and the beaches near Olympos in Antalya. You can also see monk seals in the caves near Antalya, though they are rare. For bird watchers, both coasts have herons and cormorants. The water is clear in both, with visibility of 10 to 20 metres in summer. Snorkelling is good near rocky shores. If you want to see large marine life, a longer charter to the open sea from Antalya is better. For dolphin-watching in Spain, the Strait of Gibraltar is world-class.

Food and dining on board and ashore

On board, the skipper can arrange a barbecue lunch for an extra fee. In Marmaris, the typical menu is grilled fish, chicken, salad, and rice. In Antalya, you get more meze: hummus, baba ghanoush, stuffed vine leaves, and grilled meat. Ashore, Marmaris has a huge range of international restaurants, from Indian to Italian, along the marina. Antalya's Kaleici has traditional Turkish meyhanes with raki and seafood. For a special dinner, Marmaris has the atmosphere of a party strip. Antalya has quieter, romantic settings. If you want to combine a boat trip with a food tour, Antalya is better for authentic Turkish cuisine. In Marmaris, you pay more for the view than the quality. For a food-focused boat trip in Spain, you can charter a boat to dine at a beach club in Puerto Banus.

Safety and skipper qualifications

In both Marmaris and Antalya, skippers are licensed by the Turkish government. They have at least 5 years of experience and speak basic English. All boats have life jackets, fire extinguishers, and a VHF radio. In Marmaris, the harbour patrol is active and checks boats for safety equipment. In Antalya, the coast guard is less visible but still present. For night charters, both ports require the boat to have navigation lights and a backup radio. Weather cancellations are rare but happen if winds exceed 30 knots. The skipper has the final say on safety. You should always listen to their advice. For a safe and reliable charter in Spain, BoatHire24 works with vetted skippers who have similar qualifications.

Accessibility and transport to the ports

Marmaris is easy to reach. Dalaman Airport is 90 km away, a 1.5-hour drive. Taxis cost around EUR 60. Antalya Airport is right in the city, 15 minutes from Kaleici Marina. Kemer is 40 km from the airport, a 40-minute drive. If you are flying into Turkey, Antalya is more convenient for the airport. Marmaris requires a longer transfer. Both airports have rental cars and shuttles. For a day charter, you can walk to the marina from most hotels in central Marmaris. In Antalya, you need a taxi from the old town to Kemer. For a stress-free trip, choose Marmaris if you want to stay near the marina. Choose Antalya if you want a shorter airport transfer. For a similar setup in Spain, Malaga Airport is close to Marbella, like Antalya.

Booking platforms and how to compare

For Turkey, use local booking sites like Boat Rental Turkey or Click&Boat. Compare prices across at least 3 platforms. In Marmaris, you can also walk to the marina and negotiate directly, especially in low season. In Antalya, direct negotiation is harder because the marina is smaller. Always read the cancellation policy: some require 48 hours notice for a full refund. Check if the price includes VAT, which is 18 per cent in Turkey. Some platforms show prices without VAT. For a similar platform in Spain, BoatHire24 shows all-inclusive prices with no hidden fees. You can filter by boat type, port, and price. The key is to compare total cost, not just the charter fee, including fuel and extras.

title: Turkey Bareboat Charter Guide: Licence & Costs
excerpt: A practical guide to bareboat chartering in Turkey: licence requirements, costs, and tips for sailing the Turquoise Coast without a skipper.
metaDescription: Turkey bareboat charter guide: licence requirements, costs, and tips for sailing the Turquoise Coast. Rent a yacht without a skipper from EUR 1,500/week.
author: Mardo Soo
content:
The 30-second answer

You can charter a bareboat (no skipper) in Turkey if you hold a valid International Certificate of Competence (ICC) or a Turkish licence. Costs start from around EUR 1,500 per week for a 10 m sailing yacht in low season, rising to EUR 5,000+ for a 15 m catamaran in August. You must also pay a transit log fee (approx. EUR 50-100 per week) and a refundable deposit (EUR 1,000-3,000). Departure ports include Gocek, Fethiye, Marmaris, and Bodrum. The Turquoise Coast offers calm seas, reliable winds, and hundreds of anchorages. This guide covers everything you need to know to plan your own bareboat adventure.

What is a bareboat charter in Turkey?

A bareboat charter means you rent a yacht without a professional skipper or crew. You take full responsibility for navigation, safety, and operations. In Turkey, this is popular for experienced sailors who want freedom to explore the coast at their own pace. Unlike a skippered charter, you handle everything from mooring to meal prep. The boat is usually equipped with basic safety gear, charts, and a tender. You bring your own provisions and pay for fuel, water, and mooring fees. The minimum charter period is typically one week, though some companies offer shorter bookings in low season. You must be at least 25 years old and have relevant sailing experience. The boat size ranges from 9 m to 18 m, with monohulls and catamarans available. Popular bases are Gocek, Fethiye, and Marmaris. For a similar experience in Spain, see our BoatHire24 marketplace, though note that skippered charters are more common there.

Licence requirements for bareboat charter in Turkey

To charter a bareboat in Turkey, you need a valid International Certificate of Competence (ICC) or a Turkish sailing licence. The ICC is the most widely accepted document and can be obtained through a short course in the UK or EU. You must also have a VHF radio certificate (SRC) if the boat has a fixed VHF. Some charter companies may accept a US Sailing certification or an RYA Day Skipper qualification. For Turkish nationals, a local licence is required. Non-Turkish residents can use their home country licence if it meets the ICC standards. You will be asked to provide proof of experience, such as a logbook or a skipper's reference. The charter company may also conduct a short sea trial to assess your skills. If you lack a licence, you can still enjoy a skippered charter. For options in Spain, check our boat search page. Always confirm licence requirements with the charter company before booking, as rules can vary by region.

Bareboat charter costs in Turkey

The cost of a bareboat charter in Turkey varies by season, boat size, and duration. In low season (March-April and October-November), prices start from around EUR 1,500 per week for a 10 m sailing yacht. In high season (July-August), expect EUR 3,000-5,000 for the same boat. Catamarans are more expensive, starting from EUR 3,000 in low season and up to EUR 8,000 in August. Larger yachts (15 m+) can cost EUR 6,000-12,000 per week. Additional costs include the transit log fee (EUR 50-100 per week), fuel (EUR 200-500 per week depending on usage), mooring fees (EUR 10-30 per night in marinas), and provisions. A refundable deposit of EUR 1,000-3,000 is required, which covers damage. Some companies offer all-inclusive packages with insurance and cleaning fees. For budget-conscious sailors, consider early booking or last-minute deals. To compare prices with Spanish charters, visit our blog for more guides. Always ask for a detailed quote to avoid surprises.

Popular departure ports and itineraries

The Turquoise Coast is the heart of Turkish bareboat chartering. Key departure ports include Gocek, Fethiye, Marmaris, and Bodrum. Gocek is a favourite for its calm bays and proximity to 12 Islands. A typical week-long itinerary from Gocek might include stops at Gocek Island, Cleopatra's Bay, and Yassica Islands. From Fethiye, you can sail to Oludeniz, Butterfly Valley, and St. Nicholas Island. Marmaris offers access to Dalyan River and the ancient city of Kaunos. Bodrum is ideal for those wanting nightlife and history, with routes to Kos (Greece) and the Bodrum Peninsula. Each port has well-equipped marinas with fuel, water, and provisioning. The sailing distance between ports is usually 15-30 NM, making for relaxed day sails. The best time is May to October when winds are steady from the north-west at 10-20 knots. For a different experience, consider the Costa del Sol in Spain, where skippered charters are standard. Check our boat search for options in Marbella, Puerto Banus, and Estepona.

Insurance and deposit requirements

Bareboat charters in Turkey require a refundable security deposit, typically EUR 1,000-3,000. This covers damage to the hull, rigging, and equipment. Some companies offer a damage waiver (EUR 100-200) that reduces your liability to the deposit amount. Third-party liability insurance is included in the charter fee. You can also purchase additional insurance for personal belongings and travel cancellation. The deposit is held by credit card or cash and returned after the charter, minus any damages. Always inspect the boat before departure and document any existing damage. The charter company will provide a damage list for you to sign. If you cause damage, the cost is deducted from the deposit. For peace of mind, consider a comprehensive insurance policy from a specialist provider. For skippered charters in Spain, insurance is usually handled by the operator. Learn more on our blog about insurance tips for boat rentals.

What's included in a bareboat charter?

A standard bareboat charter includes the boat, safety equipment (life jackets, flares, fire extinguisher), navigation charts, a tender with outboard engine, and basic galley equipment. Some companies also provide bed linen, towels, and a first-aid kit. Not included are fuel, water, food, mooring fees, and the transit log fee. The transit log is a mandatory document that tracks your movements and must be returned at the end of the charter. You are also responsible for cleaning the boat before return or paying a cleaning fee (EUR 50-100). Some charter companies offer optional extras like a hostess, fishing gear, or a paddleboard. Check the inventory list before booking. For a hassle-free experience, consider a skippered charter where everything is taken care of. In Spain, for example, you can rent a boat with skipper from BoatHire24 in Marbella or Puerto Banus, which includes fuel and insurance.

Tips for a successful bareboat charter in Turkey

Plan your itinerary in advance but stay flexible. The Turquoise Coast has many anchorages, but some can be crowded in August. Book moorings in advance for popular spots like Oludeniz or Fethiye Marina. Check weather forecasts daily, especially for meltemi winds which can reach 30 knots. Bring sunscreen, a hat, and a reusable water bottle. Learn basic Turkish phrases like "merhaba" (hello) and "tesekkur ederim" (thank you). Respect local customs, especially in conservative areas. Use the transit log to clear in and out of ports. Keep a copy of your licence and passport on board. For provisioning, buy supplies in the departure port as supermarkets are limited in smaller villages. Finally, consider a trial sail with a skipper if you are new to the area. For a similar experience in Spain, our search page offers skippered and bareboat options in the Costa del Sol.

Common questions

  • Do I need a licence to charter a bareboat in Turkey? Yes, you need an ICC or equivalent. Some companies may accept a logbook of experience.
  • Can I charter a bareboat without a licence? No, but you can hire a skipper for an additional fee.
  • What is the minimum age for bareboat charter? Usually 25 years old.
  • How much does a bareboat charter cost in Turkey? From EUR 1,500 per week in low season for a 10 m sailing yacht.
  • What is a transit log? A mandatory document that records your entry and exit from ports.
  • Is fuel included? No, you pay for fuel separately. Budget EUR 200-500 per week.
  • Can I take the boat to Greece? Yes, but you need a Greek visa and must clear customs. Check with the charter company.

Choosing the right boat for your Turkey bareboat charter

Your choice of boat depends on your crew size, budget, and sailing style. A 10-12 m monohull is ideal for a family of four, offering a balance of comfort and performance. Bavarias, Beneteaus, and Dufours are common in Turkish fleets. For larger groups, a 13-15 m catamaran like a Lagoon or Fountaine Pajot provides more space and stability, perfect for families with children or two couples. Catamarans have shallower drafts (1.2 m vs 2 m for monohulls), letting you anchor closer to beaches. However, they cost 40-60% more per week. If you're a solo sailor or a couple, consider a 9-10 m yacht like a Jeanneau Sun Odyssey. Most boats have 2-4 cabins, a galley, and a heads (toilet). Check the inventory for a dinghy with outboard, snorkelling gear, and a GPS chart plotter. For a different experience, try a gulet (traditional Turkish yacht) with a skipper, available in Gocek and Fethiye. For motor yacht options in Spain, see our BoatHire24 marketplace.

Seasonal timing and weather patterns on the Turquoise Coast

The best season for bareboat charter in Turkey is May to October. May and June offer pleasant temperatures (25-30°C), lighter winds (10-15 knots), and fewer crowds. July and August are peak season with 30-35°C heat, stronger meltemi winds (15-25 knots), and busy anchorages. Book moorings in advance for popular spots like Gocek Island or Fethiye. September and October are ideal with warm weather (25-30°C), steady winds, and quieter bays. The meltemi wind blows from the north-west, creating choppy seas in open waters but manageable conditions for experienced sailors. Avoid November to March when many charter companies close and weather can be unpredictable. For a winter escape, consider the Costa del Sol in Spain, where temperatures stay above 15°C. Check our boat search for year-round options in Marbella and Puerto Banus.

Detailed breakdown of additional costs and hidden fees

Beyond the base charter fee, budget for several extras. The transit log fee is EUR 50-100 per week, paid at the marina office. Fuel costs vary: a 10 m monohull uses 5-10 litres per hour under engine, totalling EUR 200-400 per week. Catamarans use 10-20 litres per hour, costing EUR 400-600. Mooring fees in marinas like Gocek or Fethiye are EUR 20-40 per night; anchoring is free. Water refills cost EUR 10-20 per 100 litres. Provisioning for a week for four people runs EUR 300-500, depending on eating out. Cleaning fee is EUR 50-100 if you don't clean the boat before return. Some companies charge a damage waiver (EUR 100-200) to reduce deposit liability. Always ask for a full price list before booking. For a comparison with Spanish charters, visit our blog on cost-saving tips.

Specific itineraries: Gocek to Fethiye and back

A classic week-long route from Gocek covers the 12 Islands and Fethiye Gulf. Day 1: Depart Gocek Marina, sail 5 NM to Gocek Island for lunch and swimming. Anchor in Cleopatra's Bay (named after the Egyptian queen). Day 2: Sail 10 NM to Yassica Islands, known for clear water and turtle sightings. Day 3: Head 15 NM to Fethiye, stopping at Oludeniz beach for paragliding views. Moor at Fethiye Marina (EUR 25/night). Day 4: Explore Butterfly Valley and St. Nicholas Island, 8 NM from Fethiye. Day 5: Sail 12 NM back to Gocek via Tersane Island, a former shipyard with ruins. Day 6: Relax at Gocek's coves like Hamam Bay or Sarsala Bay. Day 7: Return to Gocek Marina by noon. This route covers 50-60 NM total, with 10-20 NM per day. For a longer trip, continue to Marmaris (30 NM south). For Spanish itineraries, see our boat search for routes from Marbella to Estepona.

Boat handling and navigation tips for Turkish waters

Turkish waters are generally calm, but the meltemi wind can create sudden gusts in open bays. Always reef sails early and use the engine when manoeuvring in marinas. The coast has many rocks and shallow patches; rely on your chart plotter and keep a lookout. Anchor in sandy or muddy bottoms (avoid seagrass to protect the ecosystem). Use 3:1 scope in calm weather, 5:1 in wind. Most anchorages are well-protected, but check the forecast for swell. In Gocek, the 12 Islands offer sheltered bays with depths of 5-10 m. In Fethiye, the gulf can be choppy near the entrance. Always carry a paper chart as backup. Learn to tie a bowline and cleat hitch for mooring. For a refresher, take a one-day skipper course before your charter. For similar tips on the Costa del Sol, read our blog on sailing in Spain.

Provisioning and dining options along the Turquoise Coast

Stock up on provisions in the departure port. Gocek has a Migros supermarket near the marina, open 8 am-10 pm. Buy fresh bread, fruit, vegetables, cheese, and local olive oil. For meat and fish, visit the market in Fethiye on Tuesdays and Fridays. Smaller villages like Gocek Island have only basic shops. Many bays have waterfront restaurants (lokanta) serving grilled fish, meze, and raki. A meal for two costs EUR 20-40. Popular spots include Orfoz Restaurant in Gocek and Kaya Restaurant in Fethiye. For a special dinner, try a fish restaurant on the water. Bring a cooler for perishables. Most boats have a gas stove and fridge. For a different dining experience, consider a skippered charter where the skipper can recommend local eateries. For Spanish dining tips, check our BoatHire24 guide to Marbella restaurants.
