title: Marbella Snorkeling Tips for Beginners: Boat Trips
excerpt: New to snorkeling in Marbella? This guide covers beginner tips, the best spots accessible by boat, what to pack, and how to book a charter with a skipper.
metaDescription: Marbella snorkeling tips for beginners: best spots by boat, what to pack, safety advice, and how to book a yacht charter. Start your underwater adventure here.
author: Mardo Soo
content:
The 30-second answer

Marbella snorkeling tips for beginners: pick a calm day, use a well-fitted mask, and stick to shallow rocky coves like Cala del Faro or the Cabopino reef. A boat charter with a skipper gets you to the clearest water without the swim. You don't need experience, just a bit of common sense and a good sunscreen.

Why a boat trip makes snorkeling easier for beginners

If you are new to snorkeling, wading in from a beach can be a faff. Waves, currents, and the constant worry about your stuff on the sand. A boat trip solves that. You anchor directly over the best spots, step off the swim platform, and you are in the water. No long swim required. On a BoatHire24 charter, the skipper knows where the water is calmest and clearest on any given day. That matters more than the exact cove name. They also carry safety gear and can give you a quick briefing if you have never used a snorkel before. Most beginners find they relax much faster when they are not also trying to navigate back to shore.

Best snorkeling spots near Marbella for first-timers

The Costa del Sol has a handful of spots that are perfect for beginners because they are shallow, sheltered, and have decent marine life. Here are the ones you can reach by boat from Marbella or Puerto Banús.

  • Cala del Faro, a rocky cove just east of Marbella. Water depth 2 to 5 metres. Lots of small fish and the occasional octopus. Sheltered from the prevailing westerly wind.
  • Cabo Pino reef, off the coast of Cabopino marina. An artificial reef that attracts bream, wrasse, and sometimes rays. Calm in the morning before the sea breeze kicks up.
  • Isla de las Palomas (Tarifa), a longer trip but the water is crystal clear. Dolphins often pass by on the crossing. Best for a full-day charter.
  • Playa de la Carihuela (Torremolinos), a sandy bottom with patches of seagrass. Good for spotting seahorses if you look carefully.

Your skipper on a boat charter can adjust the plan based on wind and visibility. Do not fixate on one spot; go where the conditions are right.

What to pack for a Marbella snorkeling trip

You do not need much gear for a beginner snorkeling trip, but a few items make the difference between a good day and a miserable one. Most charters supply masks, snorkels, and fins, but they are often basic. If you have your own mask, bring it. A proper fit stops fogging and leaks. Here is a short list.

ItemWhy you need it
Rash guard or thin wetsuit (1-2 mm)Water is 18-22°C in spring and autumn. You get cold after 30 minutes without one.
Reef-safe sunscreenStandard sunscreen damages coral and marine life. Use mineral-based SPF 50.
Polarised sunglassesYou see the bottom before you jump in. Reduces glare.
Dry bagFor your phone, keys, and towel. Boats have storage but a bag gives you peace of mind.
Water and snacksSnorkeling dehydrates you faster than you think. Most charters include drinks, but check.

If you are prone to seasickness, take a motion sickness tablet an hour before departure. The Mediterranean can get choppy in the afternoon.

Safety tips you should actually follow

Snorkeling looks easy, and it mostly is, but the sea has its own rules. Here are the non-negotiable ones for beginners in Marbella.

  • Never snorkel alone. Even if you are a strong swimmer. Stick with the group or at least one buddy.
  • Check the flag. Look for red and yellow beach flags before you go out. If a red flag is flying, do not enter the water. The skipper will know, but it is good to check yourself.
  • Boat traffic. Stay well clear of propellers. When you surface, look up and listen. In busy areas like Puerto Banús, boats come through even in marked swimming zones.
  • Currents. The Mediterranean does not have strong tides, but wind-driven currents can push you away from the boat. If you feel yourself drifting, swim diagonally towards the boat, not straight against the current.
  • Hyperventilation. Do not breathe fast before a dive. It can cause shallow water blackout. Breathe normally and relax.

Your skipper on a boat hire will do a safety briefing. Listen to it. They know the local conditions better than any guidebook.

How to book a boat for snorkeling in Marbella

Booking a boat for snorkeling is straightforward. On BoatHire24, you filter by boat type and duration. For a half-day trip, a motor yacht or catamaran works well. Both have plenty of deck space and a swim platform. If you want to cover more ground, a RIB or speedboat gets you to the spots faster. All charters come with a licensed skipper, so you do not need a boating licence. Prices start from around EUR 300 for a half-day on a small motor yacht, and go up to EUR 1,500 or more for a full day on a catamaran with a crew. For beginners, a half-day is usually enough. You get two to three snorkeling stops, a light lunch or snacks, and time to relax. Check the Marbella boat blog for seasonal tips on water clarity and marine life.

What marine life you can expect to see

You are not going to find coral reefs like the Red Sea, but the Mediterranean has its own charm. Around Marbella, you can see:

  • Bream and wrasse, common around rocky bottoms and seagrass.
  • Octopus, shy but visible if you look under rocks. Do not disturb them.
  • Moray eels, they hide in crevices. Move slowly and you might spot one.
  • Seahorses, rare but present in seagrass meadows near Cabopino.
  • Dolphins, not underwater but often seen on the crossing to Tarifa or Estepona.

Do not touch anything. Some sea urchins and jellyfish sting. If you see a jellyfish, back away slowly and tell the skipper. Most are harmless but a few species can cause a painful rash.

Best time of year for snorkeling in Marbella

Water temperature is the main factor. June to September is the warmest, with surface temperatures around 22-26°C. You can snorkel in just a swimsuit. May and October are cooler, 18-20°C, so a thin wetsuit helps. From November to April, the water drops to 14-16°C. Only experienced snorkelers with proper wetsuits bother. Visibility is best in late spring and early autumn because there is less plankton bloom. July and August have more boat traffic and the water can be a bit hazy near the shore. For beginners, a morning trip in June or September is ideal. The sea is calm, the sun is not too harsh, and the marine life is active.

Common questions

Do I need to know how to swim to snorkel? Basic swimming helps, but you can use a life jacket or buoyancy aid. The boat will be anchored in shallow water, so you can stand up in most spots.

What if I get seasick on the boat? Take motion sickness medication an hour before departure. Choose a catamaran instead of a motor yacht, as they roll less. Stay on deck and look at the horizon.

Can I bring my own snorkel gear? Yes. Most charters provide it, but your own mask will fit better. Make sure you have a dry snorkel if you are a beginner, as it stops water from getting in.

Is it safe to snorkel near Puerto Banús? Yes, but stay away from the marina entrance and the main navigation channel. The skipper will anchor in a quiet cove away from traffic.

How long does a typical snorkeling trip last? Half-day trips are 4 hours, full-day trips 8 hours. You usually get 2-3 snorkeling stops of 30-45 minutes each.

What happens if the weather is bad? The skipper will cancel or reschedule. You get a full refund on BoatHire24 if the trip is cancelled due to weather. Do not go out in strong wind or thunderstorms.

Do I need a wetsuit in summer? Not strictly, but a 1 mm rash guard or shorty wetsuit keeps you warmer and protects against sunburn and jellyfish stings.

Choosing the right boat type for your snorkeling trip

The boat you pick affects how easy the snorkeling is. For beginners, a catamaran is the most stable option. It does not roll much at anchor, so you can get in and out of the water without wobbling. A motor yacht also works well, especially those with a wide swim platform and a ladder. Avoid RIBs or speedboats if you are nervous about water entry. They sit lower in the water and can be trickier to climb back onto. On a BoatHire24 charter, you can filter by boat type. For a group of four to six, a 9-metre motor yacht from around EUR 400 for a half-day gives you enough space. For larger groups, a 12-metre catamaran from around EUR 800 is better. The skipper will handle the anchoring and safety, so you just focus on the water.

How to prepare for your first snorkeling session on the boat

Before you jump in, spend a few minutes on the boat getting your gear right. Put your mask on and adjust the straps so it sits snug but not tight. Breathe through the snorkel on the deck to check it does not leak. If your mask fogs, spit into it, rub it around, and rinse with seawater. It works better than any anti-fog spray. When you are ready, sit on the swim platform and slide in backwards. Do not jump or dive, especially in shallow water. Once in, float face down and breathe slowly. Panic is the main reason beginners struggle. If water gets into your snorkel, blow it out sharply. The skipper on your boat charter can show you this in 30 seconds. It is worth asking for a demo if you have never done it.

Snorkeling near Puerto Banús: what to expect

Puerto Banús is the biggest departure port on the Costa del Sol. If you start from here, the snorkeling spots are within 10 to 20 minutes by boat. The water near the marina itself is not great for snorkeling because of boat traffic and murky water. But the coves to the east, like Cala del Faro and Playa de la Fontanilla, are clean and calm. Your skipper will avoid the busy areas. One advantage of leaving from Puerto Banús is that you can combine the trip with a walk around the port afterwards. The marina has plenty of restaurants and shops. For a half-day trip, you can be back by lunchtime. Prices for a motor yacht from Puerto Banús start around EUR 350 for four hours. That includes fuel, skipper, and snorkel gear. Check the Marbella boat blog for the best departure times to avoid afternoon wind.

Snorkeling from Cabopino: a quieter option

Cabopino is a small marina east of Marbella, near the Cabopino dunes. It is less crowded than Puerto Banús and closer to the artificial reef. The reef is about 500 metres offshore, so the boat ride is short. The water here is usually 3 to 6 metres deep, perfect for beginners. You can see bream, wrasse, and sometimes small rays. The seabed is sandy with patches of seagrass. If you are lucky, you might spot a seahorse. Cabopino is also a good choice if you want a more relaxed atmosphere. The marina has a few chiringuitos (beach bars) for after the trip. A half-day charter from Cabopino costs from around EUR 300 for a small motor yacht. The skipper knows the reef well and can anchor right over the best spots. For a private trip, this is a solid option.

Snorkeling from Estepona: clearer water and fewer crowds

Estepona is west of Marbella, closer to the Strait of Gibraltar. The water here is often clearer because there is less river runoff. The rocky coves near Estepona, like Playa del Cristo and Playa de la Rada, have good visibility. You can also head to the Punta de la Doncella area, where the seabed drops off quickly. That means you can see deeper water without swimming far. Estepona old town is worth a visit after the trip, with its flower-filled streets and tapas bars. A half-day charter from Estepona costs from around EUR 350. The trip takes about 15 minutes to the best spots. If you want a full-day trip, you can combine snorkeling with a visit to the Strait of Gibraltar to watch dolphins. That is a popular option on boat hire listings.

Snorkeling from Sotogrande: luxury and marine life

Sotogrande is a high-end marina on the western side of the Costa del Sol, near Gibraltar. The snorkeling here is less known but good. The rocky areas around Punta Chullera and the Sotogrande river mouth have clear water and plenty of fish. You might also see sea turtles, though they are not common. The advantage of Sotogrande is that it is quieter than Marbella. You get more privacy on the boat and the water is less crowded. Charters from Sotogrande start from around EUR 400 for a half-day. The skipper can take you to the best spots based on the wind. If you are staying in Sotogrande or nearby, this is a convenient choice. The marina itself has a golf course and several restaurants for after the trip.

Snorkeling from Benalmádena: family-friendly option

Benalmádena is east of Marbella, near Torremolinos. The marina here is large and has a good selection of charter boats. The snorkeling spots are close by, including Playa de la Carihuela and the rocky area near the Castillo de Bil Bil. The water is shallow, 2 to 4 metres, so it is safe for children. You can see bream, wrasse, and sometimes small octopus. Benalmádena is a good choice if you have kids because the boat trips are short and the water is calm. A half-day charter from Benalmádena costs from around EUR 300. The skipper will provide life jackets for children and can adjust the stops based on the group. The marina also has a sea life centre and a cable car if you want to extend the day.

Cost breakdown for a beginner snorkeling boat trip

Here is a rough guide to what you pay for a snorkeling boat trip in Marbella. Prices vary by boat size, duration, and season.

Catamaran (10-14 m)EUR 600-1,000EUR 1,200-2,000

Sailing yacht (10-12 m)EUR 400-700EUR 800-1,400

These prices include skipper, fuel, and basic snorkel gear. Drinks and food are sometimes extra. Check the listing on BoatHire24 for what is included. For beginners, a half-day on a small motor yacht or catamaran is the best value. You get enough time to snorkel at two or three spots without getting tired.

What to do if you see a jellyfish or sea urchin

Jellyfish are common in the Mediterranean in late summer. If you see one, stay calm and swim away slowly. Do not touch it, even if it looks dead. Most stings from local species are mild, like a nettle sting. If you get stung, rinse the area with seawater, not freshwater, and remove any tentacles with a credit card or tweezers. Vinegar can help, but the skipper will have a first aid kit. Sea urchins are more of a risk because you can step on them in shallow water. Wear water shoes or fins to protect your feet. If you get a spine stuck, soak the area in hot water to soften it and see a doctor if it does not come out. Your skipper on a boat charter will brief you on local hazards before you go in.

title: Marbella Fishing Season Species by Month: Catch Guide
excerpt: A practical month-by-month guide to Marbella fishing season species, covering what you can catch, peak times, and how to book a charter with a licensed skipper on the Costa del Sol.
metaDescription: Marbella fishing season species by month: a complete catch guide. Learn what fish are biting, peak months, and book a charter with a licensed skipper at BoatHir
author: Mardo Soo
content:
The 30-second answer

Marbella fishing season runs year-round, but the species change with the water temperature. From January to March you target dentex and sea bass in cooler waters. April to June brings amberjack and bonito. July to September is peak for bluefin tuna and dorado. October to December sees a return of red snapper and grouper. You can book a charter with a licensed skipper through BoatHire24 any month and expect a decent catch.

January to March: cool water, big predators

Water temperature drops to 14-16 degrees C off the Costa del Sol in winter. That pushes the baitfish deeper, and the predators follow. Your main targets in this window are dentex, sea bass, and some early-season bluefish. Dentex can hit 10-15 kg and fight hard near rocky bottoms around Cabopino and the reefs off Marbella Marina. Sea bass are more common in the sandy areas off Estepona.

You want to fish slow. Use live bait or deep-jigging lures at 30-50 metres depth. Most charters from Puerto Banús will head out to the deeper grounds south of the port. The wind can be a factor in January and February, but the days are usually calm enough for a half-day trip. You can find available boats for fishing charters on our search page that are equipped for winter fishing with heaters in the cabin.

A typical winter catch might be 2-4 dentex in a morning session, plus some smaller sea bass. The action is not as fast as summer, but the quality is higher. If you want a relaxed trip with fewer tourists on the water, this is your season.

April to June: warming waters, fast action

April sees water temperatures climb to 17-19 degrees C. The baitfish schools start to form, and with them come the predators. Amberjack become active around the rocky pinnacles near Cala del Faro and the cliffs east of Marbella. Bonito also arrive in May, often in large schools that feed on the surface. You can spot them by the diving gannets.

Bonito are a blast on light tackle. They run fast and jump. Expect to land 5-10 fish in a session if you hit the right spot. Amberjack are heavier, up to 20 kg, and require more brawn. Most charters out of Sotogrande or Estepona will target both species in a single trip.

June is the transition month. The first bluefin tuna show up near the Strait of Gibraltar, and the dorado (mahi-mahi) start appearing around floating debris. Water temps hit 21-22 degrees C by late June. You can combine a fishing trip with a dolphin-watching excursion because the same currents bring pods of common dolphins into the area. Our blog has more details on combining wildlife with fishing.

July to September: peak season for big game

This is the prime window for Marbella fishing season species by month. Water temperature peaks at 24-26 degrees C. The bluefin tuna run hard from July through September, with fish from 30 kg up to 100 kg possible. The best grounds are 15-20 nautical miles south of Puerto Banús, near the underwater seamounts. You need a powerful motor yacht or a well-equipped fishing boat for these trips.

Dorado are thick in July and August. They school around weed lines and floating logs. You can catch 10-15 in a day, with average weights of 5-8 kg. They are spectacular jumpers and excellent eating. Also in season: wahoo, which appear in August around the deeper drop-offs off Benalmádena.

Skippers will often run half-day trips in the morning to avoid the afternoon heat. Prices for a full-day bluefin charter start from around EUR 800 for a boat with a crew of two. You can also book a catamaran for a more comfortable experience with shade and a galley. Check the search page for options with fishing gear included.

One tip: book early. July and August are the busiest months on the Costa del Sol, and good skippers get snapped up weeks in advance. You can reserve through BoatHire24 with a deposit and pay the balance on the day.

October to December: autumn bounty

October water temperature drops to 20-22 degrees C, and the big tuna start to move south. But the fishing does not stop. Red snapper and grouper become active again on the rocky reefs. These are bottom-dwellers, so you will be fishing at 40-60 metres with heavy lead heads and cut bait. Grouper can exceed 15 kg and put up a stubborn fight.

November brings the first of the winter sea bass run. Schools of bass move into shallower waters around the river mouths, particularly the Río Verde near Marbella and the Guadiaro near Sotogrande. You can also catch pouting and whiting, which are smaller but good for a family trip.

December is quieter but still productive. The water is 15-17 degrees C, and the fish are less aggressive. You can still hook dentex and some late-season bonito if you find the right conditions. Many locals prefer this month because the crowds are gone and the coastline is peaceful. You can anchor off Estepona old town and fish in the lee of the harbour wall.

A half-day winter charter from Cabopino might cost from around EUR 400 for a boat that fits four people. Skippers provide all tackle and bait. You just show up with sunscreen and a jacket.

What you need to know about licences and skippers

In Spain, you need a recreational fishing licence if you fish from the shore or from a private boat. But here is the loophole: if you book a charter with a licensed skipper, the skipper holds a commercial fishing permit that covers everyone on board. So you do not need your own licence. Every charter on BoatHire24 includes a licensed skipper, which means you can fish legally without any paperwork.

The skipper will also know the local marks and the best bait for the day. They will have the boat equipped with rods, reels, and terminal tackle. Some boats have live-bait tanks for catching mackerel or sardines on the spot. You should ask when booking whether live bait is included or if you need to buy it separately.

Departure ports matter for fishing grounds. From Puerto Banús you can reach the deep tuna grounds quickly. From Estepona you are closer to the Strait of Gibraltar and the dolphin-rich waters. From Benalmádena you have easy access to the reefs off the Costa del Sol. Each port has its advantages. You can filter by port on the search page to find the best option for your target species.

Best bait and tackle for each season

Winter (Jan-Mar): Live mackerel or squid for dentex and sea bass. Use 30-50 lb braid with a 60 lb leader. Deep-jigging with slow-pitch jigs works well in 30-50 metres.

Spring (Apr-Jun): For bonito, use small feathers or spoons trolled at 6-8 knots. For amberjack, live bait or poppers. Medium-heavy spinning gear, 20-30 lb.

Summer (Jul-Sep): Bluefin tuna require 80-130 lb stand-up gear with lever-drag reels. Dorado can be taken on lighter tackle, 15-25 lb, with ballyhoo or lures. Wahoo need wire leaders to prevent bite-offs.

Autumn (Oct-Dec): Red snapper and grouper need heavy bottom gear, 50-80 lb, with cut bait or whole squid. Sea bass can be taken on light jigs or live shrimp in the shallows.

Your skipper will have all this gear. You do not need to bring anything except a hat, sunglasses, and motion-sickness tablets if you are prone to queasiness.

Booking tips for fishing charters on the Costa del Sol

Book through BoatHire24 to compare boats and skippers across all ports. Prices vary by boat size, duration, and season. A half-day (4 hour) trip on a RIB for up to 6 people starts from around EUR 500 in low season and EUR 700 in high season. A full-day (8 hour) trip on a motor yacht for bluefin tuna can be EUR 1,200 to EUR 2,000.

Look for boats that list "fishing gear included" and "catch and release" if you prefer that. Some charters let you keep your catch; others release everything. Ask before booking. Also check the cancellation policy: most require 48 hours notice for a full refund.

If you are staying in Marbella, the marina at Puerto Banús is the most convenient departure point. For a quieter day, try Cabopino or Estepona. The fishing is good from all ports, but the travel time to the best grounds varies.

Common questions

What is the best month for big bluefin tuna in Marbella?
August and September are the peak months. Water temperatures are highest and the tuna are feeding heavily before their migration. You need a full-day charter.

Do I need a fishing licence for a charter in Marbella?
No. The skipper holds a commercial permit that covers all passengers. You can fish legally without your own licence.

What is the cheapest type of fishing boat to rent?
A RIB or speedboat with a skipper is the most affordable option. Half-day trips start from around EUR 500 for up to 6 people.

Can I fish from a catamaran?
Yes, some catamarans are equipped for trolling for dorado and bonito. They are more stable and comfortable for groups or families.

What fish can I catch in winter in Marbella?
Dentex, sea bass, and some bluefish. The action is slower but the quality is high.

Is catch and release common?
Many skippers practice catch and release, especially for bluefin tuna. You can keep your catch on some charters if you ask in advance.

How far offshore do you go for fishing?
For tuna, 15-20 nautical miles. For inshore species like dentex, 5-10 nautical miles. The skipper chooses based on conditions and targets.

What should I bring on a fishing charter?
Sunscreen, a hat, sunglasses, a light jacket, and any food or drink you want. The boat provides all tackle and bait.

Puerto Banús vs Estepona: which port for which species

Puerto Banús is the most famous marina on the Costa del Sol, and it gives you fast access to the deep waters south of Marbella. From here, you can reach the tuna grounds in about 30-40 minutes at 20 knots. The downside is the crowds and the higher mooring fees, which get passed on to charter prices. A half-day trip from Puerto Banús might cost from around EUR 600 for a RIB, compared to EUR 500 from Estepona.

Estepona is quieter and closer to the Strait of Gibraltar. That means you can target the migratory species earlier in the season. The waters off Estepona are also richer in plankton, which attracts baitfish and then the predators. If you want amberjack in April or bonito in May, Estepona is a better bet. The port itself is a working fishing port, so the charter skippers there have generations of local knowledge. You can walk from the harbour wall into Estepona old town for lunch after your trip.

For a family trip targeting smaller species like sea bass and pouting, Cabopino is ideal. It is a small, sandy-bottomed marina east of Marbella with easy access to the reefs. The boats there tend to be smaller and cheaper, and the whole vibe is more relaxed. You can combine a half-day fishing trip with a beach afternoon at Cabopino beach, which is one of the few nudist-friendly beaches in the area.

How to choose the right boat for your fishing trip

Not all boats on BoatHire24 are built for fishing. A luxury motor yacht with a flybridge and teak decks might look appealing, but the crew may not have the right gear or the knowledge of the best marks. You want a boat that is purpose-built or at least well-equipped for fishing. Look for boats that list rod holders, a live-bait tank, a fishfinder, and a fighting chair. The best fishing boats are usually the older, workmanlike RIBs and centre-console boats that have been doing this for years.

RIB boats are fast and stable, and they can get you to the grounds quickly. They are also cheaper. But they have limited shade and no toilet, so a full-day trip can be uncomfortable in the July heat. A motor yacht with a cabin gives you air conditioning, a galley, and a proper head. That extra comfort costs more, but it makes a full-day bluefin charter bearable. Catamarans are the most stable platform for fishing, and they have plenty of deck space for a group. You can troll for dorado from a catamaran without worrying about seasickness.

When you book through BoatHire24, you can filter by boat type and amenities. Check the photos for rod holders and a fighting chair. If in doubt, message the skipper through the platform and ask what gear they provide. Most will send you a list of rods and reels they have on board.

Water temperature and fish behaviour: the science bit

Fish are cold-blooded, so their metabolism and activity levels depend directly on water temperature. When the water is 14-16 degrees C in winter, fish like dentex and sea bass are sluggish and feed less often. That is why you need to fish slow and use live bait. As the water warms to 18-20 degrees C in spring, the fish become more active and start feeding aggressively to build up energy for spawning. This is when you get the fast bonito action.

At 22-26 degrees C in summer, the big pelagics like bluefin tuna and dorado are in full feeding mode. They need to consume huge amounts of calories to sustain their high-speed lifestyle. A bluefin tuna can eat up to 5% of its body weight per day. That is why summer fishing is so productive. The fish are constantly on the move, searching for baitfish schools, and they will hit almost anything that looks like a meal.

In autumn, as the water cools back to 20 degrees C, the tuna start their migration south, but the bottom-dwellers like grouper and red snapper become active again. They prefer the cooler water and will move into shallower reefs to feed. The key is to match your fishing technique to the water temperature. Your skipper will check the sea surface temperature charts every morning to decide where to go.

What happens on a typical fishing charter day

You arrive at the marina 15 minutes before your scheduled departure. The skipper greets you at the boat and does a safety briefing. You stow your gear in the cabin or under the seats. The boat leaves the harbour and heads out at cruising speed. For a tuna trip, that means 20-30 minutes of travel time. For inshore species, it might be 10 minutes.

Once on the grounds, the skipper sets up the rods. If you are trolling, they will deploy lures or baits from outriggers and the boat will move at 6-8 knots. When a fish hits, the rod bends and the reel screams. You grab the rod and fight the fish. The skipper will coach you on when to reel and when to let the fish run. For bottom fishing, the skipper anchors or drifts over a reef and you drop your bait down. You wait for the bite, set the hook, and haul it up.

At the end of the trip, the skipper cleans any fish you want to keep. You can take it to a local restaurant in Puerto Banús or Estepona and they will cook it for you for a small fee. Some charters include a ceviche or sashimi snack made from your catch. That is a nice touch on a summer day.

Cost breakdown: what you actually pay for

The price you see on BoatHire24 includes the boat, the skipper, fuel, and basic fishing gear. It does not usually include food and drink, though some charters provide water and soft drinks. You should bring your own lunch or ask the skipper if they can arrange a catering option. For a half-day trip, you probably do not need food, just water and snacks.

Gratuity is not included. The standard is 10-15% of the charter price if you had a good day. Skippers work hard and rely on tips. If you catch a big tuna, consider tipping more. The skipper will also appreciate a cold beer at the end of the trip, but that is optional.

Fuel surcharges can apply in high season when fuel prices spike. Ask before booking. Some charters include fuel in the price; others add a surcharge if you travel more than a certain distance. For a bluefin tuna trip that goes 20 miles offshore, the fuel cost can be significant, so check the fine print.

title: Deep Sea Fishing Charter Marbella Tips: What to Know
excerpt: Practical tips for booking a deep sea fishing charter in Marbella. What to bring, where to go, how to choose a boat, and what species you might catch off the Costa del Sol.
metaDescription: Deep sea fishing charter Marbella tips: what to bring, which port to depart from, what you might catch, and how to pick the right boat. Book with a skipper.
author: Andra Kiirkivi
content:
The 30-second answer

For a deep sea fishing charter in Marbella, you need a licensed skipper, a suitable boat (typically a fishing boat or a RIB), and a bit of local knowledge. Depart from Puerto Banús or Marbella Marina for bluefin tuna, swordfish, and dorado. Bring sunscreen, a windbreaker, and your own snacks. Most charters include tackle and bait. Expect to pay from around EUR 400 for a half-day trip, depending on boat size and season.

Why Marbella for Deep Sea Fishing

Marbella sits on the Costa del Sol, right where the Mediterranean meets the Atlantic near the Strait of Gibraltar. That mixing of waters creates a nutrient-rich zone that attracts big pelagic fish. You can hook bluefin tuna (some over 200 kg), swordfish, amberjack, and dorado. The season runs from April to October, with peak tuna action in summer. The coast here is dotted with ports like Puerto Banús, Marbella Marina, and Estepona, each offering quick access to deep water. Within 20 minutes of leaving the marina, you can be in 100 metres of water. That is not something you get everywhere. The local skippers know the hotspots around the Río Verde mouth, the Cala del Faro drop-off, and the underwater ridges off Cabopino. You do not need to be a seasoned angler; the skippers will set the lines and talk you through the fight. But you do need to be ready for a long day in the sun with no shade. A deep sea fishing charter in Marbella is a proper physical outing, not a booze cruise. The reward is fresh fish for dinner and a story about the one that got away.

What to Bring and Wear

You will be on the water for 4 to 8 hours. The sun is intense, even in spring and autumn. Bring high-SPF sunscreen (factor 50), a hat with a brim, and polarised sunglasses. A windbreaker or a light fleece is useful because the sea breeze can feel cold at 25 knots, even when the air is 30 degrees C. Wear non-slip deck shoes or trainers with good grip. No flip-flops. The deck gets wet and fish slime is slippery. Bring a small bag with a towel, a change of dry clothes for the ride back, and a cooler if you plan to keep your catch. Most charters provide water and soft drinks, but you should bring your own lunch or snacks. The skipper will have basic tackle and bait, but if you have a favourite reel or lure, bring it. They will also have a fish-finder and GPS. You do not need a fishing licence for a charter with a skipper in Spain; the boat licence covers you. But you do need to respect the catch limits. The skipper will tell you what is legal. If you catch a bluefin tuna under the minimum size, you must release it. That is not a suggestion; it is the law.

Choosing Your Boat and Port

Not all boats are built for deep sea fishing. You want a vessel with a deep V hull, a decent-sized deck, and a fighting chair. The most common options are purpose-built fishing boats (around 8 to 12 metres) and RIBs with outboards. RIBs are faster and cheaper, but they offer less comfort for a full day. Fishing boats have a cabin for shade, a toilet, and a galley. Catamarans are not ideal for fishing because the twin hulls create turbulence that spooks fish. Sailing yachts are also unsuitable; you need motor power to chase the fish. For departure ports, Puerto Banús is the most convenient if you are staying in Marbella or the Golden Mile. Marbella Marina is also good and usually less crowded. Estepona port gives you quick access to the deep water off the Strait of Gibraltar, where the dolphins and tuna gather. Cabopino is quieter and closer to the Cala del Faro reef. Sotogrande is a bit further south but offers a direct route to the Gibraltar currents. Benalmádena is more of a tourist port with a long run to the best fishing grounds. To compare options, use BoatHire24 to filter by boat type and port.

PortDistance to deep waterBest for
Puerto Banús15 minBluefin tuna, dorado
Marbella Marina20 minSwordfish, amberjack
Estepona10 minGibraltar currents, dolphins
Cabopino25 minReef fishing, seabream
Sotogrande15 minBig game, marlin
Benalmádena30 minMixed species

What You Might Catch

The Costa del Sol offers a mix of migratory and resident species. Bluefin tuna are the main draw. They pass through from May to October, with the best runs in June and July. You can also catch swordfish, especially at night or at dawn using deep-set lines. Dorado (mahi-mahi) are common in summer around floating debris or weed lines. Amberjack and greater amberjack hang around the rocky reefs and wrecks. If you want something smaller, try for seabream, red mullet, or mackerel. The skippers know the marks: the Río Verde estuary for bass, the Cala del Faro drop-off for amberjack, and the Gibraltar strait for tuna and swordfish. You might also see dolphins, pilot whales, and even orcas if you are lucky. The Strait of Gibraltar is a migration corridor for marine mammals. Do not expect to catch a marlin every trip; that is rare. But a 50 kg tuna is a realistic prize for a half-day charter. The skipper will gut and fillet your catch on the way back, or you can arrange to have it prepared at a local restaurant. Many places in Puerto Banús will cook your fish for a small fee.

Cost and Booking Tips

Prices vary by boat size, duration, and season. A half-day (4-hour) charter on a RIB starts from around EUR 400. A full-day (8-hour) trip on a proper fishing boat costs from EUR 700 to EUR 1,200. Superyacht fishing charters are price on request and can run into thousands. Always confirm what is included: fuel, bait, tackle, ice, drinks, and crew tips. Some operators charge extra for fillet service or for keeping the catch. Book at least a week in advance in summer. The best slots are early morning departures (7 or 8 am) because the fish feed in the cooler hours. Check the weather forecast: wind over 20 knots makes the sea uncomfortable and the fishing poor. Most skippers will cancel if the sea state is dangerous, but some will still go out if you insist. Do not insist. A rough sea means a miserable day and fewer fish. For a reliable booking, use BoatHire24 to compare boats and read the skipper profiles. Look for skippers with at least 5 years of experience in the area and good reviews. Avoid any charter that does not include a licensed skipper; it is illegal to fish without one in Spanish waters.

Best Time of Year and Day

The prime season for deep sea fishing in Marbella is from late April to early October. May and June are best for bluefin tuna. July and August are hot but the fish are still active, especially early in the morning. September and October bring dorado and swordfish. November to March is quieter, but you can still catch amberjack and seabream if the weather holds. The water temperature ranges from 16 degrees C in winter to 26 degrees C in August. Fish are more active in warmer water, but they also go deeper during the heat of the day. That is why dawn trips are more productive. The best tide periods are the two hours either side of high tide and low tide. The skipper will plan around that. For a full-day charter, expect to be out from 8 am to 4 pm. Half-day trips are usually 8 am to midday or 2 pm to 6 pm. The afternoon trips are less popular because the fish are deeper and the sun is brutal. If you are prone to seasickness, take a motion-sickness pill an hour before departure. Ginger biscuits also help. The Mediterranean can be calm, but the area around the Strait of Gibraltar can get choppy.

Local Knowledge and Etiquette

The skippers in Marbella know the local marine protected areas and the no-fishing zones around the Cabo de Gata and the Strait of Gibraltar. Do not ask them to break the rules. They will not. Respect the catch limits and release undersized fish carefully. The crew works hard; a tip of 10-15% of the charter fee is standard if you are happy. Do not bring glass bottles on board; they break and cut feet. Do not play loud music; it scares the fish. And do not expect the skipper to clean your catch if you are not keeping it. If you want to release the fish, say so before the trip so they can use circle hooks that reduce injury. The best spots change with the season and the currents. The skippers communicate with each other by radio, so they know where the fish are biting. Trust their judgment. If they say the tuna are 10 miles south of the Cala del Faro, go there. The scenery is a bonus: you can see the Sierra Blanca mountains, La Concha peak, and the coast of Africa on a clear day. For more reading on Marbella boating, check the BoatHire24 blog.

Common questions

Do I need a fishing licence for a deep sea fishing charter in Marbella?
No, the boat's licence covers you when you are with a licensed skipper. You do not need to bring any documents.

Can I keep the fish I catch?
Yes, within legal size and bag limits. The skipper will advise you. Most charters let you keep your catch, but some charge extra for fillet service.

What happens if the weather is bad?
The skipper will cancel or reschedule for safety. You should get a full refund or a credit. Do not insist on going out in rough conditions.

Are there toilets on the boat?
Fishing boats usually have a small toilet. RIBs often do not. Check before booking if this matters to you.

What is the minimum age for children?
Most skippers accept children over 6 years old. Younger kids can be a safety risk on a moving boat. Ask the operator.

Can I bring my own fishing gear?
Yes. Most charters have good tackle, but if you have a favourite reel or lure, bring it. The skipper will help you set it up.

How far offshore do you go?
Typically 5 to 15 nautical miles, depending on where the fish are. That is about 30 to 60 minutes from the port.

Understanding the Boat Types for Deep Sea Fishing

If you are booking a deep sea fishing charter in Marbella, the boat matters more than you think. Purpose-built fishing boats, usually between 8 and 12 metres, are the gold standard. They have a deep V hull to cut through chop, a wide transom for fighting fish, and rod holders built into the gunwales. Most have a small cabin with a toilet and a basic galley, which is a lifesaver on a hot day. RIBs are the budget option: faster, lighter, and cheaper, but you get bounced around more. A 7-metre RIB with twin 200 hp outboards will get you to the fishing grounds in 15 minutes, but you will feel every wave. For tuna fishing, you want a boat with a fighting chair bolted to the deck. Without it, you will struggle against a 50 kg fish. Superyachts are available for the price-on-request crowd, but they are more about comfort than catch rates. The crew on a superyacht will set the lines, but you are paying for the champagne and the sun deck, not the fishing expertise. Stick to a dedicated fishing boat or a well-equipped RIB if you are serious about catching fish.

The Specifics of Fishing Around Puerto Banús

Puerto Banús is the most famous departure point for a deep sea fishing charter in Marbella. The marina is packed with luxury yachts, but the fishing boats are tucked away at the eastern end. You leave through the narrow entrance and within 10 minutes you are past the breakwater and into deep water. The key spot here is the drop-off about 2 nautical miles south of the port, where the seabed falls from 50 metres to 200 metres in a short distance. That ledge holds amberjack and dentex. Further out, around 8 nautical miles, you hit the tuna grounds. The Río Verde river mouth, just west of Banús, is good for bass and bream after a rain when the freshwater flushes out. The local skippers know these marks blindfolded. They also know that the best tuna action is often 10 to 15 nautical miles south-west, towards the Strait of Gibraltar. If you are staying in Marbella or the Golden Mile, Puerto Banús is the most convenient port. Parking is expensive, around EUR 30 for the day, so factor that in. Or get dropped off.

How the Season Affects Your Catch

The timing of your deep sea fishing charter in Marbella dictates what you might land. Bluefin tuna arrive in May, peak in June and July, and taper off in August. If you want a trophy tuna, book for late June. Swordfish are more of a night-time proposition from June to September, using deep-set electric reels. Dorado show up in July and August when the water hits 24 degrees C or more. Amberjack are resident year-round, but they are most active in spring and autumn when the water is cooler and they feed closer to the surface. Winter fishing (November to March) is for the hardy: you can still catch seabream, red mullet, and the occasional dentex, but the wind can be a problem. The best window for consistent action is from mid-May to mid-September. Within that, the first two hours after dawn are the most productive. The fish are feeding near the surface before the sun gets high. By 11 am, they often drop to 30 or 40 metres. If you are on a half-day trip, ask for the 7 am to 11 am slot. It makes a real difference.

Practical Tips for a Successful Trip

Book your deep sea fishing charter in Marbella at least a week ahead in peak season. The best skippers get snapped up. When you book, ask the operator what species are running and what tackle they provide. For tuna, you need heavy gear: 50 lb class rods and reels with 80 lb braid. For dorado, lighter spinning gear works. Confirm whether the charter includes bait. Most do, but some charge extra for live bait like mackerel or squid. Arrive at the port 30 minutes early to sort out paperwork and meet the crew. Take a seasickness pill even if you think you do not need it; the Mediterranean can be flat calm at the dock and choppy 5 miles out. Ginger tea or biscuits help settle the stomach. Do not drink alcohol before or during the trip. It dehydrates you and makes seasickness worse. The skipper will appreciate a sober crew. If you catch a fish, listen to the crew's instructions on how to fight it. Do not wind when the fish is running; let the drag do the work. And if the skipper says to release a fish, do it quickly and carefully. The conservation rules are strict, and repeat offenders can get the boat fined.

title: Marbella Fishing Licence Requirements: Complete Guide
excerpt: Need a fishing licence in Marbella? Here is the complete guide to permits, exemptions, boat types, and how to book a charter with a skipper who handles it all.
metaDescription: Complete guide to Marbella fishing licence requirements: permits, exemptions, boat types, and charters with skippers. Book your trip with BoatHire24.
author: Andra Kiirkivi
content:
The 30-second answer

If you are fishing from a private boat or from the shore in Marbella, you need a recreational fishing licence issued by the Junta de Andalucía. The licence costs from around EUR 30 a year and covers rod fishing from the coast or from a boat up to certain limits. However, if you book a charter with a licensed skipper through BoatHire24, the skipper holds a commercial fishing licence that covers everyone on board. That means you can fish without your own permit on a guided trip. This guide covers who needs what, how to apply, and what happens if you do not have the right paperwork.

Who needs a fishing licence in Marbella

Anyone aged 14 or over fishing in Andalusian waters needs a recreational fishing licence unless they are on a licensed charter boat. The licence is personal and non-transferable. It covers rod and line fishing from the shore, from a private boat, or from a kayak. If you are under 14, you can fish without a licence but must be supervised by a licenced adult. The licence is issued by the Delegación Territorial de la Consejería de Sostenibilidad, Medio Ambiente y Economía Azul in Málaga. You can apply online or in person at designated offices. The annual fee is around EUR 30 to EUR 50 depending on the type and duration. A one-day licence is also available for around EUR 10. For tourists, a short-term licence may be a better option than a full year. But if you plan to fish more than a few times, the annual licence works out cheaper. The licence is valid across Andalusia, not just Marbella. So you can use it in Estepona, Sotogrande, or even up the coast in Nerja. Keep a digital or printed copy with you at all times. Inspections by the Guardia Civil or the Junta's environmental agents are common at popular fishing spots like the Cabopino pier or the rocks near Puerto Banús.

Exemptions: When you do not need a licence

The main exemption is fishing on a commercial charter boat with a licensed skipper. The skipper's commercial licence covers all passengers. That is why most tourists and casual anglers choose a charter boat in Marbella rather than dealing with the paperwork themselves. Other exemptions include fishing from a public pier or harbour wall with a rod, provided you are not using a boat. But you still need a recreational licence for that in Andalusia. The only real exemption is for children under 14. There is no exemption for EU citizens or non-residents. Everyone must have a licence regardless of nationality. If you are a resident of another Spanish region, your home licence may not be valid in Andalusia. Check before you travel. The same applies to international visitors: you cannot use a licence from your home country. You must get an Andalusian licence. The only exception is for organised competitions with prior authorisation from the Junta. But those are rare for tourists. In practice, the easiest way to avoid the hassle is to book a charter. The skipper handles the licence, the tackle, and the bait. You just show up and fish.

Types of recreational fishing licences in Andalusia

The Junta de Andalucía issues several types of recreational fishing licences. The most common is the Licencia de Pesca Recreativa de Superficie (surface fishing licence), which covers rod and line fishing from the shore or from a boat. There is also a Licencia de Pesca Submarina for spearfishing, which requires a separate medical certificate. And a Licencia de Pesca desde Embarcación for fishing from a private boat, which includes specific rules about gear and catch limits. For most tourists, the surface licence is enough. It costs EUR 31.95 for one year, EUR 17.50 for three months, or EUR 8.75 for one day. You can purchase it online via the Junta's website or at any authorised office. The process takes about 10 minutes. You need your NIE or passport number, a Spanish address (can be a hotel), and a credit card. The licence is issued immediately as a PDF. Print it or save it on your phone. If you plan to fish from a private boat, you also need the boat's registration documents and a valid seguro (insurance). The boat owner usually handles that. But if you are renting a boat without a skipper, you must ensure the boat is licensed for recreational fishing. Some rental companies include a fishing permit in the price. Ask before you book.

Fishing from a charter boat: No licence needed

When you book a fishing charter through BoatHire24, the boat operates under a commercial fishing licence. That licence covers all passengers. You do not need your own recreational licence. The skipper is a professional who knows the local waters, the best spots, and the regulations. Most charters include rods, reels, bait, and tackle. Some even clean and pack your catch. The typical charter lasts 4 to 8 hours and costs from around EUR 400 to EUR 800 for a group of up to 6 people. Popular target species in Marbella include sea bass, bream, mackerel, and sometimes tuna or swordfish. The season matters: summer is good for surface fish, winter for bottom fish. The skipper will advise on what is biting. Departure ports include Puerto Banús, Marbella Marina, Cabopino, and Estepona. Some charters also offer trips to the Strait of Gibraltar where you can see dolphins and whales while fishing. If you want a relaxed day on the water without the paperwork, a charter is the way to go. You also avoid the risk of a fine for fishing without a licence. The fine for unlicensed fishing in Andalusia ranges from EUR 150 to EUR 3,000 depending on the severity. Not worth it.

How to apply for a Marbella fishing licence

Applying for a recreational fishing licence in Andalusia is straightforward. Go to the Junta de Andalucía's online portal (Ventanilla Electrónica) and search for 'licencia de pesca recreativa'. You will need a digital certificate or a Cl@ve login. If you do not have those, you can apply in person at the Delegación Territorial in Málaga (Avenida de la Aurora, 47) or at any Oficina de Turismo. The form asks for your personal details, type of licence, and duration. You pay by card. The licence is issued instantly as a PDF. Print it or keep a copy on your phone. For non-residents, the process is the same. You use your passport number. The address can be your hotel or a rental apartment. The licence is valid for the entire region of Andalusia. So if you are staying in Marbella and want to fish in Sotogrande or Benalmádena, you are covered. The licence is also valid for fishing from a kayak or a paddleboard, as long as you are not using a motor. If you plan to fish from a private boat, you need to ensure the boat has a valid registration and insurance. The licence does not cover the boat itself. That is a separate requirement. If you are renting a boat from a private owner, ask them to include a fishing permit in the rental agreement. Some owners offer it as an add-on. But most tourists find it easier to book a charter and skip the bureaucracy.

Catch limits and regulations

Andalusia has specific catch limits for recreational fishing. You can keep up to 5 kg of fish per person per day, plus one fish over 5 kg. Some species have minimum sizes. For example, sea bass must be at least 36 cm, bream 23 cm, and mackerel 20 cm. If you catch a fish below the minimum size, you must release it immediately. The same applies to protected species like groupers or certain sharks. You are not allowed to sell your catch. It is for personal consumption only. Fishing is prohibited in marine reserves like the Cabo de Gata-Níjar or the Strait of Gibraltar Special Area of Conservation. However, most of the Marbella coast is open for fishing. The Guardia Civil and the Junta's environmental agents conduct random inspections. They check licences, catch sizes, and gear. If you are on a charter, the skipper will handle compliance. If you are fishing from shore or a private boat, it is your responsibility. The penalties for exceeding catch limits or taking undersized fish range from EUR 150 to EUR 3,000. In serious cases, your gear can be confiscated. So follow the rules. If you are unsure, ask the skipper or check the Junta's website. Most charters also have a conservation ethic: they release what they do not eat and only take what is legal.

Best fishing spots near Marbella

Marbella offers a variety of fishing spots, from shore to offshore. From the shore, popular locations include the rocks near Puerto Banús, the Cabopino pier, and the beach at San Pedro de Alcántara. These spots are accessible and often yield bream, sea bass, and mackerel. For boat fishing, the waters off the Costa del Sol are rich with marine life. The Río Verde estuary is a good spot for bass and mullet. The Cala del Faro area near Estepona has rocky bottoms that attract larger fish. Heading west toward the Strait of Gibraltar, you can find tuna, swordfish, and even sharks. The Strait is also famous for dolphin and whale watching. Many fishing charters in Marbella offer trips to the Strait as part of their itinerary. If you want a peaceful day on the water, the area around Cabopino is quieter than Puerto Banús. For a more social experience, the Marbella Marina has several charter boats that depart daily. The best times to fish are early morning and late afternoon, especially during the summer months when the heat can slow the bite. Winter fishing is good for bottom fish like sea bream and grouper. The water temperature in Marbella ranges from 15°C in January to 25°C in August. That affects what fish are active. The skipper will know the seasonal patterns.

Common questions about Marbella fishing licences

Do I need a licence to fish from the shore in Marbella? Yes, anyone aged 14 or over needs a recreational fishing licence to fish from the shore in Andalusia. The licence is issued by the Junta de Andalucía and costs from around EUR 8.75 for one day. You can apply online or in person.

Can I use my EU fishing licence in Spain? No, you cannot use a fishing licence from another country in Andalusia. You must obtain a licence from the Junta de Andalucía. The process is quick and can be done online. The only exception is if you are on a licensed charter boat.

What happens if I fish without a licence? Fishing without a licence in Andalusia can result in a fine of EUR 150 to EUR 3,000. The Guardia Civil and the Junta's environmental agents carry out inspections. It is not worth the risk. Either get a licence or book a charter.

How much does a fishing charter cost in Marbella? A typical 4-hour charter for up to 6 people costs from around EUR 400 to EUR 800. The price includes the skipper, licence, rods, bait, and tackle. Some charters also include food and drinks. Check the listing on BoatHire24 for details.

What fish can I catch in Marbella? Common species include sea bass, bream, mackerel, and tuna. In the Strait of Gibraltar, you can also catch swordfish and sharks. The season affects availability. Summer is best for surface fish, winter for bottom fish. The skipper will advise on the best spots.

Can I keep the fish I catch? Yes, you can keep up to 5 kg of fish per person per day, plus one fish over 5 kg. Minimum sizes apply. You cannot sell your catch. On a charter, the skipper will help you clean and pack the fish. Some charters include a fish-cleaning service.

Do I need a licence for spearfishing? Yes, spearfishing requires a separate licence (Licencia de Pesca Submarina) and a medical certificate. It is more regulated than rod fishing. Most tourists stick to rod fishing. If you are interested in spearfishing, check with the Junta de Andalucía for the specific requirements.

Is fishing allowed in Puerto Banús? Fishing is allowed from the rocks and breakwaters around Puerto Banús, but not from the marina itself. You need a licence. The area is popular for shore fishing, especially for bream and sea bass. Be careful of the rocks and the waves. Always prioritise safety.

What is the best time of year for fishing in Marbella? Fishing is good year-round in Marbella. Summer (June to September) is best for surface fish like mackerel and tuna. Winter (November to February) is better for bottom fish like sea bream and grouper. Spring and autumn offer a mix. The water temperature ranges from 15°C to 25°C.

Do I need insurance to fish from a private boat? Yes, private boats must have valid insurance and registration. The fishing licence covers you, not the boat. If you rent a boat without a skipper, check that the rental includes insurance and a fishing permit. Many rental companies offer this as an add-on. For more information, see our blog on boat rental tips.

title: Marbella Dolphin Watching Best Camera: Photo Tips
excerpt: Catch dolphins off Marbella with the right camera. We rate DSLR, mirrorless, GoPro, and phone options for boat trips from Puerto Banús to Estepona.
metaDescription: Find the Marbella dolphin watching best camera for your boat charter. DSLR, GoPro or phone tips for clear shots from Puerto Banús to Estepona. Book now.
author: Andra Kiirkivi
content:
Browse the full fleet at BoatHire24.

The 30-second answer

For Marbella dolphin watching, the best camera is a mirrorless or DSLR with a 70-300mm zoom lens and fast autofocus, paired with a polarising filter and a floating strap. If you want something smaller, a GoPro Hero12 or a recent iPhone (Pro model) with burst mode will get you solid shots. The key is preparation: set shutter speed to 1/1000s or faster, shoot in raw if you can, and brace against the boat's motion. You can rent gear locally or bring your own. Ready to book your trip? Check out available charters from Puerto Banús, Marbella Marina, or Estepona.

Why camera choice matters on dolphin tours

Dolphins off the Costa del Sol are fast, unpredictable, and often backlit against the Mediterranean glare. A phone camera can work, but you'll miss the detail and reach you need for a keeper shot. The Strait of Gibraltar and waters around Marbella host common and striped dolphins, plus occasional pilot whales. They surface for seconds, so your camera's autofocus speed and burst rate matter more than megapixels. A slow lens or laggy shutter means blurry fins and missed moments. You also need to deal with spray, salt, and boat vibration. A weather-sealed body and a lens with image stabilisation help. For most people, a mid-range mirrorless with a 70-200mm or 100-400mm zoom is the sweet spot. It's light enough to hold one-handed while you steady yourself, but gives you the reach to fill the frame from 20-50 metres away. If you're hiring a private charter from Puerto Banús or Estepona, you can ask the skipper to position the boat at a good angle, but you still need gear that can keep up.

Top camera types for dolphin photography

Here is a quick breakdown of what works and what doesn't on a boat off Marbella.

Camera typeProsConsBest for
DSLR (e.g. Canon EOS 90D, Nikon D7500)Fast autofocus, long battery life, optical viewfinderBulky, heavy, harder to handle with one handSerious shooters who want full control
Mirrorless (e.g. Sony A6700, Fuji X-T5, OM System OM-1)Compact, excellent AF, in-body stabilisationBattery drains faster, lens selection variesVersatility and portability
Compact superzoom (e.g. Sony RX10 IV, Panasonic FZ300)All-in-one lens, light, good reachSmaller sensor, less low-light performanceTravel light without changing lenses
GoPro / action cam (Hero12, DJI Osmo Action 4)Waterproof, wide angle, easy to mountNo zoom, wide field means tiny dolphinsUnderwater or POV shots, not primary camera
Smartphone (iPhone 15 Pro, Samsung S24 Ultra)Always with you, burst mode, easy sharingDigital zoom degrades quality, less reachBackup or casual snaps

Your choice depends on how much gear you want to carry. A mirrorless with a 70-300mm lens is the most flexible for a half-day charter from Puerto Banús or Cabopino. If you're on a RIB or speedboat, a compact superzoom or phone with a wrist strap is safer. For a catamaran or motor yacht, you have more space to use a DSLR with a monopod.

Best settings for dolphin shots at sea

Getting sharp images from a moving boat requires specific settings. Start with shutter priority mode and set it to 1/1000s or faster. Dolphins breach fast, and boat motion adds blur. If the light is good, go up to 1/2000s. Use a wide aperture (f/5.6 to f/8) to let in enough light while keeping the dolphin in focus. Set ISO to auto with a max of 1600 or 3200 depending on your camera's noise performance. On sunny days off Marbella, ISO 400-800 is typical. Use continuous autofocus (AF-C or AI Servo) with a zone or tracking mode. Burst mode at 5-10 frames per second gives you a sequence to pick the best frame. If your lens has image stabilisation, turn it on for handheld shots. For telephoto lenses, stabilisation is essential. A polarising filter reduces glare from the water and boosts contrast in the dolphin's skin. It also helps with the harsh midday sun. Avoid using a UV filter unless it's a high-quality multi-coated one, because cheap filters add flare. Shoot in raw format if you can edit later, or fine JPEG if you want to share straight away. Check your histogram to avoid blown highlights on the white bellies of dolphins.

Gear you should bring besides the camera

A camera body and lens are not enough for a day on the water off Marbella. You need a floating strap or a lanyard that attaches to your life jacket. Drop a camera overboard near the Strait of Gibraltar and it is gone. A dry bag for your gear when not in use is cheap insurance. Salt spray can kill electronics, so pack a microfiber cloth and a small blower to clean the lens between shots. A lens hood reduces flare and protects the front element. If you use a DSLR or mirrorless, bring at least two fully charged batteries. A morning charter from Benalmádena or Estepona can last four hours, and you will shoot a lot. A fast SD card (UHS-II or V60) with 64GB or more ensures your buffer does not choke during burst mode. A small beanbag or a clamp mount can help stabilise your camera on the boat's railing. For phone users, a waterproof case and a grip handle make a difference. Some charters from Puerto Banús provide sun protection, but bring your own sunscreen and a hat. The glare off the sea is intense even with a polariser.

Where and when to see dolphins off Marbella

Dolphin watching is best from May to October, when the sea is calm and visibility is high. The most reliable spots are the waters between Marbella and Estepona, near the Strait of Gibraltar, and around the Cabo de Plata area. Departure ports like Puerto Banús, Marbella Marina, and Estepona offer dedicated dolphin-watching charters. The trip usually takes 2-3 hours, and skippers know the feeding grounds. Early morning trips (9-11am) have better light and calmer seas. Afternoon trips can be choppier but the light is warmer. Dolphins are wild, so sightings are not guaranteed, but the success rate from local operators is high. The Strait of Gibraltar is a migration corridor for cetaceans, so you might also see pilot whales or even orcas in late summer. If you are on a private charter from Sotogrande or Cabopino, the skipper can adjust the route based on recent sightings. Bring binoculars to spot the dorsal fins first, then aim your camera. The best shots often come when the boat slows down and the dolphins approach the bow wave. That is when you get close, eye-level compositions.

How to compose dolphin photos that stand out

Technical settings only get you so far. Composition matters. Fill the frame with the dolphin if you can. Use a fast burst to capture a jump or a tail slap. Try to get the eye in focus. A dolphin's eye is small, but if it is sharp, the image works. Include the horizon or a landmark like La Concha mountain or the coast of Africa for context. A low angle from a RIB or small boat makes the dolphin look larger and more dynamic. If you are on a catamaran, lean over the side (safely) to shoot at water level. Use the rule of thirds: place the dolphin where it is moving into the frame, not out of it. Watch the background. A busy shoreline or another boat can distract. On a cloudy day, the light is softer and more flattering. On bright days, expose for the dolphin's skin and let the water blow out slightly. Black and white conversions can work well for high-contrast shots. Do not delete images on the boat. Review them later on a larger screen. You might miss a keeper because of the small preview. For video, shoot at 60fps or 120fps for slow-motion playback. A GoPro mounted on a pole can get underwater shots if the water is clear, which it often is off the Costa del Sol.

Rental vs buying gear for a one-off trip

If you are visiting Marbella for a week and do not own a suitable camera, renting can save you money and hassle. Camera rental shops in Marbella and Málaga city offer bodies and lenses by the day. Expect to pay from around EUR 30-80 per day for a mirrorless body and a telephoto zoom. You can also rent GoPros and accessories. Some charters include a photographer or provide a GoPro for guests, but check before booking. If you plan to shoot a lot, buying a used mirrorless kit might make sense if you will use it later. For most holidaymakers, a recent smartphone with a telephoto lens (like the iPhone 15 Pro or Samsung S24 Ultra) plus a clip-on telephoto adapter is enough. The adapter adds 2x to 3x optical magnification without the digital crop. It costs around EUR 50-100. Pair it with a waterproof case and you have a lightweight setup. For serious enthusiasts, a rental from a shop like Foto Málaga or Marbella Camera Hire gives you access to high-end gear like a Sony A1 or Canon R5 with a 100-400mm lens. Book ahead in summer, because stock runs low. And remember to insure the rental against accidental damage or loss.

Common questions

What is the best camera for dolphin watching in Marbella on a budget?
A used Sony A6000 with a 55-210mm lens costs around EUR 400-500 total and delivers great results. It is small, fast, and has good autofocus. Pair it with a floating strap and a dry bag.

Can I use my phone for dolphin photography on a boat?
Yes, but use burst mode and tap to lock focus. A phone with a dedicated telephoto lens (like the iPhone 15 Pro or Samsung S24 Ultra) works best. Avoid digital zoom. Hold the phone with both hands and brace against the boat.

Do I need a waterproof camera for a dolphin tour?
Not necessarily, but a splash-proof camera or a waterproof housing gives peace of mind. Salt spray can damage electronics. A GoPro is fully waterproof and good for wide-angle shots, but not for zooming in on distant dolphins.

What time of day is best for dolphin photos off Marbella?
Early morning (9-11am) offers calm seas and soft light. Late afternoon (4-6pm) gives warm golden light. Midday is harsh and creates glare. Check the weather forecast for wind, because choppy water makes photography harder.

Should I use a polarising filter?
Yes, a circular polariser reduces glare from the water and enhances the dolphin's skin texture. It also deepens the blue of the sea. It costs from around EUR 30 for a good one. Make sure it matches your lens thread size.

How close do boats get to dolphins in Marbella?
Boats must keep a minimum distance of 60 metres by law, but dolphins often approach the boat. Expect them to be 10-50 metres away. A 200mm lens is usually enough to fill the frame. A 100-400mm gives more flexibility.

What if I drop my camera in the sea?
Do not try to retrieve it unless it is very shallow and you have a dry bag. A floating strap prevents this. If it happens, remove the battery and memory card immediately. Rinse with fresh water and dry it thoroughly. Rice does not work. Get it to a repair shop within 24 hours.

Why Puerto Banús charters give you a photography edge

Departing from Puerto Banús puts you closer to the dolphins' favourite feeding grounds off the Costa del Sol. The marina's location means you reach the deeper waters of the Alboran Sea in under 20 minutes, cutting down travel time and giving you more shooting opportunity. Private motor yacht charters from Banús often include a flybridge, which gives you a higher vantage point for shooting down at dolphins riding the bow wave. This angle is hard to get from a low-sided RIB. On a 12-metre Sunseeker or Azimut, you have a stable platform with a railing you can brace against. The skipper can also cut the engines when dolphins are nearby, reducing vibration and letting you shoot at slower shutter speeds if needed. For photographers, a half-day charter from Puerto Banús from around EUR 600-1200 for a group of six is a solid investment. You get space to move, shade from the bimini top, and a cooler for drinks. The light in the late afternoon from Banús is warm and golden, with the Sierra Blanca mountains as a backdrop.

How to handle a RIB or speedboat for dolphin shots

If you book a RIB or speedboat from Cabopino or Benalmádena, you trade stability for speed and agility. These boats get you to the dolphins fast, but the ride is bumpy. Your camera setup needs to be compact and secure. A mirrorless body with a 70-200mm f/4 lens is better than a heavy DSLR. Use a neck strap wrapped around your arm, not just around your neck. A monopod with a quick-release plate can help, but only if the boat has a flat deck. On a RIB, the inflatable tubes absorb some shock, but you still need to keep your knees bent and your elbows tucked. Shoot bursts of 3-5 frames to avoid wasting buffer. The low height of a RIB gives you a water-level perspective that makes dolphins look huge. If the sea is calm, you can lean over the side and shoot at eye level. Some RIB charters from Cabopino include a guide who spots dolphins with binoculars. Watch their hand signals and pre-focus on the direction they point. A polarising filter is essential on a RIB because the spray creates extra glare.

Best seasons and weather windows for clear shots

June and September are the best months for dolphin photography off Marbella. The sea temperature is warm, the wind is light, and the visibility underwater is at its peak. July and August are hotter and busier, but the morning charters are still good. Avoid December to February unless you are after dramatic storm light. The winter swell makes it hard to keep the camera steady. Check the Levante wind forecast. When the easterly wind blows, the sea gets choppy and the dolphins dive deeper. A Poniente wind from the west brings calm, flat water and clear skies. Use Windy.com or the AEMET marine forecast before you book. If you are on a catamaran charter from Estepona, the skipper will often head toward the Strait of Gibraltar where the water is deeper and the dolphin pods are larger. In late summer, you might spot orcas hunting tuna, which is a once-in-a-lifetime photo opportunity. Bring a 400mm lens for those shots, because the orcas stay further out.

Editing dolphin photos for maximum impact

Raw files from your camera need some tweaking to look their best. Start with exposure: dolphins have dark backs and white bellies, so use the highlight slider to recover detail in the white areas. Boost the shadows slightly to bring out the eye and the dorsal fin texture. Increase contrast by 10-15% to make the dolphin pop against the blue water. Use the dehaze slider lightly to cut through atmospheric haze, especially on humid days. For colour, warm up the white balance slightly to remove the cool blue cast from the sea. Boost the saturation of the blues and cyans, but keep the dolphin's skin natural. Crop tightly to remove empty water and focus on the action. If the horizon is tilted, straighten it. For black and white conversions, use a red filter effect to darken the sky and make the dolphin's grey tones stand out. Software like Lightroom Mobile or Snapseed works on a tablet or phone. Do not over-sharpen. A light sharpening mask applied only to the dolphin's edges is enough. Export at 2000px on the long side for social media, or keep the full resolution for prints.

What to pack in your camera bag for a Marbella dolphin tour

Beyond the camera and lens, pack a small toolkit. A lens cleaning pen and a microfiber cloth are essential for wiping off salt spray between shots. A rocket blower removes dust from the sensor if you change lenses. Bring a small tripod or a clamp mount for the boat railing. A Joby GorillaPod with a ball head is light and versatile. Pack a spare memory card and a portable hard drive or tablet for backups. A power bank for your phone and camera batteries is useful on longer charters. Sunscreen with SPF 50 and a wide-brimmed hat protect you, but also keep your gear cool. A light jacket or windbreaker is useful even in summer because the wind on the water is cooler. For phone users, a lens cleaning wipe and a waterproof pouch are enough. Some charters from Sotogrande provide a dry box for valuables, but bring your own dry bag to be safe. Label your gear with your name and a phone number in case you leave it on the boat.
