title: Marbella Dolphin Species Guide: Common Sightings
excerpt: A practical guide to the dolphin species you're likely to see on a boat charter off Marbella and the Costa del Sol, with tips on behaviour and the best spots.
metaDescription: Your Marbella dolphin species guide: common sightings of bottlenose, striped, and common dolphins off the Costa del Sol. Tips for spotting them on a boat charte
author: Andra Kiirkivi
content:
The 30-second answer

You will most likely see three dolphin species on a boat trip from Marbella: the common bottlenose dolphin, the striped dolphin, and the short-beaked common dolphin. All three are resident or semi-resident in the Alboran Sea, and the Strait of Gibraltar is a global hotspot for them. A half-day charter from Puerto Banús or Marbella Marina almost guarantees a sighting between April and October, though they are present year-round. For the best experience, book a boat charter with a licensed skipper who knows where the pods tend to feed.

Why the Costa del Sol is a dolphin hotspot

The waters off Marbella sit in the Alboran Sea, the westernmost basin of the Mediterranean. That narrows down to the Strait of Gibraltar, where Atlantic and Mediterranean currents mix and create an upwelling of nutrients. That means plankton, which means sardines and anchovies, which means dolphins. The geography is simple: deeper channels near the coast, underwater canyons like the one off Estepona, and the convergence of two water masses. You do not need to go far offshore. Many pods hunt within 2-5 nautical miles of the coast, especially around Cabopino and the Río Verde estuary. A typical sighting happens 20-30 minutes after leaving port. The water temperature ranges from 15°C in winter to 24°C in summer, which suits the dolphins fine. For context, the entire Mediterranean population of bottlenose dolphins is estimated at around 10,000 individuals, and a significant chunk of them passes through the Strait. So the odds are in your favour.

Bottlenose dolphin (Tursiops truncatus)

This is the one you picture when someone says dolphin. Grey body, short beak, curved dorsal fin. Bottlenose dolphins are the most common species on Marbella charters. They are resident in the area, meaning you can see them any month of the year. They travel in pods of 5 to 30 individuals, but you sometimes see super-pods of 50 or more during the summer feeding frenzy. They are curious and will approach boats, riding the bow wave or surfing the wake. That is not just showing off. It saves them energy. They can reach speeds of 30 km/h bursts. Adults are 2.5 to 3.5 metres long and weigh up to 600 kg. They feed on fish and squid, hunting at depths of 10-50 metres. In the Alboran Sea, they often follow trawlers for scraps, which is why you see them near fishing boats. If you charter a BoatHire24 vessel from Puerto Banús, the skipper will likely cut the engine to let them approach. Do not expect them to jump through hoops. They are wild animals. But a pod swimming alongside your catamaran is a solid 9/10 experience.

Striped dolphin (Stenella coeruleoalba)

Striped dolphins are the acrobats of the group. They are smaller than bottlenose, at 1.8 to 2.5 metres, with a distinctive pattern: a dark grey back, lighter sides, and a black stripe running from the eye to the tail. They also have a second stripe from the eye to the flipper, which gives them the name. In the Alboran Sea, they are the most abundant dolphin species, with estimates of 100,000 individuals in the western Mediterranean. They prefer deeper waters, 200 metres or more, so you see them further out, around 5-10 nautical miles from Marbella. They travel in large pods of 50 to 100, and they are fast swimmers, hitting 40 km/h. They are also the ones you see leaping high out of the water, spinning, and doing flips. That is not just for Instagram. It helps them communicate and dislodge parasites. The best area for striped dolphins is off Estepona, where the continental shelf drops sharply. A half-day charter from Estepona port will get you there in 20 minutes. They are present year-round but more visible in summer when the water is warmer and the fish are near the surface.

Short-beaked common dolphin (Delphinus delphis)

Short-beaked common dolphins are the ones with the hourglass pattern on their sides: a yellow-tan patch forward, grey behind, and a dark cape on the back. They are slightly smaller than bottlenose, at 1.7 to 2.4 metres, and very social. They used to be the most common dolphin in the Mediterranean, but their numbers crashed in the 20th century due to overfishing and bycatch. In the Alboran Sea, they have recovered somewhat, and you see them in pods of 20 to 200 individuals. They are fast and energetic, often bow-riding and breaching repeatedly. They prefer the upper 50 metres of the water column and feed on small schooling fish like anchovies and sardines. The best spot for them is the Strait of Gibraltar, around Tarifa and the waters off Sotogrande. If you charter a speedboat or RIB from Sotogrande, you can reach the Strait in 30 minutes. They are seasonal visitors, more common from May to October, but some pods stay year-round. They are also the species most likely to appear in large mixed groups with striped dolphins.

Other species you might see

You might also spot the common bottlenose dolphin's larger cousin, the Risso's dolphin (Grampus griseus), which has a blunt head and a tall, falcate dorsal fin. They are less common but appear in the deeper waters off Cabopino and Cala del Faro. They are grey with white scars from social interactions. Then there is the long-finned pilot whale (Globicephala melas), which is technically a dolphin. They travel in tight family groups of 10 to 30 and are often seen in the Strait. They are black with a bulbous head and can be 6 metres long. You might also see the occasional killer whale (Orcinus orca) in the Strait, but that is rare. More likely, you will see common dolphins and striped dolphins together, sometimes with bottlenose nearby. If you want to maximise your chances, book a private charter from Estepona or Sotogrande and ask the skipper to head toward the deeper channels. Do not expect a guaranteed sighting on a shared trip, but the success rate on private charters is well above 90%.

When and where to go for the best sightings

Timing matters. Dolphins are active year-round, but the best months are April through October, when the sea is calm and the fish are near the surface. Morning trips, between 9am and 12pm, often yield more sightings because the water is calmer and the dolphins are feeding. Afternoon trips can be good too, but the sea breeze picks up and makes the water choppy. Location: the waters off Puerto Banús and Marbella Marina are fine, but the real hotspots are the Strait of Gibraltar (from Sotogrande), the area off Estepona, and the deep water off Cabopino. The Strait is a migratory corridor, so you see larger pods there. Estepona has the underwater canyon, which attracts fish and dolphins. Cabopino is quieter, with less boat traffic, so dolphins are less shy. If you are on a catamaran charter from Benalmádena, you will likely head south toward the Strait. On a sailing yacht from Marbella, you might go east toward Cala del Faro. Either way, the skipper will know the coordinates. They use fish-finding sonar sometimes, but mostly they rely on local knowledge. You can also look for seabirds diving, which indicates a school of fish below, and dolphins will be nearby. Do not forget binoculars. And a windbreaker, because even in August it gets cold offshore.

How to behave around dolphins

Spanish law regulates dolphin watching. Boats must keep a distance of at least 60 metres from dolphins, and you cannot chase them, cut off their path, or make sudden turns. The skipper will follow these rules. You should not try to swim with them, feed them, or touch them. They are wild animals, and close contact stresses them. If a pod approaches the boat, stay seated and do not lean over the side. Do not throw anything into the water. Do not shout or make loud noises. The best way to enjoy the sighting is to sit still, watch, and take photos without flash. The dolphins will often stay for 10 to 20 minutes if the boat is quiet. If you are on a RIB or speedboat, the engine noise is louder, so the dolphins may not approach as closely. On a sailing yacht or catamaran, the engine is quieter, and they are more likely to come right up to the hull. Some charters offer hydrophones to listen to their clicks and whistles. Ask your skipper if they have one. It adds a layer to the experience. And remember: if you do not see dolphins, do not blame the skipper. They are wild animals, not a theme park attraction. But on the Costa del Sol, the odds are very good.

Common questions

What is the most common dolphin species off Marbella?

The striped dolphin is the most abundant in the Alboran Sea, but the bottlenose dolphin is the one you are most likely to see on a typical charter because it stays closer to shore.

Can you guarantee seeing dolphins on a boat trip from Marbella?

No one can guarantee wildlife, but the success rate on private charters from Estepona or Sotogrande is over 90% between April and October. Shared trips have a lower rate, around 70%.

What is the best time of day to see dolphins in Marbella?

Morning trips from 9am to 12pm give the best chances because the sea is calmer and dolphins are feeding. Afternoon trips can work but the wind often picks up.

How far offshore do you need to go to see dolphins?

Usually 2 to 5 nautical miles from the coast. The areas off Estepona and Cabopino are particularly good, with deeper water close to shore.

Are there any dolphin-watching regulations in Spain?

Yes. Boats must keep at least 60 metres from dolphins, and you cannot chase or harass them. Licensed skippers on BoatHire24 charters follow these rules.

What other marine life might you see alongside dolphins?

You might see pilot whales, fin whales (rare), loggerhead sea turtles, and seabirds like Cory's shearwater. In the Strait of Gibraltar, you can also spot orcas, but it is not common.

Do you need a special type of boat for dolphin watching?

No. Any motor yacht, catamaran, or RIB can work. But quieter boats like sailing yachts and catamarans allow closer approaches because they make less noise. Read more tips in our blog.

How much a dolphin-watching charter costs

A shared dolphin-watching trip from Puerto Banús or Marbella Marina runs from around EUR 50 to EUR 80 per person for a two-hour outing on a RIB or small motor yacht. Private charters cost more. A half-day private trip on a 10-metre motor yacht for up to eight people starts at around EUR 600 from Cabopino or Estepona. A full-day catamaran charter from Benalmádena for 12 guests sits at roughly EUR 1,200 to EUR 1,800, depending on the season and onboard extras. The price includes the licensed skipper, fuel, and usually basic insurance. You pay extra for food, drinks, or a photographer. July and August are peak season, so prices can be 20% higher. Book a private charter from Sotogrande if you want to target the Strait of Gibraltar without the Puerto Banús premium. You save money and get better odds of seeing larger pods.

Which ports give you the fastest dolphin access

Estepona port is your best bet for speed. The continental shelf drops sharply just 1.5 nautical miles offshore, so you reach deep water in under 10 minutes. Striped dolphins and common dolphins are frequent there. Sotogrande is second best: you are 15 minutes from the Strait of Gibraltar, where dolphin density is highest. Cabopino is quieter and less crowded, with pods often seen 2-3 nautical miles out. Marbella Marina and Puerto Banús are fine but require a longer run to the deeper channels, about 4-5 nautical miles, which adds 20-30 minutes of cruising. Benalmádena is the furthest from the hotspots, needing a 45-minute ride south to reach the same waters. If you charter from there, you will want a full-day trip to make it worthwhile. The skipper on your BoatHire24 vessel will factor this into the route and give you a realistic timeline before you set off.

What to pack for a dolphin-watching trip

Bring sunscreen SPF 50, a hat with a strap, polarised sunglasses, and a windproof jacket even in summer. The wind chill offshore can drop the perceived temperature by 5-10 degrees C. Binoculars with 7x or 8x magnification help you spot dolphins at distance before they reach the boat. A dry bag for your phone and camera is smart, especially on a RIB where spray is common. Do not bring glass bottles. Most charter boats have a coolbox for drinks. If you are prone to seasickness, take a motion-sickness tablet an hour before departure. The Alboran Sea can get choppy in the afternoon, with waves of 0.5 to 1.5 metres. A half-day morning trip from Cabopino or Estepona avoids the worst of it. And bring a camera with a fast shutter speed. Dolphins move at 30-40 km/h, so a smartphone video in 4K at 60 fps works better than still photos for capturing the action.

title: Marbella Whale Watching Winter Guide: Best Spots
excerpt: Winter whale watching in Marbella is prime time for spotting fin whales, pilot whales, and dolphins in the Strait of Gibraltar. This guide covers the best spots, tips, and boat rental options for your trip.
metaDescription: Plan your Marbella whale watching winter guide: best spots like Estepona and Gibraltar, plus tips for spotting fin whales and dolphins. Rent a boat with a skipp
author: Mardo Soo
content:
The 30-second answer

Winter is the best season for Marbella whale watching because the Strait of Gibraltar becomes a migratory highway for fin whales, pilot whales, and common dolphins. You can see these animals from December to March, often just a few nautical miles from Puerto Banús or Estepona. The key is hiring a boat with a licensed skipper who knows the local hotspots, and the good news is that BoatHire24 has vessels departing from Marbella Marina, Puerto Banús, and Sotogrande that are perfect for the trip.

Why winter is prime for whale watching in Marbella

You might think summer is best for spotting marine life, but winter in the Costa del Sol brings cooler water temperatures and a concentration of plankton that draws whales and dolphins closer to shore. The Strait of Gibraltar is a bottleneck for migratory species, and from November to March, fin whales (the second-largest animal on Earth) pass through regularly. Pilot whales and striped dolphins are resident year-round, but winter sightings are more frequent because the animals are feeding heavily before breeding seasons. Water temperatures hover around 15-18 degrees C, which is still mild enough for a comfortable boat ride if you dress in layers. The key factor is the wind: the Levante wind can kick up choppy seas, so check forecasts and choose a morning departure when conditions are calmer. Most local skippers recommend heading west from Puerto Banús towards the Strait, where the continental shelf drops off and creates upwelling currents that concentrate prey. You can expect to see fin whales surfacing every 10-15 minutes, often in pairs or small groups, and common dolphins riding the bow wave of your boat. For the best experience, rent a motor yacht or catamaran from our search page that has a covered deck and a heated cabin, because winter mornings can be brisk.

Best departure ports for winter whale watching

You have five main ports to choose from, each with different advantages for a winter whale watching trip. Puerto Banús is the most glamorous and has the widest selection of motor yachts and superyachts, but it also gets busy on weekends. Estepona Marina is quieter and closer to the Strait of Gibraltar, which means less travel time to the prime feeding grounds. Sotogrande is the southernmost port, offering the shortest route to the Strait and the best access to the deep waters where fin whales congregate. Cabopino is a smaller, more relaxed marina with limited boat options but a more private feel. Marbella Marina (Puerto Deportivo) is central and has a good mix of catamarans and sailing yachts that are stable in winter swells. For a winter trip, you want a boat that is at least 10-12 metres long to handle the sea state, with a covered cockpit and a heater if possible. Prices for a half-day charter with a skipper start from around EUR 600 for a motor yacht, and from EUR 400 for a RIB or speedboat (which is faster but less comfortable). Most operators include a basic lunch or tapas, but bring your own warm drinks and snacks. Book at least 48 hours in advance because winter charters are popular with local enthusiasts and visiting photographers.

Top whale watching spots near Marbella

The Strait of Gibraltar is the obvious hotspot, but there are specific locations within a 20-30 nautical mile radius of Marbella that consistently deliver sightings. The first is the area around the Isla de las Palomas in Tarifa, where the Atlantic meets the Mediterranean and creates a nutrient-rich mixing zone. Fin whales and pilot whales are common here, and you can often see them from December to February. The second is the waters off Punta Carnero, just west of Algeciras, where the continental shelf drops to 800 metres and attracts deep-diving sperm whales in winter. Third, the bay of Estepona itself has resident common dolphins and occasional fin whale sightings close to shore, especially in January and February when the water is coldest. Fourth, the area between Cabo de Gracia and the Rock of Gibraltar is a migration corridor for fin whales and orcas (killer whales) that hunt bluefin tuna from December to March. Orca sightings are rarer but happen every winter, and they are unforgettable. Fifth, the waters around the Banco de la Concepción, a seamount about 50 nautical miles south of Marbella, are a winter feeding ground for fin whales and sei whales, but this requires a full-day charter. Most half-day trips from Puerto Banús or Estepona will target the first three spots, which are within 15-20 nautical miles and can be reached in 45 minutes to an hour at cruising speed. Keep in mind that winter daylight is shorter, so aim for a 9am departure to maximise your time on the water.

What species you can see in winter

You are most likely to see fin whales, which are the second-largest whale species after blue whales, reaching up to 27 metres in length. They migrate through the Strait from November to March, heading south to breed and feed in warmer waters. Pilot whales are resident year-round but more visible in winter because they form larger pods of 20-50 animals. Common dolphins are everywhere and often approach boats, while striped dolphins are more common in deeper waters. Bottlenose dolphins are also present, especially around the Bay of Gibraltar. Sperm whales are less common but are spotted in winter when they follow squid migrations into the Mediterranean. Orcas are the highlight, but they are seasonal and appear mainly from December to March when they hunt tuna near the Strait. You might also see sea turtles (loggerheads) and sunfish in winter, though they are less common. The variety is impressive for such a small area, and many charters guarantee sightings or offer a free repeat trip if you don't see anything. The key is to go with a skipper who uses hydrophones or has local knowledge of recent sightings. Check the BoatHire24 blog for recent reports from other charterers to know what is being seen that week.

How to choose the right boat for winter conditions

Winter sea conditions in the Costa del Sol can be unpredictable, with the Levante wind creating waves of 1-2 metres in the Strait. For comfort and safety, you need a boat that is at least 10 metres long, with a deep V-hull for cutting through chop and a covered cabin to shelter from wind and spray. Motor yachts are the best option because they are stable, fast, and have indoor seating. Catamarans are also excellent because they have a wide beam that reduces rolling, and they offer a stable platform for photography. Sailing yachts are slower and less comfortable in winter, but they are quieter and can approach whales without startling them. RIBs and speedboats are fast and agile, but they are exposed and cold, so only choose one if you are prepared for a rougher ride and have proper waterproof gear. For a half-day trip, a motor yacht between 12 and 15 metres is ideal, with a flybridge for viewing and a heated saloon for breaks. Prices for a motor yacht charter with skipper start from around EUR 700 for a half day, while a catamaran is slightly more at EUR 800. All charters on BoatHire24 include a licensed skipper, fuel, and basic insurance. You should also ask about the boat's heating system and whether blankets are provided. Most skippers will cancel or reschedule if winds exceed 20 knots, so book with a flexible policy.

Tips for a successful winter whale watching trip

Dress in layers: a thermal base layer, a fleece, and a windproof jacket are essential, even if the day starts sunny. Bring a hat, gloves, and a scarf because the wind chill on the water can be 5-10 degrees C colder than on land. Sunglasses are crucial for spotting whale blows on the horizon, and a polarising filter helps reduce glare. Bring binoculars with at least 8x magnification to see details like fin shapes and dorsal fins. A camera with a telephoto lens (200mm or more) is recommended, but keep it in a dry bag between shots. Motion sickness can be a problem in winter swells, so take medication an hour before departure if you are prone to seasickness. Ginger chews and acupressure bands also help. Listen to your skipper's briefing about safety and whale etiquette: never approach closer than 100 metres, do not chase animals, and cut engines when whales are nearby. Winter trips are shorter, so use your time wisely: scan the horizon for blows, splashes, and seabird activity, which often indicates feeding fish and whales. If you see a slick of calm water or a patch of ripples, that can be a whale just below the surface. Most sightings happen within the first two hours, so be patient and keep your eyes open.

Combining whale watching with other winter activities

Marbella in winter is not just about whales. You can combine a morning charter with an afternoon visit to Estepona old town, which has charming cobblestone streets and flower-filled plazas. The walk along the Paseo Marítimo is pleasant even in winter, and there are several tapas bars where you can warm up with a bowl of salmorejo or fried fish. If you depart from Puerto Banús, you can spend the afternoon browsing the luxury boutiques or having a late lunch at a marina restaurant with views of the superyachts. For a more adventurous day, drive to the Strait of Gibraltar after your trip and look for dolphins from the shore at Tarifa, or visit the Pillars of Hercules viewpoint. The Nerja caves are about an hour east of Marbella and are a good indoor option if the weather turns bad. Winter is also the season for hiking in the Sierra de las Nieves, where you can see snow on La Concha mountain. If you want to extend your trip, consider a weekend charter that includes overnight accommodation on a catamaran or sailing yacht, which allows you to anchor in a sheltered cove like Cala del Faro and watch for whales at dawn. The winter light is beautiful for photography, and the lack of summer crowds makes the experience more intimate.

Common questions

Is winter really the best time for whale watching in Marbella? Yes, because fin whales and orcas migrate through the Strait from November to March, and resident pilot whales are more active. The cooler water concentrates plankton, which attracts feeding animals closer to shore.

What is the success rate for seeing whales in winter? Most charters report a 90-95% success rate for seeing at least dolphins, and 70-80% for fin whales or pilot whales. Orca sightings are less predictable but happen every winter.

How long is a typical winter whale watching charter? Half-day charters are 4-5 hours, departing at 9am and returning by 1-2pm. Full-day charters are 8-10 hours and can reach the Banco de la Concepción seamount.

Do I need a special licence or experience to rent a boat? No, because all charters on BoatHire24 include a licensed skipper who handles the navigation and spotting. You just sit back and enjoy.

What happens if the weather is bad on the day of my booking? Most operators offer a free reschedule or full refund if conditions are unsafe. Check the cancellation policy before booking.

Can I bring children on a winter whale watching trip? Yes, but children under 5 may struggle with cold and motion sickness. Choose a motor yacht with a heated cabin and bring warm clothes and snacks.

Are there any ethical concerns with whale watching in winter? Responsible operators follow the Strait of Gibraltar cetacean code of conduct, which limits approach distance and time spent with animals. Avoid boats that chase or surround whales.

The best winter whale watching boats on BoatHire24

If you browse BoatHire24, you will find specific vessels that are ideal for winter whale watching. For example, the Azimut 55 motor yacht from Puerto Banús has a heated saloon, a flybridge with wind protection, and a cruising speed of 22 knots, meaning you can reach the Strait in under an hour. The Lagoon 42 catamaran from Marbella Marina is another favourite because its twin hulls reduce rolling to almost nothing, and its cockpit is fully enclosed with clear vinyl curtains. For a more budget-friendly option, the Quicksilver 755 RIB from Cabopino is fast and nimble but has no cabin, so you need full waterproofs. Prices for these boats range from around EUR 400 for the RIB to EUR 1,200 for the Azimut for a half-day charter. All include a skipper who knows the winter hotspots, and many provide hot drinks and blankets as standard. Book via the search page and filter by "winter" or "heated cabin" to narrow your options.

How to read winter weather windows for whale watching

Winter weather in the Costa del Sol is dominated by the Levante wind, which blows from the east and can create steep, choppy waves in the Strait of Gibraltar. The ideal conditions for whale watching are a light Poniente wind (from the west) at 5-10 knots, which produces flat seas and good visibility. You can check the Windy app or the AEMET forecast for Tarifa and Estepona. Look for days when the wave height is below 1.5 metres and the wind speed is under 15 knots. Morning departures between 9am and 12pm are best because the sea breeze has not yet built up. If the forecast shows Levante at 20 knots or more, reschedule because the boat will be uncomfortable and whales will be harder to spot. Many skippers on BoatHire24 monitor conditions daily and will proactively offer a move if the weather turns. January and February have the most settled days, while December and March can be more variable due to passing fronts.

What to do if you see orcas in winter

Orca sightings in the Strait of Gibraltar are a winter highlight, but they come with specific rules. These orcas are a small, endangered population of around 50 individuals that hunt bluefin tuna. If your skipper spots them, the boat must maintain a distance of at least 100 metres and cut engines if the orcas approach. You should not make loud noises, throw objects, or try to feed them. Orcas often surface in a predictable rhythm, blowing every 30-60 seconds, and they may breach or slap their tails. The best spots for orcas are between Punta Carnero and the Rock of Gibraltar, especially in January and February when tuna are migrating. A half-day charter from Sotogrande or Estepona gives you the best chance because you are already close to the Strait. If you are lucky enough to see them, stay calm and enjoy the moment. Most skippers will stay with the pod for 15-20 minutes before moving on to avoid disturbing them. Check the BoatHire24 blog for recent orca reports to time your trip.

title: Marbella Boat Photoshoot Wedding Ideas: Sunset Shots
excerpt: Planning a wedding photoshoot on a boat in Marbella? We cover the best spots, timing, boat types, and practical tips for sunset shots that actually look good.
metaDescription: Marbella boat photoshoot wedding ideas for sunset shots. Best ports, boat types, timing, and tips for a stunning wedding photoshoot on the Costa del Sol.
author: Andra Kiirkivi
content:
The 30-second answer

If you want wedding photos that don't look like every other hotel-lobby-and-beach combo, a boat photoshoot in Marbella is your move. The golden hour over the Mediterranean, with Puerto Banús or La Concha mountain in the background, gives you lighting and scenery that a studio can't fake. You can charter a motor yacht, catamaran, or sailing yacht with a skipper for a couple of hours, shoot from the bow or the flybridge, and be back at port for champagne before the sun fully drops. Budget from around EUR 500 for a basic 2-hour charter, not including the photographer. Book early, avoid August weekends, and check the wind forecast.

Why a boat photoshoot works for weddings

A boat gives you three things a land venue can't: isolation, movement, and changing backdrops. On a boat, you control who is in the frame. No random tourists photobombing your kiss. No beach vendors. Just you, your partner, and the sea. The boat itself becomes a prop. The white hull, the teak deck, the rigging on a sailing yacht, they all add texture and structure to your shots. You can shoot from the bow looking back at the sunset, from the flybridge with the wind in your hair, or from the stern with the wake trailing behind you. A BoatHire24 charter includes a licensed skipper, so you don't have to worry about navigation or anchoring. You just show up, pose, and let the captain handle the rest. The movement of the boat at slow speed or drifting creates natural, candid moments. You'll hold each other a little tighter, laugh a little more, and the photographer catches that. It's not stiff. It's real.

Best ports and departure points for sunset photos

Your choice of departure port determines your background and your sailing route. Puerto Banús is the obvious one. The marina itself is photogenic, with superyachts and designer boutiques. You can shoot on the dock before you leave, then head west toward the sunset. The coastline from Banús to the Río Verde estuary is a mix of cliffs and sandy coves. Cala del Faro, just west of Banús, gives you a lighthouse and rock formations. Marbella Marina (Puerto Deportivo) is more relaxed. From there you head east toward Cabopino, passing the dunes and the Marbella Club beach club. The old town of Marbella is visible from the water, with La Concha mountain behind it. Cabopino itself is a small, quiet marina with a nature reserve and a long sandy beach. Good if you want fewer people in the background. Estepona is further west, closer to the Strait of Gibraltar. The old town's white buildings and flower pots are visible from the water, and the sunset over the strait is dramatic. Sotogrande is more exclusive, with larger villas and a golf course vibe. Benalmádena, east of Marbella, gives you a view of the Mijas mountains and the marina's pagoda-style buildings. Each port has its own character. Pick based on the vibe you want. For a search of available boats, filter by port and boat type.

Boat types for a wedding photoshoot

Not all boats photograph the same. A motor yacht gives you a sleek, modern look. The flybridge is great for wide shots with the horizon behind you. The bow is spacious, and you can sit on the sun pads or stand at the rail. A 15-metre motor yacht is enough for a couple and a photographer. Catamarans are stable, which means less motion sickness and sharper photos. The trampoline netting at the front is a unique spot for lying down or sitting cross-legged. The wide beam gives you more space to move around. Sailing yachts look romantic. The mast, the sails, the ropes, they all add a classic, timeless feel. You can shoot from the cockpit or on the bow with the sails up. The photographer needs to be comfortable on a heeling boat, though. RIBs and speedboats are smaller and faster. They work for action shots, like jumping off the boat or speeding away. Not ideal for a full wedding dress. Licence-free day boats are the cheapest option. They are small, open boats with an outboard motor. You can anchor in a cove and shoot from the beach. Superyachts are for the budget. They have multiple decks, a jacuzzi, and a crew that can help with styling. Prices on request. For a photoshoot, a 10-15 metre motor yacht or a 12-metre catamaran is the sweet spot.

Timing and light for sunset shots

The golden hour on the Costa del Sol runs from about 90 minutes before sunset to 30 minutes after. In summer, that means 20:00 to 21:30. In winter, it's earlier, 17:00 to 18:30. You want to be on the water and at your chosen spot 60 minutes before sunset. That gives you time to settle, do a few test shots, and then catch the best light. The sun sets over the sea if you are west of Marbella, which is most ports except Benalmádena. From Benalmádena, the sun sets behind the mountains, which can still look good but is less dramatic. Check the wind forecast. A light breeze (5-10 knots) is fine. Strong wind (15+ knots) will make the boat rock and mess up hair and dresses. The photographer should use a fast lens (f/1.4 or f/1.8) to shoot in low light without flash. Flash on a boat at sunset kills the mood. Use natural light and reflectors. The sea reflects the colours of the sky, so you get orange, pink, and purple tones on the water. That is your backdrop. After sunset, you have about 20 minutes of blue hour. That is when the sky turns deep blue and the marina lights come on. Shoot from the dock or from the boat with the lights of Puerto Banús behind you. Two hours is enough for a full session: one hour of golden hour, 30 minutes of blue hour, and 30 minutes of dock shots.

What to wear and what to bring

Boat decks get hot. The sun reflects off the water. You will sweat. Bring a backup outfit. For the bride, a lightweight dress with a train that can be bustled. Avoid heavy silk or satin that shows sweat marks. Lace and chiffon work well. For the groom, linen or cotton. No wool suits. Barefoot or flat shoes on the boat. Heels damage the deck and are dangerous. You can put heels on for dock shots. Bring a shawl or jacket for after sunset. The wind picks up and the temperature drops. Bring sunscreen, even at sunset. You still get UV reflection off the water. Bring water and a snack. The photographer should bring a polarising filter to reduce glare on the water and a lens hood to block flare. A drone adds another dimension. You can get aerial shots of the boat against the sunset. Check the drone laws. In Spain, you need a licence for drones over 250 grams and you cannot fly over people or built-up areas. Your skipper can help find a spot away from the marina where you can fly. A blog post on drone photography covers the regulations in more detail.

Legal and practical considerations

You need a permit to get married on a boat in Spain. That is a separate process. A photoshoot does not require a permit. You just charter the boat and go. The boat must have a valid licence and insurance. All charters on BoatHire24 include a licensed skipper. You cannot take the boat out yourself. The skipper will handle the anchor, the route, and safety. You need to tell the skipper and the charter company that it is a photoshoot. They may have rules about where you can stand or what you can do on the boat. Some boats do not allow jumping off the bow or sitting on the gunwale. Ask before you book. The photographer needs to be comfortable on a boat. If they get seasick, the shoot is over. Test them on a short charter first. The boat will have a toilet, but it is small. Plan for that. You will be on the water for 2-3 hours. No one wants to be in a wedding dress trying to use a marine head. Bring a change of clothes for the ride back. And tip the skipper. They are working the whole time, positioning the boat for your light and keeping you safe.

Cost breakdown for a Marbella boat wedding photoshoot

ItemEstimated cost (EUR)
Boat charter (2 hours, motor yacht 12 m)500 - 800
Boat charter (2 hours, catamaran 14 m)700 - 1,200
Boat charter (2 hours, sailing yacht 12 m)600 - 1,000
Photographer (2 hours, professional)400 - 1,000
Drone operator (30 minutes)200 - 400
Hair and makeup (on-site)200 - 500
Flowers and props100 - 300
Total estimated1,500 - 4,200

Prices vary by season, boat, and photographer. July and August are peak. You pay more and the marinas are busier. May, June, September, and October are better. The light is still good, the weather is warm, and the crowds are smaller. Book at least 4 weeks in advance for a weekend slot. Weekdays are easier. The photographer should scout the boat and the route before the shoot. Some photographers charge extra for travel to the port. Clarify that upfront. The charter company may charge a cleaning fee if you bring confetti or glitter. Do not bring either. They end up in the sea. Use real flower petals or nothing.

Common questions

Can we get legally married on a boat in Marbella?
Yes, but it requires a civil ceremony with a judge or a religious ceremony with a priest, and the boat must be registered as a venue. Most couples do the legal part on land and use the boat for the photoshoot only. The charter company can help arrange a symbolic ceremony on board if you want.

What if I get seasick?
Take an anti-nausea tablet an hour before departure. Choose a catamaran, which is more stable than a monohull. Stay on the deck, not inside the cabin. Look at the horizon. The skipper can keep the boat at anchor or at slow speed to minimise movement.

Can we bring our own drinks?
Most charters allow you to bring your own food and drink. Some include a basic drinks package. Check with the charter company. Do not bring glass bottles on board. Use plastic or cans. The skipper will provide a cooler and ice.

How many people can be on the boat?
It depends on the boat's licence. A 12-metre motor yacht typically holds 10-12 passengers. A catamaran the same size holds 12-14. The photographer and skipper count. For a photoshoot, you only need the couple, the photographer, and maybe a stylist. Keep it small.

What happens if the weather is bad?
The skipper decides if it is safe to go out. If the wind is over 20 knots or there is a storm warning, the charter will be cancelled or rescheduled. Most companies have a weather policy. You get a refund or a new date. Have a backup plan for a land-based shoot on the same day.

Do we need to speak Spanish?
No. The charter companies and skippers on BoatHire24 speak English. The photographer should speak English or Spanish, depending on your preference. Confirm before booking.

Can we see dolphins during the photoshoot?
Possibly. The Strait of Gibraltar and the waters off Estepona are known for dolphins and whales. The skipper can head toward areas where they are often spotted, but there is no guarantee. If you see them, it makes for incredible photos. Do not chase them. It is illegal to approach within 60 metres.

How to plan the shoot around the wind and swell

The wind on the Costa del Sol follows a predictable pattern. The morning is calm, the afternoon picks up with the sea breeze, and by late afternoon you often get a steady 10-15 knots from the west. For a sunset shoot, that means you are dealing with afternoon chop. The swell is usually short and choppy, not long rolling waves. A 12-metre motor yacht handles that fine. A smaller RIB or day boat will bounce. If you are in a sailing yacht, the skipper can use the main sail as a stabiliser by keeping it sheeted tight. For the smoothest ride, stay inside the bay of Marbella, where the coastline shelters you from the open sea. The area between Puerto Banús and Cabopino is the most protected. If you go further west toward Estepona, the swell increases as you approach the Strait of Gibraltar. Check the wind forecast on Windy or Windguru the day before. Look for wind under 12 knots. Anything above 15 knots and the boat will rock enough to make the photographer's job harder. Your skipper will know the local conditions. Trust them. They will position the boat bow-first into the swell to reduce movement during the key shots.

Specific photo spots along the Marbella coast

You can break the coastline into distinct zones, each with a different look. The stretch from Puerto Banús to Cala del Faro is the most popular. Cala del Faro has a lighthouse on a rocky point. The rocks are dark, the lighthouse is white, and the sunset behind it creates a strong silhouette. You can anchor just off the rocks and shoot from the boat with the lighthouse in the frame. The Río Verde estuary, just east of Banús, has a sandbar and dunes. The water is shallow and calm. You can anchor and walk on the sandbar if the tide is low. The dunes give you a desert-like backdrop. The area off the Marbella Club Hotel has a series of small coves with pine trees coming down to the water. The trees add green to the golden light. Cabopino has a nature reserve with sand dunes and a long beach. The beach is less crowded than Marbella's main beaches. You can anchor and wade ashore for beach shots. Estepona has a longer stretch of coastline with cliffs and small coves. The sunset from Estepona is pure, with no land blocking the horizon. The Strait of Gibraltar is visible in the distance. If you time it right, you can get a shot with the Atlas Mountains of Morocco faintly visible across the strait. That is a unique backdrop you cannot get anywhere else on the coast.

title: Marbella Boat Trip for Teenagers: Adventure Ideas
excerpt: Teenagers bored on a boat trip in Marbella? Not with jet skis, cliff jumping, snorkelling, and dolphin spotting. Here are the best adventure ideas for a teen-friendly charter on the Costa del Sol.
metaDescription: Plan a Marbella boat trip for teenagers with adventure ideas: jet skiing, cliff jumping, snorkelling, and dolphin watching. Find teen-friendly charters with ski
author: Mardo Soo
content:
The 30-second answer

Teenagers need action, not a slow cruise. A Marbella boat trip for teenagers works best when you include fast RIBs, cliff jumping at Cala del Faro, snorkelling in clear coves, and a jet ski add-on. Private charters from Puerto Banús or Marbella Marina let you set the pace, and every boat comes with a licensed skipper who knows the best spots for dolphin spotting near the Strait of Gibraltar. Expect to pay from around EUR 600 for a half-day on a motor yacht or speedboat, with fuel and skipper included.

Why a Marbella boat trip works for teenagers

Teenagers have a short attention span for scenery. You need activities that get them moving. A Marbella boat trip for teenagers solves that by combining speed, water sports, and wildlife. The Costa del Sol coast has calm waters in the morning, ideal for water skiing or wakeboarding behind a RIB. After lunch, the wind picks up, which is perfect for sailing or just speeding along the coast. The key is to book a boat that offers flexibility: a motor yacht with a swim platform, a RIB for thrills, or a catamaran with space to lounge. Every charter includes a skipper, so you can relax while the crew handles navigation and safety. Departure ports like Puerto Banús and Estepona are close to the best coves, meaning less travel time and more fun.

Best boat types for teenagers: speed and space

Not all boats suit teenagers. Here is a quick guide to what works and why.

Boat typeWhy it works for teensTypical cost (half day)
RIB or speedboatFast, bumpy rides. Ideal for water sports and cliff jumping. Limited shade.From around EUR 500
Motor yachtStable, with a swim platform and cabin for changing. Good for snorkelling trips.From around EUR 800
CatamaranHuge deck space, stable, slow. Best for dolphin watching and lounging, not thrills.From around EUR 900
Sailing yachtHands-on sailing experience for older teens. Slower pace.From around EUR 600

For a Marbella boat trip for teenagers, a RIB or a small motor yacht is usually the sweet spot. You get speed when you want it and comfort when you need a break from the sun.

Adventure idea 1: cliff jumping at Cala del Faro

Cala del Faro is a rocky cove near Marbella, just west of Puerto Banús. The cliffs here are around 5 to 8 metres high, safe for jumping if you check the water depth first. Your skipper will anchor close to the rocks, and teens can take turns leaping into the clear water. The cove is sheltered from the wind, so the water is usually calm. Bring water shoes because the rocks can be sharp. This is one of the most popular stops on a Marbella boat trip for teenagers because it requires no equipment and delivers instant adrenaline. You can combine it with snorkelling in the same spot, where you might see small fish and octopus. The nearby beach of El Ancón is also good for a quick swim.

Adventure idea 2: jet ski add-on and water sports

Many boat charters in Marbella offer jet ski add-ons. You rent a jet ski for an hour and follow the boat, or you tow a wakeboard or a ringo (inflatable tube) behind the RIB. Teenagers love the ringo because it flips over when you hit a wake. Wakeboarding requires a bit of skill, but most teens pick it up in 15 minutes. The best area for water sports is off the coast of Cabopino, where the water is flat and there are fewer boats. Your skipper can arrange the equipment in advance. Expect to pay around EUR 100 to EUR 150 extra per hour for a jet ski or wakeboard package. This turns a simple Marbella boat trip for teenagers into a full action day.

Adventure idea 3: dolphin spotting and the Strait of Gibraltar

If your teens are into wildlife, a trip towards the Strait of Gibraltar is a must. From Estepona or Sotogrande, you can reach the strait in about 45 minutes by speedboat. The area is famous for common dolphins, striped dolphins, and even pilot whales. The best time is early morning when the sea is calm. Your skipper will know the hotspots near the Tarifa coast. Dolphin watching is not guaranteed, but the success rate is high, around 90 percent in summer. Bring binoculars and a camera with a zoom lens. This adds an educational element to your Marbella boat trip for teenagers, and it is a lot more exciting than a museum visit. After dolphin spotting, you can anchor at a quiet beach like Playa de Valdevaqueros for a swim.

Adventure idea 4: snorkelling in the Cabopino marine reserve

The Cabopino marine reserve, just east of Marbella, is a protected area with seagrass meadows and rocky reefs. The water clarity is good, often 10 to 15 metres visibility in summer. Teens can snorkel here and see bream, groupers, and sometimes rays. The reserve is shallow, around 3 to 8 metres deep, so it is safe for beginners. Your skipper will provide masks, fins, and snorkels. Combine this with a stop at the nearby Cabopino sand dunes, which are a protected natural area and a good spot for a short walk. Snorkelling is a low-energy activity, so it works well after a morning of cliff jumping or jet skiing. For a Marbella boat trip for teenagers, this is the calm before the next adrenaline hit.

Adventure idea 5: fishing trip for competitive teens

Teenagers who love competition will enjoy a fishing charter. You can book a fishing boat from Marbella Marina or Estepona. The target species are sea bass, bream, mackerel, and sometimes tuna. The skipper provides rods, bait, and basic instruction. The best spots are around the reefs off Cabopino or near the rocky outcrops of Calahonda. Fishing is a patience game, but teens who land a fish get a rush. You can keep the catch and ask a local restaurant to cook it for dinner. A half-day fishing trip costs from around EUR 400 for a small boat. This is a different kind of adventure for a Marbella boat trip for teenagers, one that teaches patience and respect for the sea.

Practical tips for a teen-friendly charter

Book a private charter, not a shared tour. Teenagers want control over the itinerary, not a fixed route with strangers. Look for boats with a sun deck or a bimini top for shade, because Spanish sun is intense. Bring sunscreen, hats, and plenty of water. A cooler with soft drinks and snacks is usually provided, but check with the charter company. Allow for a flexible schedule: start at 10am, have a late lunch on board or at a beach club, and return by 5pm. Teenagers get bored if the trip is too long, so a half-day (4 to 5 hours) is often better than a full day. Your skipper can adjust the speed and stops based on the group's mood. Check out our search page to filter boats by type and price.

Where to eat and hang out on the water

Teenagers get hungry. Many charters include the option to stop at a beach club for lunch. Popular choices include Nikki Beach Marbella (Puerto Banús area) or the chiringuitos at Cabopino. These places serve burgers, pizza, and fresh seafood, which appeal to most teens. You can also bring your own food on board. If you want a quick bite, Estepona's old town has ice cream shops and bakeries. For a more relaxed vibe, anchor near the dunes at Cabopino and have a picnic on the boat. The key is to keep the food simple and fast. No long sit-down meals. This keeps the energy up for the next activity. Read more about boat trip ideas on our blog.

Common questions

What is the minimum age for a Marbella boat trip for teenagers?
There is no legal minimum age for a private charter, but most companies recommend children be at least 4 years old. For activities like jet skiing, the minimum age is usually 16 with parental consent.

Can teenagers drive the boat?
No. The licensed skipper is in charge at all times. However, on a sailing yacht, teens can help with the sails and steering under supervision, which is a great learning experience.

Is sea sickness common for teenagers?
Less common than for adults, but it can happen. Choose a calm day (check the forecast) and avoid heavy meals before the trip. A RIB or motor yacht in calm waters is safer than a catamaran in choppy conditions.

How do I book a Marbella boat trip for teenagers?
Use BoatHire24 to compare boats and prices. Filter by boat type, departure port, and duration. Most charters can be booked online with instant confirmation.

What should teenagers bring on the boat?
Swimwear, a towel, sunscreen, a hat, sunglasses, a change of clothes, and a waterproof phone case. A dry bag is useful for keeping valuables safe.

Are there toilets on the boats?
Most motor yachts and catamarans have a toilet (head) and a small cabin. RIBs and speedboats usually do not, so plan bathroom stops at beach clubs or coves with facilities.

Can we add extra activities on the day?
Yes, but it is better to arrange jet skis, wakeboards, or fishing gear in advance. Your skipper can help coordinate this. Last-minute requests may not be available.

Why Puerto Banús is the best departure port for teens

Puerto Banús is a magnet for teenagers. The marina is packed with superyachts, flash cars, and designer shops, which creates a buzz before you even leave the dock. Departing from here means you can grab a coffee at a waterfront cafe while waiting for your skipper to prepare the boat. The port is also close to the best adventure spots: Cala del Faro is 10 minutes by speedboat, and the Cabopino marine reserve is 15 minutes east. For a Marbella boat trip for teenagers, starting in Puerto Banús adds a layer of glamour that teens appreciate. The downside is that parking is expensive and the marina can be crowded in July and August. Book your charter for a 10am departure to avoid the worst of the crowds. Marbella Marina is a quieter alternative, with free parking and easy access to the same coves.

How to keep costs under control for a group of teens

A Marbella boat trip for teenagers can get expensive if you add every extra. Here is how to budget. A half-day RIB charter from Benalmádena costs from around EUR 500 for up to 8 people, which works out at roughly EUR 62 per person. Add a jet ski for EUR 120 per hour, and the total for a group of four is EUR 620 for a half-day. If you want a motor yacht with a swim platform, expect from around EUR 800 for a half-day from Estepona. To save money, book a longer trip: a full-day charter often costs only 30 percent more than a half-day, giving you more time for activities. Bring your own food and drinks instead of buying from the boat's bar, which can charge EUR 5 for a can of Coke. Check our search page for boats that include fuel and water toys in the price.

Best time of year for a teen boat trip in Marbella

The best months for a Marbella boat trip for teenagers are June, July, August, and September. June and September are ideal because the water temperature is around 22 to 24 degrees C, the sea is calm, and the beaches are less crowded than in July and August. July and August are hotter, with air temperatures hitting 35 degrees C, so you need a boat with good shade and a swim platform for cooling off. The wind is lightest in the morning, making 10am to 2pm the best window for water sports. After 3pm, the afternoon breeze (poniente) picks up, which is good for sailing but choppy for RIBs. Avoid October and November unless you are booking a fishing trip, because the sea gets rougher and the water drops to 18 degrees C. Winter trips are possible but rare, and you will need a boat with a heated cabin, which is hard to find in Marbella.

What to do if your teen gets bored on the boat

Even the best Marbella boat trip for teenagers can hit a lull. If your teens start scrolling their phones, change the plan. Ask the skipper to increase speed for a few minutes, or head to a cove with a rope swing or cliff jump. Many skippers carry a Bluetooth speaker, so let the teens play their own music. Bring a waterproof camera for underwater photos, or a GoPro for filming jumps and dolphin sightings. Some boats have a small inflatable kayak or paddleboard that you can tow along, which gives teens something to do on the water. If all else fails, head to a beach club like Nikki Beach or Ocean Club, where they can get a mocktail and watch the people go by. The key is to keep the itinerary flexible and not overplan. Your skipper is your best resource for on-the-fly adjustments.

Safety tips for teens on a boat in Marbella

Safety is your responsibility, even with a licensed skipper on board. Make sure every teen wears a life jacket when the boat is moving, especially on a RIB or speedboat. The skipper will provide life jackets, but check the sizes fit properly. Sunburn is a real risk: the Spanish sun is strong, and teens often forget to reapply sunscreen. Use SPF 50 and reapply every two hours. Dehydration is common, so bring at least 2 litres of water per person. Alcohol is not recommended for teens, but if you have older teens (18+), the skipper will enforce a limit. Cliff jumping at Cala del Faro is safe only if you check the water depth first, which the skipper will do. Never let teens jump near rocks or in murky water. For a Marbella boat trip for teenagers, a quick safety briefing at the start sets the tone for a fun and accident-free day.

How to choose the right skipper for a teen group

Not all skippers are good with teenagers. When booking a Marbella boat trip for teenagers, ask the charter company if the skipper has experience with younger groups. A good skipper will be patient, energetic, and willing to let teens take the helm under supervision. They should speak English and Spanish, and be able to explain dolphin behaviour or marine life in a way that engages teens. Avoid skippers who are too strict or formal, as they can kill the vibe. On the day, introduce the teens to the skipper and let them ask questions about the boat and the route. A skipper who cracks jokes and lets teens help with anchoring or tying ropes will earn their respect. You can read reviews on BoatHire24 to find skippers who are rated highly for family and teen charters.

title: Marbella Boat Trip to Cabo Pino Guide: Marina Visit
excerpt: Plan your Marbella boat trip to Cabo Pino guide: visit the marina, beach bars, and nature reserve. Practical tips for a day on the water.
metaDescription: Plan your Marbella boat trip to Cabo Pino guide: visit the marina, beach bars, and Cabopino dunes. Book with a licensed skipper on BoatHire24.
author: Mardo Soo
content:
The 30-second answer

You can charter a boat from Marbella or Puerto Banús to Cabo Pino marina in under 30 minutes. Cabopino is a small, quiet harbour with a protected dune system, a handful of beach bars, and no mega-yacht circus. The trip is ideal for a relaxed half-day or sunset outing. Book a motor yacht or catamaran with a skipper through BoatHire24 and tie up at the marina’s visitor berth for a few hours.

Why Cabo Pino instead of Puerto Banús

Puerto Banús is the Costa del Sol’s bling capital, superyachts, designer shops, and crowds. Cabo Pino, five nautical miles east, is the opposite. The marina is small, with about 300 berths, mostly for local fishing boats and modest cruisers. You won’t find a Louis Vuitton store or a paparazzi scrum. What you get is a chilled-out vibe, a sandy beach (Playa de Cabopino), and the Artola-Cabopino dunes, a protected natural area with walking trails. If you want a boat trip that feels like a proper escape from the Marbella scene, this is it. The approach by sea is straightforward, the entrance channel is dredged to about 2.5 metres depth, so most motor yachts and catamarans under 20 metres can enter. You’ll need to radio the marina office on VHF channel 9 for berth availability. They usually have space for visitors midweek, though weekends in July and August can be tight. Expect to pay around EUR 30-50 for a day berth for a 10-metre boat. The marina has water and electricity hook-ups, plus basic showers.

How to get there by boat from Marbella

Your Marbella boat trip to Cabo Pino starts from one of the main departure ports: Puerto Banús, Marbella Marina (Puerto Deportivo), or even Benalmádena if you’re coming from further east. From Puerto Banús, it’s a straight run east along the coast, about 5 NM. At a cruising speed of 20 knots, you’ll be there in 15 minutes. From Marbella Marina, it’s roughly 7 NM, about 20 minutes. The coastline is easy to follow: you’ll pass Cala del Faro (a small cove with a lighthouse) and the long stretch of Playa de las Dunas. Keep an eye out for the distinctive tower of the Cabopino dune system, it’s the tallest sand dune on the Costa del Sol, standing about 20 metres high. The marina entrance is just east of the dune. If you’re on a sailing yacht, tacking against the prevailing westerly wind might take 45-60 minutes. The wind is usually light in summer, 8-12 knots, so it’s a gentle sail. For a RIB or speedboat, you can do the trip in 10 minutes flat, but you’ll want to slow down inside the harbour limits (5 knots).

What to do once you arrive

Cabopino marina isn’t a destination for shopping or nightlife. It’s about beach, food, and nature. Tie up at the visitor pontoon, then walk the 200 metres to Playa de Cabopino. The beach is wide, with fine golden sand and a dune backdrop. There are two chiringuitos (beach bars): Chiringuito Cabopino and Los Canos. Both serve grilled fish, salads, and cold beer. Expect to pay around EUR 4-5 for a caña (small beer) and EUR 12-15 for a grilled dorada. The dunes behind the beach are part of the Artola-Cabopino Natural Monument. You can walk the marked trails, it takes about 30 minutes to do the loop. The viewpoint at the top gives you a clear sightline back to Marbella and La Concha mountain. If you’re feeling energetic, continue east along the coastal path to Cala del Faro. That’s a 20-minute walk from the marina. The cove is rocky, but good for snorkelling. Water clarity is usually 5-8 metres in summer. For lunch, skip the marina’s restaurant (it’s overpriced) and head to Los Canos on the beach, it’s casual, sandy-floored, and the paella is decent. After eating, you can swim off the boat if you drop anchor in the bay outside the marina. The seabed is sandy, so holding is good. Depth is 3-5 metres about 100 metres off the beach.

Best boats for the trip

Your choice of boat depends on how you want to spend the day. For a fast run, a RIB or speedboat (6-8 metres) is fine, you’ll arrive in 10 minutes and can beach the tender on the sand. For a more comfortable cruise, a motor yacht around 10-12 metres gives you a sunpad, a small cabin, and a toilet. Catamarans are stable and spacious, a 40-foot cat can carry up to 12 guests and has a shallow draft (1.2 metres), so you can get close to the beach. Sailing yachts are slower but quieter; if you want to feel the wind, a 35-foot Beneteau or Bavaria works. Fishing boats (6-8 metres) are practical if you plan to drop a line off the dune. Licence-free day boats (under 6 metres, up to 15 hp) are an option if you have a skipper’s licence, but you’ll need to check the engine power limit. Superyachts (over 24 metres) can’t enter the marina; they’d need to anchor offshore and use a tender. For most people, a 30-40 foot motor yacht or catamaran is the sweet spot. Prices start from around EUR 400 for a half-day on a 10-metre motor yacht, including skipper. Check availability on the search page to compare options.

When to go and what to bring

The best time for a Marbella boat trip to Cabo Pino is May to October. Sea temperatures in summer are 22-26 degrees C. July and August are hot (30-35 degrees C) and the marina can be busy, but the beach crowd is manageable compared to Marbella. June and September are ideal, warm, fewer boats, and the water is still pleasant. Wind is usually light in the morning (5-10 knots from the west), picking up to 12-15 knots in the afternoon. If you’re sailing, go early. For a motorboat, any time works. Sunset trips are popular, the sun sets over La Concha mountain, and the marina lights up. Bring sunscreen (SPF 50), a hat, a towel, and swimwear. The marina has a small shop for water and snacks, but it’s limited. If you want lunch at a beach bar, cash is useful, not all chiringuitos accept cards. For snorkelling, bring a mask and fins, the water off Cala del Faro is clear. If you’re prone to seasickness, note that the sea state is usually calm (1-2 on the Douglas scale) inside the bay, but the swell can pick up if the wind blows from the east. A typical half-day trip from Marbella costs from around EUR 350-500 for a 4-hour charter. You can book via BoatHire24, all charters include a licensed skipper, so you don’t need a licence.

Other stops to combine with Cabo Pino

Cabopino is small enough that you’ll probably want to combine it with another spot. A common itinerary is to leave Puerto Banús, head east to Cabo Pino for lunch and a swim, then go further east to Benalmádena or Fuengirola. Benalmádena marina is 8 NM from Cabopino, a 15-minute cruise. Fuengirola is another 3 NM east. Both have larger marinas with more restaurants and shops. Alternatively, go west after Cabopino to Estepona. That’s 15 NM from Cabopino, about 30 minutes at 20 knots. Estepona’s old town is worth a walk, whitewashed streets, flower pots, and a good tapas scene. You can tie up at Estepona marina (call ahead on VHF 9). Another option is to anchor off Cala del Faro for a quiet swim before or after the marina. If you have a full day, you could push east to Nerja, but that’s 30 NM from Marbella, a 90-minute cruise one way. The Nerja caves are a famous landmark, but you’d need a full day for that trip. For a half-day, stick to Cabo Pino plus one other stop. For a longer trip, consider going south towards the Strait of Gibraltar, dolphin sightings are common there. Check the blog for more itinerary ideas.

Practical tips for the skipper

If you’re the one driving the boat (or your skipper is), here are the specifics. The entrance to Cabo Pino marina is at 36° 30.8′ N, 04° 40.0′ W. The channel is marked by two green buoys (starboard) and two red buoys (port). Depths are 2.5-3 metres in the channel, dropping to 1.5 metres at the inner ends of the pontoons. The marina has a maximum length limit of 20 metres. If your boat is bigger, anchor in the bay (36° 30.6′ N, 04° 40.2′ W) in 5-7 metres of water, sand bottom, and use a tender. The holding is good in moderate weather. Beware of the easterly swell in winter, it can push boats onto the beach. In summer, it’s calm. The marina office is open 0800-2000 in summer. Fuel is available at the pump on the north quay, diesel and petrol. The pump is open 0900-1800. Water and electricity are included in the berth fee. There’s a small chandlery for basic supplies. If you need a mechanic, the nearest is in Puerto Banús. For a relaxed day, Cabo Pino is hard to beat. It’s not glamorous, but that’s the point. Book your boat on BoatHire24 and enjoy a proper Costa del Sol beach day without the fuss.

Common questions

How long does a Marbella boat trip to Cabo Pino take?

From Puerto Banús, it’s about 15 minutes by motorboat (5 NM). From Marbella Marina, 20 minutes (7 NM). A sailing yacht will take 45-60 minutes depending on wind. The trip is short enough for a half-day charter.

Can I take a large yacht to Cabo Pino?

The marina has a 20-metre length limit. Larger yachts must anchor in the bay and use a tender. The bay has good holding in sand at 5-7 metres depth, but it’s exposed to easterly winds.

What is there to do at Cabo Pino besides the beach?

You can walk the Artola-Cabopino dune trails (30-minute loop), visit Cala del Faro cove for snorkelling, or eat at the beach bars. The marina itself is quiet, no shops or nightlife.

Do I need a boat licence to charter a boat to Cabo Pino?

No. All charters on BoatHire24 include a licensed skipper. You can relax while the skipper handles navigation, berthing, and radio communication with the marina.

How much does it cost to charter a boat from Marbella to Cabo Pino?

A half-day (4-hour) charter for a 10-metre motor yacht starts from around EUR 400, including skipper. Prices vary by boat size and season. Check the BoatHire24 search page for current options.

Is Cabo Pino marina safe for mooring?

Yes, the marina is well-maintained with a dredged channel, pontoons in good condition, and security cameras. In summer, it’s calm. Avoid during strong easterly storms in winter.

Can I see dolphins on the trip to Cabo Pino?

Dolphins are more common in the Strait of Gibraltar, further south. You might see them off Cabo Pino occasionally, but it’s not guaranteed. For reliable sightings, head towards Estepona or Tarifa.

Comparing departure ports for your Cabo Pino trip

Your choice of departure port affects the total trip time and the scenery along the way. From Puerto Banús, you leave the glitzy superyacht harbour and head east past the Rio Verde estuary. The water there can be a bit murky after rain, but it clears within a few hundred metres. Marbella Marina (Puerto Deportivo) is a more relaxed starting point, with cheaper parking (around EUR 15 per day versus EUR 30 in Banús) and a fuel dock that is usually less busy. If you depart from Cabopino itself, you skip the sea leg entirely, but you miss the coastal views of La Concha mountain from the water. Benalmádena is a solid option if you want a longer day on the water, it adds about 8 NM each way, making the round trip roughly 26 NM. That extra distance pushes a half-day charter into a full-day one, so budget accordingly. Estepona is further west, 15 NM from Cabo Pino, and works well if you want to combine a marina visit with a stop at the Estepona old town. The run from Estepona to Cabo Pino takes you past the Cala del Faro lighthouse and the long beach of San Pedro de Alcántara. Each departure port has its own vibe, so pick the one that matches your morning mood.

What to eat and drink at Cabo Pino

Food at Cabo Pino is all about simple, fresh seafood eaten with sand between your toes. Chiringuito Cabopino does a decent espetos de sardinas (sardines grilled on a stick) for around EUR 10 for a skewer of six. The sardines are caught locally and grilled over olive wood, giving them a smoky flavour. Los Canos serves arroz con bogavante (lobster rice) for about EUR 22 per person, but you need to order it in advance. Both places have cold Cruzcampo beer on tap for EUR 3.50 a pint. If you want something more substantial, the marina’s own restaurant, La Taberna del Puerto, offers paella mixta for EUR 15 and grilled octopus for EUR 18. The quality is okay but the prices are higher than the beach bars. For a proper feast, bring your own food and drinks on the boat. Most charter boats have a cooler, so you can pack a picnic of jamón ibérico, manchego cheese, and a bottle of local white wine from the Ronda region. Eat on deck while anchored in the bay, then wade ashore for a post-lunch ice cream from the kiosk near the dunes. The ice cream is average, but the view makes up for it.

Weather and sea conditions for a smooth trip

The Costa del Sol is known for calm seas, but conditions vary by season. In summer (June to September), the prevailing wind is the Poniente, a light westerly that blows 5-10 knots in the morning and picks up to 12-15 knots by early afternoon. This creates a gentle chop of 0.3-0.5 metres in the bay off Cabo Pino, which is fine for most boats. In spring and autumn, the Levante wind from the east can blow stronger, 15-25 knots, with a swell of 1-2 metres. That makes the approach to Cabo Pino bumpy, especially if you are in a RIB or small speedboat. Check the AEMET forecast before you go. Sea temperature in summer is 22-26 degrees C, perfect for swimming. In May and October, it drops to 18-20 degrees C, still swimmable if you are hardy. Visibility underwater is best in calm conditions, around 5-8 metres. If the wind has been blowing for a few days, the water can get murky. For the most reliable conditions, book a morning trip in June or September. You get flat water, fewer boats, and a gentle breeze by lunchtime.

Cost breakdown for a half-day charter to Cabo Pino

Prices for a Marbella boat trip to Cabo Pino depend on the boat type, season, and duration. A half-day (4 hours) on a 8-metre RIB or speedboat starts from around EUR 350 in low season (May, June, September) and EUR 450 in high season (July, August). A 10-metre motor yacht with a cabin and toilet costs from EUR 400 in low season and EUR 550 in high season. A 40-foot catamaran for up to 12 guests starts at EUR 600 for half a day in low season and EUR 800 in high season. Sailing yachts are generally cheaper, from EUR 350 for a 35-foot Beneteau. All prices include a licensed skipper, fuel, and basic insurance. Extras like food, drinks, and marina berth fees (EUR 30-50) are not included. If you want a full day (8 hours), expect to pay roughly 1.5 times the half-day rate. The total cost for a couple on a motor yacht, including lunch and drinks, is typically EUR 500-700. For a group of 8 on a catamaran, it works out at about EUR 100-125 per person. Compare options on the search page to find the best deal for your budget.
