title: Marbella Boat Trip to Puerto Banus Guide: Distance
excerpt: Plan your Marbella boat trip to Puerto Banus with this guide. Learn distances, routes, costs, and tips for a smooth day on the water in Costa del Sol.
metaDescription: Plan your Marbella boat trip to Puerto Banus guide: distances, routes, costs, and tips. Book your charter with a skipper for a day on the Costa del Sol.
author: Andra Kiirkivi
content:
The 30-second answer

You can sail from Marbella Marina to Puerto Banus in about 20-30 minutes, depending on your boat type and speed. The distance is roughly 3 nautical miles (5.5 km) along the coast, passing landmarks like La Concha mountain and the Rio Verde estuary. A motor yacht or RIB will get you there faster, while a sailing yacht offers a more leisurely trip. All charters include a licensed skipper, so you can relax and enjoy the views of the Costa del Sol.

Why take a boat trip from Marbella to Puerto Banus

Puerto Banus is the glitzy marina that everyone talks about, and getting there by boat from Marbella is the best way to arrive. You skip the traffic on the A-7 and the hassle of parking, plus you get to see the coastline from the water. The trip is short but scenic, with the Sierra Blanca mountains on one side and the Mediterranean on the other. You can stop for a swim at Cala del Faro or just cruise past the mega-yachts docked at Banus. It is a practical route for a day trip, and many charters offer flexible timing, so you can spend a few hours exploring the shops and restaurants at Puerto Banus before heading back. The skipper handles everything, from docking to navigation, so you don't need any experience. Just bring your sunscreen and a sense of adventure.

Distance and route details

The straight-line distance from Marbella Marina (Puerto Deportivo) to Puerto Banus is about 3 nautical miles (5.5 km). The actual sailing route follows the coast, so you will pass by the Rio Verde beach and the mouth of the Rio Verde river. The trip takes 20-30 minutes on a motor yacht or RIB, and 30-45 minutes on a sailing yacht or catamaran, depending on wind conditions. You will see La Concha mountain rising behind Marbella, and the skyline of Puerto Banus becomes visible as you approach. The water depth is shallow near the shore, but the channel into Puerto Banus is well-marked. Skippers know the local currents and any sandbanks, so you are in safe hands. If you are departing from other ports like Estepona or Sotogrande, the distance is longer, but Marbella to Banus is the classic short hop.

What you will see along the way

On a Marbella boat trip to Puerto Banus, the views are the main attraction. To your left, the Sierra Blanca mountains, with La Concha peak at 1,215 metres, dominate the skyline. To your right, the Mediterranean stretches to Africa, and on a clear day you can see the Strait of Gibraltar. You will pass the Rio Verde beach, a quieter spot popular with locals, and the Cala del Faro cove, which is good for a quick swim if you ask your skipper. As you near Puerto Banus, you will see the marina's entrance, flanked by the iconic Banco Santander building and the Casino. The water in the marina is calm, and the skipper will dock smoothly. Keep an eye out for dolphins, especially in the summer months, as they often play near the coast. The whole trip is a photo opportunity, so have your camera ready.

Costs and charter options

Boat hire prices vary by type and season. A RIB or speedboat for a half-day charter might cost from around EUR 400, while a motor yacht from around EUR 800. Catamarans and sailing yachts are often priced from EUR 600 for a half day, and superyachts are price on request. All charters include a licensed skipper, fuel, and insurance. You can book through BoatHire24 for a wide selection of boats in Marbella and Puerto Banus. The trip itself is short, so many people book a half-day charter that includes time in Banus. You can also arrange a one-way trip, where the skipper drops you at Banus and you return by taxi, but most charters are return journeys. For the best value, book in advance, especially in July and August when demand is high.

Best time of year for this trip

The Costa del Sol has a Mediterranean climate, so you can do this trip from April to October. Summer months (June to September) are the most popular, with temperatures around 30 degrees C and calm seas. Spring and autumn are also good, with fewer crowds and cooler temperatures, around 20-25 degrees C. Winter trips are possible but less common, as the water is cooler and winds can be stronger. The sea breeze picks up in the afternoon, so morning trips are often smoother. For the best light for photos, aim for late afternoon, when the sun is behind you as you approach Puerto Banus. Check the wind forecast before booking, but skippers will not go out if conditions are unsafe. The trip is short enough that even a slightly choppy day is manageable.

How to book your Marbella boat trip to Puerto Banus

Booking is straightforward. Use BoatHire24's search to filter by boat type, capacity, and departure port. For this trip, set departure port to Marbella Marina or Puerto Banus. You can also book directly through the platform, which handles payments and communication with the owner. Most charters require a deposit, with the balance paid on the day. Cancellation policies vary, so read the terms. You can also contact the owner directly to ask about custom routes, like stopping for lunch at a beach club in Banus. The platform lists boats with photos, specs, and reviews from previous renters. For a group of 6-10, a motor yacht or catamaran works well. For a couple, a RIB or small sailing yacht is more intimate. The skipper will meet you at the marina, so arrive 15 minutes early.

Tips for a smooth trip

Bring sunscreen, a hat, and sunglasses, as the sun reflects off the water. Pack a light jacket for the breeze, even in summer. If you plan to swim, bring a towel and change of clothes. Most boats have a small cooler, but you can bring your own drinks and snacks. The skipper can recommend a spot to anchor for a swim, like off the coast of Rio Verde. In Puerto Banus, you can dock and explore the marina, which has shops, restaurants, and a casino. The skipper will stay with the boat, so you can wander for a few hours. Tipping is not mandatory but appreciated, typically 10-15% of the charter fee. If you are prone to seasickness, take a motion sickness pill an hour before departure, though the short trip is usually fine. For more tips, check our blog on boat trip planning.

Common questions

How long does it take to get from Marbella to Puerto Banus by boat?

The trip takes about 20-30 minutes on a motor boat or RIB, and 30-45 minutes on a sailing yacht or catamaran, depending on wind and sea conditions.

Can I swim during the trip?

Yes, many charters allow a stop for swimming, especially at Cala del Faro or off Rio Verde beach. Ask your skipper in advance to plan a swim break.

Do I need a boating licence?

No, all charters on BoatHire24 include a licensed skipper, so you do not need any licence or experience. The skipper handles everything.

What is the cost of a boat trip from Marbella to Puerto Banus?

Prices vary by boat type. A RIB or speedboat from around EUR 400 for a half day, a motor yacht from around EUR 800, and catamarans from around EUR 600. Superyachts are price on request.

Can I depart from Puerto Banus instead?

Yes, you can also charter a boat from Puerto Banus to Marbella. The distance and time are the same, and the route is just as scenic.

What is the best time of day for this trip?

Morning trips are smoother with calmer seas, while late afternoon offers better light for photos. Summer afternoons can be windier.

Are dolphins common on this route?

Dolphins are seen occasionally, especially in the Strait of Gibraltar area, but less so on the short Marbella-Banus route. Your skipper can advise on recent sightings.

Departing from other ports: Estepona, Sotogrande, and Benalmádena

While Marbella Marina is the obvious starting point, you can also do this trip from other Costa del Sol ports. From Estepona, the distance to Puerto Banus is about 10 nautical miles (18.5 km), taking 40-60 minutes on a motor yacht or 1-1.5 hours on a sailing yacht. You will pass the Estepona old town skyline and the Sierra Bermeja mountains before reaching the Banus channel. From Sotogrande, it is roughly 15 nautical miles (28 km), a 50-70 minute motor boat trip or 2 hours under sail. This route takes you past the Gibraltar Strait, where dolphins are more common. From Benalmádena, the distance is about 8 nautical miles (15 km), a 30-40 minute motor boat ride. Each departure port offers a different perspective on the coastline, with the Sierra Blanca mountains as a constant backdrop. The skipper will adjust the route based on wind and current, but all these trips end at the same glitzy marina. For a longer day out, start from Sotogrande and stop for lunch at a beach club near Banus.

Boat types best suited for the Marbella to Puerto Banus route

The short distance means you can use almost any boat type, but some suit the route better than others. A RIB or speedboat is ideal for a fast, direct crossing, hitting speeds of 25-35 knots, so you can be in Banus in under 20 minutes. These are good for a quick transfer or a thrill ride, but they offer less shade and comfort. Motor yachts from 30-50 feet provide a stable ride with a sun deck and cabin, perfect for groups of 6-10 who want to arrive in style. Catamarans offer more deck space and stability, making them good for families or anyone prone to seasickness. Sailing yachts are slower but more romantic, especially if you catch a breeze. For a group of 12-20, a catamaran or larger motor yacht works well. Licence-free day boats like the Quicksilver 755 are also available, but they are slower and less spacious. Check the boat capacity on BoatHire24's search to match your group size.

Stopping at Cala del Faro for a swim

One of the best additions to a Marbella boat trip to Puerto Banus is a stop at Cala del Faro, a small cove about halfway between the two marinas. The cove is tucked behind the Punta de la Mona headland, with clear water and a pebble beach. It is sheltered from the prevailing wind, so the water is usually calm for swimming. Your skipper can anchor for 15-30 minutes, giving you time to jump in and cool off. The depth is around 3-5 metres near the shore, so it is safe for swimmers. Bring a mask and snorkel to see the small fish near the rocks. The cove is popular with locals, so it is less crowded than the main beaches. After your swim, you will continue to Puerto Banus, arriving dry and refreshed. This stop adds about 20 minutes to the total trip time, but it is worth it for the experience. Most skippers will agree to this if you ask at booking.

Lunch options in Puerto Banus after your boat trip

Once you dock at Puerto Banus, you have several dining options within walking distance of the marina. For a casual meal, try the chiringuitos on the beach, like La Pesquera, which serves grilled fish and paella for around EUR 20-30 per person. For something more upscale, the marina restaurants like Ocean Club or La Sala offer Mediterranean cuisine with views of the yachts, costing EUR 50-80 per person. If you want to stay on the water, some charters allow you to moor at a beach club like Nikki Beach or Playa Padre, where you can eat at a sunbed. Your skipper can recommend a spot based on your budget and preferences. Most restaurants are open from 1pm to 4pm for lunch and 8pm to midnight for dinner. Book ahead in summer, as tables fill up fast. After lunch, you can explore the designer shops or just watch the superyachts come and go before heading back to Marbella.

Seasonal variations in sea conditions and pricing

The Mediterranean is generally calm from May to October, but conditions vary by month. In July and August, the sea is flat, with water temperatures around 24-26 degrees C, making swimming comfortable. Winds are light in the morning, picking up to 10-15 knots in the afternoon, which can create a gentle chop. Spring (April-May) and autumn (September-October) have cooler water, around 18-22 degrees C, and more variable winds. The Levante wind from the east can bring stronger gusts, up to 20 knots, which might make the trip bumpier on a small RIB. Winter (November-March) is less popular, with water temperatures dropping to 14-16 degrees C and more frequent storms. Pricing follows demand: high season (July-August) sees rates up to 30% higher than shoulder months. A half-day RIB charter might cost EUR 400 in May and EUR 520 in August. Booking early gives you the best selection and price.

Combining this trip with a visit to Marbella's other attractions

A boat trip to Puerto Banus can be part of a larger day exploring Marbella. Start at Marbella Marina, where you can grab coffee at one of the waterfront cafes before boarding. After the boat trip and lunch in Banus, you can take a taxi back to Marbella old town (about 15 minutes, EUR 20-25) to see the Plaza de los Naranjos and the Orange Square. Alternatively, visit the Rio Verde beach for a quiet afternoon swim, or drive up to La Concha mountain for a hike with panoramic views. If you have time, book a sunset cruise back from Banus to Marbella, which takes 30-45 minutes and offers golden light on the coastline. Some charters offer a full-day package that includes a swim stop, lunch, and return. Check the blog for more ideas on combining boat trips with land activities. The key is to plan the logistics so you are not rushing between locations.

What to pack for a Marbella boat trip to Puerto Banus

Packing smart makes the trip more comfortable. Essentials include high-SPF sunscreen (SPF 50+), a wide-brimmed hat, and polarised sunglasses to reduce glare. A light cotton shirt or rash guard protects your skin from the sun. Bring a waterproof phone pouch or a dry bag for your valuables, as spray can happen on a RIB. For swimming, pack a towel, swimsuit, and a change of clothes. A light jacket or windbreaker is useful, even in summer, because the breeze on the water can feel cool. If you are prone to seasickness, take a motion sickness pill 30-60 minutes before departure; the short trip usually does not cause issues, but it is better to be safe. Most boats have a small cooler for drinks, but you can bring your own water and snacks. Leave high heels at home; boat shoes or sandals with a grip are better for moving around the deck. The skipper will have a first aid kit and life jackets on board.

How the skipper handles docking at Puerto Banus

Docking at Puerto Banus is a skill that your skipper handles, so you do not need to worry. The marina has a narrow entrance with a breakwater on the left, and the skipper will call the marina on VHF channel 9 for a berth assignment. There are visitor berths along the main pier, usually 10-15 metres long, with power and water hookups. The water depth in the marina is 3-5 metres, and the current is minimal, so docking is straightforward. The skipper will use the boat's bow thruster and stern thruster to manoeuvre into the berth, assisted by marina staff with ropes. You can help by handing the ropes to the dockhands, but it is not required. The berth fee is usually included in your charter, but confirm with the owner. Once docked, you can step off the boat and explore the marina. The skipper stays with the boat, so you are free to wander for the agreed time, usually 2-3 hours for a half-day charter.

content:
The 30-second answer

You can sail from Marbella to Estepona in about 45 minutes to 1.5 hours depending on your boat type and speed. The route hugs the coast past Cabopino, Cala del Faro, and the Río Verde estuary, with the Sierra Blanca mountains as a backdrop. Most charters include a lunch stop in Estepona old town or a swim in a secluded cove. Expect to pay from around EUR 600 for a half-day trip on a motor yacht, or EUR 1,200 for a full-day catamaran with a skipper. Book through BoatHire24 to compare options and secure a licensed skipper.

Why take a boat trip from Marbella to Estepona

The Costa del Sol coastline between Marbella and Estepona is one of the most varied stretches on the Mediterranean. You get the glitz of Puerto Banús, the quiet beaches of Cabopino, the cliffs of Cala del Faro, and the charming old town of Estepona. On a boat, you see it all from the water, without the traffic on the A-7 highway. The trip is short enough for a half-day charter but long enough to feel like a proper excursion. You can stop for a swim, spot dolphins near the Strait of Gibraltar, or tie up at Estepona Marina for a seafood lunch. For a full list of available boats, check our search page.

Route overview: Marbella to Estepona by sea

The direct route from Marbella Marina (Puerto Deportivo) to Estepona Marina is about 12 nautical miles. At a cruising speed of 20 knots on a motor yacht, you cover it in 35-40 minutes. A sailing yacht at 6-8 knots takes around 1.5 hours. Most charters take a scenic route that follows the coast, passing these landmarks:

  • Puerto Banús, the superyacht harbour and shopping hub
  • Cabopino, a small marina with a sandy beach and dunes
  • Cala del Faro, a rocky cove with a lighthouse, good for a swim
  • Río Verde estuary, a nature spot with birdlife
  • Playa del Cristo, a sheltered beach just east of Estepona
  • Estepona Marina, your destination, with restaurants and a promenade

The return trip follows the same route in reverse. You can also extend the trip to the Strait of Gibraltar to see dolphins, or head east to Cabopino for a longer day.

Departure ports and boat options

You can start your trip from any of the main ports in the area. BoatHire24 lists charters departing from Puerto Banús, Marbella Marina, Cabopino, and Estepona itself. Here is a table of typical boat types and their suitability for this route:

All charters include a licensed skipper unless you choose a licence-free day boat. Prices vary by season, boat age, and included extras like fuel, food, and drinks.

What you will see along the way

The coast between Marbella and Estepona is not just beachfront hotels. You get a mix of natural and man-made sights. From the water, you can spot La Concha mountain behind Marbella, its peak often dusted with snow in winter. The Río Verde estuary is a green patch where herons and egrets feed. Cala del Faro is a small cove with a white lighthouse on a cliff; it is a popular spot for a swim because the water is clear and the seabed is sandy. As you approach Estepona, the old town's white buildings and the church tower become visible. The marina has a long breakwater with a walkway and a few bars. If you are lucky, you might see dolphins near the Strait of Gibraltar, especially in spring and autumn when the water is cooler.

Lunch and stop options in Estepona

Estepona Marina has several restaurants with terraces overlooking the water. You can tie up at the visitor berths (call ahead or ask your skipper to arrange it). For a proper meal, try a chiringuito on the beach near Playa del Cristo, or walk into the old town (5-10 minutes from the marina) for tapas in the Plaza de las Flores. Many charters include a lunch stop as part of the itinerary. If you prefer a picnic, your skipper can anchor in a quiet cove like Cala del Faro or Playa del Cristo, where you can swim and eat on board. Some catamarans have a barbecue grill on deck, so you can cook fresh fish or meat. Check with the charter company beforehand about included meals or catering options.

Costs and booking tips

A half-day charter (4 hours) from Marbella to Estepona and back costs from around EUR 600 for a motor yacht, up to EUR 1,200 for a catamaran. Full-day charters (8 hours) range from EUR 1,000 to EUR 2,500. Fuel is usually included in the price, but confirm this when booking. Some charters charge extra for food, drinks, or water toys like paddleboards. To get the best deal, book 2-4 weeks in advance during summer (June-September) when demand is highest. For a more flexible option, consider a licence-free day boat from around EUR 250, but note that you need to stay within 2 nautical miles of the coast and cannot cross open water to Estepona directly. You can read more tips on our blog.

Weather and sea conditions

The best months for this trip are May to October, when sea temperatures range from 18°C to 26°C and winds are light. In summer, the Levante wind can pick up in the afternoon, creating choppy seas around Cabopino and Cala del Faro. Morning departures (9-10am) are calmer and give you more time for lunch. In winter, the sea is rougher and many charters run only on request. Always check the forecast before you go. Your skipper will decide if it is safe to sail, but you can also cancel or reschedule if the weather looks bad. Most charter companies have a flexible cancellation policy for weather-related issues.

Common questions

How long does the boat trip from Marbella to Estepona take?
About 35-40 minutes on a motor yacht at 20 knots, or 1.5 hours on a sailing yacht. With stops for swimming and sightseeing, a half-day charter of 4 hours is enough for a relaxed trip.

Can I see dolphins on this route?
Yes, especially near the Strait of Gibraltar, which is about 10 nautical miles west of Estepona. Your skipper can adjust the route if dolphins are spotted. Common species are common dolphins and striped dolphins.

Do I need a skipper?
All charters on BoatHire24 include a licensed skipper unless you choose a licence-free day boat. For a trip to Estepona, a skipper is recommended because of the open water crossing.

What is the cost of a boat trip from Marbella to Estepona?
From around EUR 600 for a half-day motor yacht charter. Full-day catamaran charters start at EUR 1,200. Prices vary by season, boat size, and included extras.

Can I swim during the trip?
Yes. Most charters include a stop at Cala del Faro or another cove for swimming. The water is clear and calm in summer.

What should I bring?
Sunscreen, a hat, sunglasses, a light jacket for the wind, and a swimsuit. The boat usually provides towels, water, and soft drinks. Check with the charter company.

Is Estepona old town worth visiting?
Yes. It has narrow streets with whitewashed houses, flower-filled balconies, and a central square with tapas bars. It is a 10-minute walk from the marina.

Can I book a private charter?
Yes. All charters on BoatHire24 are private, meaning only your group is on board. You can customise the route and stops with the skipper.

Choosing the right departure port for your Marbella to Estepona trip

Your departure port sets the tone for the day. Puerto Banús is the obvious choice if you want to start in the most glamorous harbour on the Costa del Sol. You can grab a coffee at a waterfront cafe while watching superyachts before you cast off. The downside is that Puerto Banús is about 2 nautical miles west of Marbella Marina, so you add a few minutes to the trip. Marbella Marina (Puerto Deportivo) is more practical for a quick start, with free parking nearby and a direct route west. Cabopino is a smaller option, about 5 nautical miles east of Marbella, with a dune-backed beach and a quieter vibe. If you are staying in Estepona itself, you can start from there and do a shorter loop east to Cala del Faro and back. Each port has its own character, and your choice affects the total distance and time. For a full list of available boats at each port, check our search page.

Best seasons for the Marbella to Estepona boat route

The route is sailable year-round, but the experience changes dramatically with the season. In high summer (July and August), sea temperatures hit 24-26°C, and the water is calm in the mornings. The catch is that the Levante wind often picks up at 2-3pm, creating short, steep waves around Cabopino and Cala del Faro. A morning departure (9-11am) avoids this. Spring (April to June) is ideal for dolphin spotting, with water temperatures around 16-20°C and lighter winds. Autumn (September to October) is similar, with fewer crowds in Estepona and lower charter prices. Winter (November to March) is for the brave: sea temperatures drop to 14-16°C, and many charters run only on request. If you do go in winter, you might have the coast almost to yourself, but bring a warm jacket. The Sierra Blanca mountains behind Marbella often have snow on La Concha in January, which is a rare sight from the water.

What to expect at Estepona Marina

Estepona Marina is a working harbour with 400 berths, a fuel dock, and a long breakwater that doubles as a promenade. When you arrive, your skipper will contact the marina office on VHF channel 9 or call ahead to arrange a visitor berth. The marina has a few restaurants and bars on the eastern side, serving grilled fish and cold beers. The old town is a 10-minute walk up Avenida de España, past the bullring and into the maze of whitewashed streets. Plaza de las Flores is the main square, with orange trees and tapas bars. For a more local experience, walk to the market hall (Mercado de Abastos) on Calle Terraza for fresh produce and jamón. If you want a beach stop, Playa del Cristo is a sheltered cove just east of the marina, with a chiringuito and calm water for swimming. Your skipper can anchor there for an hour or two before the return trip.

Extending the trip: Estepona to the Strait of Gibraltar

If you have a full-day charter, you can extend the route west from Estepona to the Strait of Gibraltar, about 10 nautical miles further. This adds 30-40 minutes each way on a motor yacht, or 1-1.5 hours on a sailing yacht. The Strait is famous for dolphin sightings, especially common dolphins and striped dolphins, and occasionally pilot whales in summer. The water here is deeper and the currents are stronger, so your skipper will need to be experienced. The reward is a view of the African coast on a clear day, with the Rif Mountains of Morocco visible across the 14-kilometre gap. You can stop for a swim in the clear water near the Punta de Europa lighthouse at the southern tip of mainland Spain. This extension is best done from May to September when the sea is calmest. It pushes the total trip to 6-8 hours, so budget for a full-day charter from around EUR 1,200 for a motor yacht or EUR 1,800 for a catamaran.

Swimming spots and coves between Marbella and Estepona

The coast between Marbella and Estepona has several coves where you can anchor for a swim. Cala del Faro is the most popular, with a sandy seabed and clear water protected by a rocky headland. The lighthouse on the cliff adds a postcard backdrop. Playa del Cristo, just east of Estepona, is a sheltered beach with a gentle slope, ideal for less confident swimmers. Further east, near Cabopino, there is a small cove called Cala de Cabopino with a rocky bottom and better snorkelling. For a more private spot, your skipper can anchor off the Río Verde estuary, where the water is calm and the beach is quiet. Most charters include a stop at one of these coves, and you can ask to spend more time at a specific spot. Bring a mask and snorkel to see the small fish around the rocks. The water is clearest in the morning before the wind picks up.

Practical tips for your Marbella to Estepona boat trip

Book your charter 2-4 weeks in advance during summer, especially for catamarans and larger yachts. Confirm what is included in the price: fuel, skipper, food, drinks, and water toys (paddleboards, snorkel gear) are sometimes extra. Most charters provide towels and soft drinks, but bring your own sunscreen and a hat. The sun is intense even in spring, and the reflection off the water can burn you quickly. If you are prone to seasickness, take a motion sickness tablet 30 minutes before departure, especially if the Levante wind is forecast. The route is sheltered in most places, but the stretch between Cabopino and Cala del Faro can be choppy. Wear non-slip shoes on the boat, as decks get wet. For a licence-free day boat, you need a valid ID and a credit card deposit, and you are limited to 2 nautical miles from the coast, so you cannot cross directly to Estepona. You can read more practical advice on our blog.

Comparing motor yachts and catamarans for this route

Motor yachts are the fastest option for the Marbella to Estepona trip, cutting the crossing time to 35-40 minutes. They are ideal if you want to maximise time in Estepona or extend to the Strait of Gibraltar. The downside is the engine noise and a slightly rougher ride in choppy seas. Catamarans are slower (8-12 knots, taking 1-1.5 hours) but offer more stability, a larger deck area, and a smoother ride. They are better for families with children or groups who want to socialise. Catamarans also have a shallower draft, so they can anchor closer to beaches. For a half-day trip, a motor yacht gives you more time at the destination. For a full-day cruise with lunch and swimming, a catamaran is more comfortable. Prices reflect this: a half-day motor yacht from around EUR 600, a half-day catamaran from around EUR 1,200. Both include a licensed skipper, and you can customise the route.

title: Marbella Boat Trip to Benalmadena Guide: Marina Trip
excerpt: Marbella boat trip to Benalmadena guide covering routes, marinas, timing, and tips. Learn how to plan a day on the water from Puerto Banus to Benalmadena Marina.
metaDescription: Marbella boat trip to Benalmadena guide: routes, marinas, timing, and tips. Plan your day on the water from Puerto Banus to Benalmadena Marina. Book now.
author: Andra Kiirkivi
content:
The 30-second answer

A Marbella boat trip to Benalmadena is a straightforward coastal hop of about 10 nautical miles, taking roughly 45 minutes to an hour depending on your boat and speed. You depart from Puerto Banus or Marbella Marina, cruise past Cala del Faro and the Torrequebrada coastline, and arrive at Benalmadena Marina, a purpose-built leisure port with restaurants, bars, and the Sea Life aquarium. The trip works well on a motor yacht, catamaran, or RIB. Every charter includes a licensed skipper, so you just sit back and enjoy the views of La Concha mountain and the Mediterranean. Expect to pay from around EUR 400 for a half-day RIB charter up to EUR 1,500 for a motor yacht with crew.

Why take a boat from Marbella to Benalmadena

Benalmadena Marina, also known as Puerto Marina, is one of the most visited leisure ports on the Costa del Sol. It was designed by the architect Miguel Sarasola and looks like something out of a fantasy novel, all winding canals and whitewashed buildings. The marina itself has over 900 berths and is packed with seafood restaurants, chiringuitos, and shops. A boat trip from Marbella gives you a different perspective on the coast. You see the Sierra de Mijas mountains rising behind Fuengirola and the Torre Bermeja lighthouse before you round the point into Benalmadena. The water is usually calm, especially in the morning before the sea breeze picks up. If you are staying in Marbella and want a day out without the hassle of driving or parking, this trip is a solid choice. You can also combine it with a stop at Cala del Faro for a swim. The route is short enough that you can do it in half a day, including a couple of hours ashore for lunch. For a longer day, you could push on to the Strait of Gibraltar to spot dolphins, but that is a different trip altogether.

Route overview and distances

The direct distance from Puerto Banus to Benalmadena Marina is approximately 10 nautical miles (18.5 km). If you are departing from Marbella Marina (Puerto Deportivo), add another 2 nautical miles east. The route is a straight line east-northeast along the coast. You pass the following landmarks:

  • Puerto Banus, departure point with luxury yachts and designer shops
  • Cala del Faro, a small cove with a lighthouse, good for a quick swim
  • Torre Bermeja, a historic watchtower on the cliffs
  • Fuengirola beachfront, you will see the castle and the long sandy beach
  • Benalmadena Marina, your destination, with the Sea Life building as a landmark

The cruising speed of a typical motor yacht is around 20 knots, so the trip takes about 30 minutes. On a sailing yacht, you are looking at 1.5 to 2 hours depending on the wind. RIBs and speedboats can do it in 20 minutes. The sea state is usually calm in summer, with wave heights under 0.5 metres. In winter, you might get a light chop, but it is still manageable. The best time to go is between May and October, when the water temperature is above 20 degrees C and the air temperature is in the high 20s. You can also go in April or November, but you might need a light jacket.

Boat types suitable for this trip

You have several options for a Marbella boat trip to Benalmadena. Each boat type gives a different experience. Here is a quick comparison:

Boat typeSpeedCapacityTypical cost (half day)Best for
Motor yacht20-30 kts8-12 guestsfrom EUR 1,200Comfort, luxury, dining on board
Catamaran15-20 kts10-18 guestsfrom EUR 1,500Stability, space, groups
Sailing yacht6-10 kts6-10 guestsfrom EUR 800Experience, silence, wind
RIB / speedboat30-45 kts4-8 guestsfrom EUR 400Speed, adrenaline, small groups
Fishing boat8-15 kts4-6 guestsfrom EUR 500Fishing, relaxed pace

For a quick day trip, a RIB or motor yacht is the most practical. If you want to make a day of it with lunch on board, a catamaran or motor yacht with a flybridge gives you more space. All charters include a licensed skipper, so you do not need a licence. You can also add water toys like a paddleboard or snorkel gear for an extra fee. Check the boat rental search page for availability and prices.

What to do in Benalmadena Marina

Benalmadena Marina is not just a place to tie up your boat. It is a destination in itself. The marina has a large central square with a fountain and palm trees, surrounded by restaurants and bars. You can eat fresh grilled fish at one of the seafront places or grab a tapas lunch at a smaller spot. The marina also has a Sea Life aquarium, which is good if you have kids. There is a small beach called Playa de la Carihuela just west of the marina, but it gets busy in summer. If you want a quieter swim, head to the small cove near the Torre Bermeja on the way back. The marina has a chandlery and a few shops selling nautical gear and souvenirs. You can also take a short walk to the Benalmadena Pueblo, the old town on the hill, but that is a 30-minute walk uphill. Most people stay in the marina area. The atmosphere is lively but not as flashy as Puerto Banus. It is more of a family and local vibe. You can easily spend 2-3 hours here before heading back to Marbella. If you want to stay longer, you can book a full-day charter and also visit Fuengirola or the Strait of Gibraltar on the same trip, but that would be a long day.

Timing and weather considerations

The best time of day for a Marbella boat trip to Benalmadena is in the morning, between 9am and noon. The sea is usually calm, and you avoid the afternoon heat. The wind picks up around 2pm, which can make the return trip choppier, especially on a RIB. In summer, the temperature can reach 35 degrees C, so bring sunscreen, a hat, and plenty of water. The boat will have shade from the bimini or cabin, but you still need protection. In spring and autumn, the temperature is milder, around 22-28 degrees C, and the water is still warm enough to swim until October. Winter trips are possible but less popular. The water temperature drops to around 15 degrees C, and you might get a light jacket. The sea is usually calm in winter too, but you have fewer daylight hours. The sunset is around 6pm in December, so plan accordingly. Always check the weather forecast before you go. The wind can pick up suddenly, especially if a poniente (west wind) blows. The skipper will handle the navigation and will decide if it is safe to go. If you are prone to seasickness, take a tablet an hour before departure. The trip is short, but the swell can be noticeable in a small boat.

Costs and booking tips

The cost of a Marbella boat trip to Benalmadena varies by boat type, duration, and season. Here are typical ranges for a half-day charter (4 hours):

  • RIB or speedboat: from EUR 400 to EUR 800
  • Motor yacht (up to 12 guests): from EUR 1,200 to EUR 2,500
  • Catamaran (up to 18 guests): from EUR 1,500 to EUR 3,000
  • Sailing yacht: from EUR 800 to EUR 1,500
  • Fishing boat: from EUR 500 to EUR 1,000

Prices are higher in July and August, when demand peaks. You can often get a better deal in May, June, or September. All prices include the skipper and fuel. Some charters include drinks and snacks, but check the listing. You might need to bring your own food or order catering. To book, use the boat rental search page to filter by boat type and date. Book at least a week in advance in summer. You can also contact the boat owner directly through the platform. The cancellation policy is usually flexible if you cancel 48 hours before. If you are a group of 6 or more, a catamaran is often the best value because it is stable and has plenty of deck space. For a couple or small family, a RIB or small motor yacht is fine. You can also book a full-day charter (8 hours) and include a stop at Cala del Faro or Fuengirola on the way back.

Local tips and alternative routes

If you have done the Marbella to Benalmadena trip before, or if you want something different, consider these alternatives:

  • Go east to Cabopino instead. It is closer to Marbella, about 5 nautical miles, and has a small marina with a dune reserve.
  • Go west to Estepona. The old town is charming, and the marina is quieter. Distance from Puerto Banus is about 10 nautical miles.
  • Combine Benalmadena with a stop at Fuengirola. You can dock at the Fuengirola marina, visit the castle, and then continue to Benalmadena.
  • If you want a longer trip, head south to the Strait of Gibraltar. You can see dolphins and maybe whales. Distance is about 30 nautical miles from Marbella, so you need a full day.

For the Benalmadena trip, a good tip is to bring a camera for the views of La Concha mountain from the sea. The mountain is visible for most of the trip. Also, bring swimwear and a towel if you want to swim at Cala del Faro or at the beach in Benalmadena. The water is clear and clean. If you are on a RIB, the ride can be bumpy, so hold onto your belongings. The skipper will provide life jackets for everyone. You can also ask the skipper to point out landmarks and tell you about the history of the coast. Many skippers are local and know the area well. For more ideas, read the BoatHire24 blog for other destination guides and tips.

Common questions

How long does it take to sail from Marbella to Benalmadena?
On a motor yacht at 20 knots, about 30 minutes. On a sailing yacht, 1.5 to 2 hours. On a RIB, about 20 minutes.

Do I need a boat licence to charter a boat for this trip?
No. Every charter on BoatHire24 includes a licensed skipper, so you just relax and enjoy the ride.

Can I swim during the trip?
Yes. Most charters allow a stop at Cala del Faro or a quiet spot for swimming. The skipper will choose a safe location.

What is the best time of year for this trip?
May to October is ideal. Water temperature is above 20 degrees C, and the sea is calm. April and November are also possible but cooler.

How much does a half-day charter cost?
From around EUR 400 for a RIB up to EUR 1,500 for a catamaran. Prices vary by season and boat type.

Can I bring my own food and drink?
Yes, most charters allow you to bring your own. Some boats have a fridge and a sound system. Check the listing for details.

Is Benalmadena Marina worth visiting?
Yes. It is a lively marina with restaurants, bars, an aquarium, and a beach. It is a popular destination for a day trip from Marbella.

Why Puerto Banus is the best departure point for this trip

Puerto Banus, the glitzy marina in Marbella, is the most convenient departure point for your Benalmadena trip. It sits just 10 nautical miles west of Benalmadena, so you are already halfway there. The marina itself is worth a look before you leave, with its superyachts, designer shops, and the famous Casino Marbella. You can grab a coffee at one of the waterfront cafes before boarding. The marina has a dedicated charter area where you meet your skipper. If you are staying in Marbella town, the journey to Puerto Banus is about 10 minutes by taxi or 20 minutes by bus. Parking is expensive, around EUR 20 for a few hours, so consider a taxi. The departure time is flexible, but the skipper will usually suggest a morning start to avoid the afternoon wind. You can also depart from Marbella Marina (Puerto Deportivo), which is closer to the town centre and has cheaper parking. The extra 2 nautical miles east means you add about 10 minutes to the trip. Both ports have good facilities, including toilets, shops, and restaurants. For a full list of boats departing from Puerto Banus, check the boat rental search page.

What to expect at Benalmadena Marina on arrival

When you arrive at Benalmadena Marina, the skipper will dock at one of the visitor berths. The marina has a dedicated area for day charters, usually near the main square. You step off the boat and straight into the action. The marina is designed like a small village, with canals, bridges, and whitewashed buildings. The central square has a large fountain and is surrounded by restaurants serving fresh seafood, paella, and grilled meats. Prices are reasonable, around EUR 15-25 per person for a main course. You can also find chiringuitos on the beach side, serving grilled sardines and beer. The marina has a Sea Life aquarium, which costs around EUR 15 for adults and EUR 10 for children. It is small but well-maintained, with a tunnel through the shark tank. If you want to shop, there are a few boutiques selling clothes and souvenirs. The marina is pedestrian-friendly, so you can wander without worrying about traffic. The atmosphere is lively but not as pretentious as Puerto Banus. You can easily spend 2-3 hours here, eating, drinking, and exploring. If you want to swim, the nearest beach is Playa de la Carihuela, a 5-minute walk west. It is a sandy beach with loungers and umbrellas for rent. The water is clean and calm, ideal for a quick dip.

How to combine this trip with a stop at Cala del Faro

Cala del Faro is a small cove about 3 nautical miles east of Puerto Banus, roughly halfway to Benalmadena. It is a popular spot for swimming and snorkelling, with a lighthouse on the cliffs above. The water is clear and deep, so you can jump in from the boat. The cove is sheltered from the wind, so it is usually calm. Most skippers will offer a stop here if you ask. You can spend 20-30 minutes swimming, snorkelling, or just floating. The cove has no facilities, so bring your own water and snacks. The seabed is rocky in places, so wear water shoes. You can also see small fish and sometimes octopus if you snorkel. After the swim, you continue east to Benalmadena. The stop adds about 30 minutes to the trip, so factor that into your charter time. If you are on a half-day charter, you can do the swim, then have lunch at the marina, and head back. On a full-day charter, you can also stop at Fuengirola on the way back. The skipper will know the best spots and can adjust the route based on your preferences. For more ideas on combining stops, read the BoatHire24 blog for other itinerary suggestions.

title: Marbella Boat Trip to Fuengirola Guide: Day Trip
excerpt: A practical guide to taking a boat trip from Marbella to Fuengirola. What to see, where to moor, how long it takes, and what you can expect on the water.
metaDescription: Plan your Marbella boat trip to Fuengirola with our guide. Distance, mooring options, things to see, and tips for a smooth day on the Costa del Sol.
author: Andra Kiirkivi
content:
The 30-second answer

A Marbella boat trip to Fuengirola takes about 45 minutes to 1.5 hours by motor yacht or RIB, depending on your speed and the sea state. You can moor at the Fuengirola marina, which has visitor berths, or anchor off the beach near the castle. The route runs west along the coast, passing Cabopino and Calahonda, and gives you a solid view of the Sierra de Mijas. You will need to book a boat with a skipper from BoatHire24, as all charters include a licensed skipper.

Why take a boat from Marbella to Fuengirola

You might think Fuengirola is just another coastal town, but it has a few things that make it worth the trip by water. The approach from the sea gives you a different perspective: the castle of Sohail sits right on the beach, and the marina is compact but functional. If you have guests who want a short, relaxed outing without committing to a full day at sea, this route works well. You can leave from Puerto Banús or Marbella Marina, cruise for less than an hour, and then spend a few hours ashore before heading back. The distance is only about 12 nautical miles from Puerto Banús to Fuengirola, so you are not burning through fuel or time. For a family or a small group, a RIB or a licence-free day boat is fine. For something more comfortable, a motor yacht gives you shade, a bathroom, and a place to sit. Check the BoatHire24 search page for boats available from Marbella and Puerto Banús.

Distance and travel time from Marbella to Fuengirola

The straight-line distance from Puerto Banús to Fuengirola marina is roughly 12 nautical miles. From Marbella Marina, it is about 10 nautical miles. At a cruising speed of 20 knots on a RIB or small speedboat, you can cover that in 30 to 40 minutes. On a motor yacht doing 10 to 15 knots, expect 45 minutes to 1 hour. A sailing yacht will take longer, 1.5 to 2 hours depending on wind. The sea state along this stretch is usually calm in summer, with a gentle swell from the west. In winter or after a Levante wind, the sea can get choppy, especially near Cabopino point. Your skipper will adjust the speed and route accordingly. The route is straightforward: head west from Marbella, keep the coast on your starboard side, pass the Cabopino marina and the Calahonda beach clubs, and you will see the Fuengirola castle and marina ahead. There are no tricky navigation points, but the skipper will handle that anyway.

Where to moor or anchor in Fuengirola

Fuengirola has a marina called Puerto Deportivo de Fuengirola, located just east of the castle. It has visitor berths, and you can usually get a spot for a few hours or overnight. The marina office is on the north side of the basin. Depth is around 3 to 4 metres, so most yachts and catamarans can enter. Fees are reasonable, around EUR 20 to 40 for a few hours for a 10-metre boat, but confirm with the marina on arrival. If you prefer to anchor, the beach west of the castle, Playa del Castillo, has good holding in sand and is sheltered from the east. You can anchor there and take a tender to shore or swim in. The beach is busy in summer, so anchor well outside the swimming area. Another option is to anchor off Playa de Los Boliches, further west, but that is more exposed. Your skipper will know the best spot based on wind and swell. For a day trip, anchoring is often simpler than dealing with marina formalities, but if you want to go into town for lunch, the marina is more convenient.

What to see and do in Fuengirola from the water

From the boat, the main landmark is the Castillo Sohail, a 10th-century Moorish fortress on a hill at the mouth of the Fuengirola river. It is lit up at night and visible from miles away. You can anchor right below it and swim to the beach. The marina itself has a few restaurants and bars, but nothing special. If you go ashore, the old town is about a 10-minute walk from the marina, with narrow streets and tapas bars. The Bioparc Fuengirola is a zoo, but you would need a taxi or a longer walk. For a boat trip, the best activity is to anchor off the castle, have lunch on board, and then cruise back. You can also head further west to the mouth of the Río Fuengirola, but it is shallow and not navigable for most boats. Dolphins are occasionally seen along this coast, especially near Cabopino, but not guaranteed. If you want a longer day, combine Fuengirola with a stop at Cabopino or even Estepona, but that would be a full day.

Best boats for a Marbella to Fuengirola trip

For a short hop like this, you do not need a superyacht. A RIB or speedboat is ideal: fast, easy to handle, and cheap to rent. You can get a 6 to 8-metre RIB from around EUR 300 for a half day. A licence-free day boat, like a small motorboat with a 15hp engine, is cheaper but slower, around EUR 200 for a half day. If you want comfort, a 10 to 12-metre motor yacht with a cabin, bathroom, and sun pads will cost from around EUR 600 for a half day. Catamarans are stable but slower, and sailing yachts are fine if you have time. Fishing boats are also available if you want to combine the trip with some fishing. For a group of 6 to 8, a motor yacht is the best balance of speed and comfort. For a couple or a small family, a RIB is fine. All boats on BoatHire24 include a skipper, so you do not need a licence. You can filter by boat type and price on the search page.

What to pack for a day trip to Fuengirola

Sun cream, a hat, and sunglasses are essential, even in spring or autumn. The sun reflects off the water and you will burn faster than on land. A light jacket or windbreaker is useful because the wind on a RIB can be cool, even in summer. Swimwear and a towel if you plan to anchor and swim. Snorkel gear is optional but the water is clear near the castle. Bring cash for the marina or beach bars, as not all places take cards. A camera or phone for photos of the castle from the sea. Food and drink: you can bring your own on most boats, but check with the skipper. Some charters offer a cool box or fridge. If you want to eat ashore, the marina has a few restaurants, but they are touristy. Better to anchor and have a picnic on board. Do not forget seasickness tablets if you are prone, though the sea is usually calm on this route.

When to go: best time of year for this trip

The best months are May to October, when the sea is warm and calm. July and August are hot, with temperatures around 30 degrees C, but the sea breeze helps. The water temperature is around 20 to 25 degrees C from June to September. Spring and autumn are cooler but still pleasant, with fewer crowds. Winter trips are possible but the sea can be rough, and many boats are laid up. The wind is a factor: the Levante (east wind) can create choppy seas, especially in the afternoon. The Poniente (west wind) is lighter and more comfortable. Your skipper will monitor the forecast and may suggest a morning departure to avoid afternoon winds. Sunrise trips are beautiful, with the sun coming up over the Sierra de Mijas. Sunset trips are popular too, with the castle lit up. For a quick day trip, aim for a 10 am departure, arrive by 11 am, anchor for a few hours, and head back by 3 pm.

How to book a boat from Marbella to Fuengirola

You can book directly on BoatHire24. Use the search filters to set your departure port to Marbella or Puerto Banús, your desired date, and the number of guests. Then select a boat type: motor yacht, RIB, or licence-free day boat. Contact the owner or charter company through the platform to confirm availability and ask about the Fuengirola trip. Most owners are flexible and will agree to a half-day charter to Fuengirola. Prices vary by boat size and season, but expect to pay from around EUR 300 for a half day on a RIB to EUR 800 for a motor yacht. All charters include a skipper, fuel, and insurance. You can also book a full day and include other stops like Cabopino or Estepona. Read the boat description carefully for amenities like a bathroom, shower, or sound system. For a short trip, you do not need a huge boat, but comfort matters if you have elderly guests or children. Book at least a week in advance in summer, as boats get booked up.

Common questions

How long does it take to get from Marbella to Fuengirola by boat? About 45 minutes to 1.5 hours, depending on the boat type and speed. A RIB can do it in 30 to 40 minutes, a motor yacht in 45 minutes to 1 hour, and a sailing yacht in 1.5 to 2 hours.

Can I anchor in Fuengirola and swim? Yes, you can anchor off Playa del Castillo near the castle. The water is clean and the beach is public. Your skipper will find a safe spot outside the swimming area.

Do I need a licence to rent a boat for this trip? No. All boats on BoatHire24 include a licensed skipper, so you can just relax and enjoy the ride.

What is the best boat for a family trip to Fuengirola? A motor yacht with a cabin and bathroom is best for families with children. A RIB is fine for older kids, but can be bumpy in choppy seas.

Are there dolphins on this route? Occasionally, especially near Cabopino. But it is not guaranteed. If you want a higher chance, book a trip towards the Strait of Gibraltar.

Can I stay overnight in Fuengirola marina? Yes, the marina has visitor berths. You will need to arrange with the marina office on arrival. Overnight fees are around EUR 30 to 60 for a 10-metre boat.

What if the weather is bad on the day? The skipper will decide if it is safe to go. If the sea is too rough, you can reschedule or cancel with a full refund, depending on the charter policy.

Why Fuengirola beats a lazy day at Puerto Banús

Let's be honest: Puerto Banús is a zoo in August. You queue for everything, the mooring fees are eye-watering, and the beach is a postage stamp. Fuengirola gives you actual space. The beach west of the castle is 200 metres wide, the water is shallow for kids, and you can anchor without a dozen jet skis buzzing your bow. The castle itself is a solid photo op: it dates back to the 10th century, and the Moors picked that spot because they could see the entire coast. From the water, you get the full scale of it, the hill, the walls, the flag. If you time it right, there is a medieval market or a music festival in the castle grounds during summer. Your skipper can drop you at the marina, you walk five minutes to the castle entrance, and you are in a different century. Compare that to sipping EUR 18 cocktails in Banús. The choice is yours.

Fuel costs and hidden fees for the Marbella to Fuengirola run

Fuel is included in most charter prices on BoatHire24, but you should confirm. For a 12-nautical-mile run, a 30-foot motor yacht burning 60 litres per hour at 15 knots will use about 48 litres. At EUR 1.50 per litre for diesel, that is roughly EUR 72 in fuel. A RIB with a 200hp outboard uses more, around 30 litres per hour at 25 knots, so about 14 litres for the trip, around EUR 25. Most half-day charters already factor this in, but if you book a full day and go further, fuel can be extra. Check the listing details. Marina fees in Fuengirola are separate: EUR 20 to 40 for a few hours for a 10-metre boat, payable in cash at the office. Anchoring is free, but you need a tender to get ashore. Some skippers have a small dinghy, others do not. Ask before you book. And tip the skipper, EUR 20 to 50 is normal for a half day.

The best departure port for your Fuengirola trip

You have three main options: Puerto Banús, Marbella Marina, and Cabopino. Puerto Banús is the flashiest, with superyachts and designer shops, but traffic to get in and out in summer is a nightmare. Marbella Marina is quieter, easier to park near, and closer to Fuengirola by 2 nautical miles. Cabopino is even closer, about 6 nautical miles from Fuengirola, but it is a small marina with fewer boat options. If you are staying in Marbella town, depart from Marbella Marina. If you are in Nueva Andalucía or want the Banús vibe, go from Puerto Banús. Cabopino is best if you are in the Artola area or want a quick trip. All three are on the search page, so you can filter by port. For a half-day trip, the time saved by leaving from Cabopino is marginal, 15 minutes versus 45 minutes, but it matters if you are on a tight schedule.

What to do if the sea is rough on your chosen day

The Levante wind can kick up 1.5-metre swells between Cabopino and Fuengirola, especially in July and August afternoons. Your skipper will check the forecast and may suggest a morning departure, say 9 am, to avoid the chop. If the sea is already rough at 8 am, you have options. First, reschedule to the next day, most charters allow that with 24 hours notice. Second, switch to a larger boat: a 12-metre motor yacht handles chop better than a 6-metre RIB. Third, take the inland route: the coast is sheltered close to shore, so the skipper can stay inside the 5-metre depth line where the swell is smaller. Fourth, cancel and get a refund if the charter company deems it unsafe. Do not pressure the skipper to go out in bad conditions. The Costa del Sol has 320 sunny days a year, so odds are in your favour. If you are flexible, book a boat with a flexible cancellation policy.

Combining Fuengirola with a stop at Cabopino

If you want more than just Fuengirola, add Cabopino to your itinerary. Cabopino is 6 nautical miles west of Fuengirola and has a small marina and a nudist beach. You can anchor off the Artola dunes, swim in the clear water, and then cruise to Fuengirola for lunch. The total distance from Marbella to Cabopino to Fuengirola and back is about 28 nautical miles, doable in a half day on a fast RIB, but a full day on a motor yacht. The advantage is variety: Cabopino is quiet and natural, Fuengirola has the castle and marina. You get two different Costa del Sol experiences in one trip. Your skipper can plan the route to avoid backtracking: leave Marbella, go to Cabopino first (30 minutes), then Fuengirola (20 minutes), then back to Marbella (45 minutes). That is a 4-hour trip with two stops. Book a full-day charter to have time for swimming and lunch.

Packing for a family with young children on this route

Children under 5 get bored on a boat after 20 minutes. Bring entertainment: a tablet with downloaded shows, a small bag of toys, and snacks. The wind on a RIB is loud, so ear protection for toddlers is a good idea. Life jackets are provided by the charter, but bring your own if your child is small, the boat ones might be too big. Sun protection is critical: a UV suit, a hat with a strap, and reef-safe sunscreen. The sun reflects off the water and can burn in 15 minutes. For swimming, bring inflatable arm bands or a float vest. The beach at Fuengirola has a gentle slope, so it is safe for paddling. If your child gets seasick, give them ginger biscuits or a seasickness patch an hour before departure. Most skippers are happy to slow down if the kids are uncomfortable. A motor yacht with a cabin is better than a RIB for young children, because they can nap inside away from the sun and noise.

title: Marbella vs Puerto Banus Boat Charter: Comparison
excerpt: Choosing between a boat charter from Marbella or Puerto Banús? Here is a direct comparison of costs, vibe, routes, and practical differences to help you decide.
metaDescription: Marbella vs Puerto Banus boat charter: compare costs, vibe, routes, and practical tips. Decide which departure port suits your day on the Costa del Sol.
author: Andra Kiirkivi
content:
The 30-second answer

Puerto Banús is flashier and more expensive, with superyachts and designer boutiques; Marbella Marina is more relaxed and slightly cheaper, with a family-friendly vibe. For a boat charter, you pay a premium in Puerto Banús for the glitz, but Marbella offers similar access to the same coastline (dolphin spotting, Cala del Faro, Cabopino) often at a lower base rate. Both ports have licensed skippers included, and the sailing time to key spots like La Concha views or Estepona is nearly identical. Your choice depends on whether you want the paparazzi vibe or a chilled start to your day.

Location and atmosphere: the real difference

Marbella Marina (Puerto Deportivo) sits right in the town centre, a short walk from the old town and its tapas bars. It is busy but not chaotic; you get a mix of local fishermen and charter boats. The atmosphere is Mediterranean-casual, with a few decent restaurants and a chandlery. Puerto Banús, five kilometres west, is a different beast. It is the superyacht capital of the Costa del Sol, where you see EUR 20 million boats parked next to Versace and Louis Vuitton. The crowd is wealthier, the music louder, and the prices higher. For a boat charter, this matters because the departure port sets the tone for your day. If you want a low-key start, Marbella wins. If you want to feel like a VIP before you even step on board, Puerto Banús delivers.

Both ports have direct access to the same sea, but the vibe on land influences your pre- and post-charter experience. In Marbella, you can grab a EUR 4 beer at a chiringuito before boarding. In Puerto Banús, a coffee might cost you EUR 6. The actual charter experience on the water is similar, but the emotional start is different.

Cost comparison: what you pay and what you get

Boat charter prices vary by season, boat type, and duration, but broad trends exist. For a 4-hour motor yacht charter (say, a 40-50 ft boat with skipper), from Marbella Marina you might pay from around EUR 800 to EUR 1,200. From Puerto Banús, the same boat could be EUR 1,000 to EUR 1,500. The premium is roughly 15-25% in Puerto Banús, partly due to higher berthing fees and demand.

Catamarans, popular for groups, follow a similar pattern. A 40 ft catamaran for half a day from Marbella might be EUR 1,200 to EUR 1,600; from Puerto Banús, EUR 1,400 to EUR 1,800. RIBs and speedboats are cheaper: a 30 ft RIB for 2 hours from Marbella could be EUR 400 to EUR 600; from Puerto Banús, EUR 500 to EUR 700. Fishing boats and licence-free day boats are less common in Puerto Banús, so Marbella has a wider selection for budget options.

Fuel is usually included in the charter price, but check. Skipper costs are always included on BoatHire24. The bottom line: if you want the cheapest possible day, Marbella wins. If you want the experience of departing from a glamorous marina, you pay extra.

Routes and sailing time: how far can you go

From both ports, you have the same coastline to explore. East: Cabopino (15-20 minutes by motor yacht), Cala del Faro (25 minutes), and Marbella beaches. West: Estepona (30-40 minutes), Sotogrande (50-60 minutes), and the Strait of Gibraltar for dolphin watching (90 minutes+).

The difference is minimal. From Puerto Banús, you are 5 km closer to Estepona and the Strait, saving about 10 minutes. From Marbella, you are 5 km closer to Cabopino and Nerja (though Nerja is 60 km east, so a 2-hour trip from either). For a standard half-day charter (4 hours), both ports let you reach the same highlights: anchor at Cala del Faro for a swim, cruise past La Concha mountain, and maybe spot dolphins near the Strait. The extra 10 minutes is irrelevant.

One practical note: Puerto Banús has a narrower entrance channel and more traffic, so departure and return can take 15 minutes extra in summer. Marbella Marina is more straightforward. For a 2-hour RIB trip, this matters. For a full-day charter, it is negligible.

Boat types and availability: which port has what

Puerto Banús has a higher concentration of superyachts (over 60 ft) and luxury motor yachts. If you want a 100 ft motor yacht with a jacuzzi and a crew of five, you go to Puerto Banús. Marbella Marina has more variety: smaller motor yachts, catamarans, sailing yachts, RIBs, fishing boats, and licence-free day boats. The reason is simple: Marbella Marina is older and more established as a working port, while Puerto Banús is a purpose-built luxury destination.

For catamarans, both ports have good options, but Marbella often has a wider range of sizes (30-50 ft) at lower prices. Sailing yachts are more common in Marbella, as the marina has a sailing club and regatta history. Fishing boats are almost exclusively in Marbella. Licence-free day boats (no skipper required) are rare in Puerto Banús because the marina management prefers skipper-operated charters for safety and insurance reasons.

If you want a specific boat type, check availability on our search before deciding on a port. In peak season (June-September), both ports are busy, but Puerto Banús books out faster for luxury boats.

Local colour and extras: beyond the boat

Your charter day can include more than just the boat. From Marbella, you can combine a morning charter with a walk through the old town, a visit to the Orange Square, or lunch at a chiringuito on the beach. The marina has a fish market and a small beach. From Puerto Banús, the extras are shopping at designer stores, people-watching at the portside cafes, and nightlife at clubs like Pangea or Ocean Club. The contrast is stark: Marbella is about culture and local life; Puerto Banús is about spectacle and luxury.

For dolphin spotting, both ports offer similar chances, but the Strait of Gibraltar is more accessible from Puerto Banús by 15 minutes. The Río Verde area, just east of Puerto Banús, is a good fishing spot. Cala del Faro, a secluded cove east of Marbella, is a 25-minute cruise from either port. Estepona old town, with its flower-filled streets, is a 30-minute walk from the Estepona marina (which is a separate departure port, not part of this comparison).

If you book through BoatHire24, you can filter by departure port and add extras like water toys, catering, or a photographer. The choice of port affects these extras: Puerto Banús charters often include champagne and gourmet catering as standard; Marbella charters are more likely to offer local seafood and beer.

Practical considerations: parking, access, and crowds

Parking is a headache in both ports in summer. Marbella Marina has a large underground car park (around EUR 25 per day in peak season). Puerto Banús has multiple car parks but charges EUR 30-40 per day and they fill up by 11 am. If you are driving, arrive early or use a taxi. Both ports are accessible by public bus from Marbella town (line L-2 connects them in 15 minutes).

Crowds: Puerto Banús is more crowded, especially on weekends and in August. The marina walkways are packed with tourists and boat crew. Marbella Marina is busier in the morning when fishing boats return, but generally less intense. For a relaxed start to your charter, Marbella wins. For a vibrant, buzzing atmosphere, Puerto Banús.

Check-in procedures are similar: you meet the skipper at the charter office, board, and depart. Both ports have security gates and require ID. No major differences here.

Which port for which type of group

If you are a couple or a small group looking for a romantic sunset cruise, Marbella Marina is quieter and more intimate. If you are a group of friends wanting a party boat with loud music and champagne, Puerto Banús is the better fit. Families with children often prefer Marbella because it is less hectic and has easier access to beaches. Business clients and corporate events lean towards Puerto Banús for the prestige factor.

Solo travellers or small groups on a budget should choose Marbella. Large groups (10-20 people) might find better value catamarans from Marbella. Superyacht charters for VIPs are almost exclusively from Puerto Banús. The rule of thumb: if you want to be seen, go to Puerto Banús. If you want to see the coast without the fuss, go to Marbella.

Common questions

Is it cheaper to charter a boat from Marbella or Puerto Banús?

Generally, Marbella is 15-25% cheaper for the same boat type and duration. A half-day motor yacht from Marbella starts around EUR 800, while from Puerto Banús it starts around EUR 1,000. The price difference reflects berthing fees and demand.

Can I see dolphins from both ports?

Yes, both ports offer access to dolphin-spotting areas, especially near the Strait of Gibraltar. Puerto Banús is about 15 minutes closer to the Strait, but the difference is small. Dolphins are most common from April to October.

Which port has more superyachts available for charter?

Puerto Banús has a much higher concentration of superyachts over 60 ft. Marbella Marina has fewer superyachts but more variety in smaller boats. If you want a 100 ft yacht with crew, Puerto Banús is your best bet.

Is it easy to get from Marbella to Puerto Banús without a car?

Yes, the local bus line L-2 runs every 15 minutes and takes 15 minutes. Taxis cost around EUR 15-20. Both ports are also connected by a coastal path for walking or cycling, though it is 5 km.

Which port is better for a family with young children?

Marbella Marina is more family-friendly because it is less crowded and has direct access to beaches and playgrounds. Puerto Banús is busier and more focused on nightlife and luxury shopping, which may not suit young children.

Do both ports have parking facilities?

Yes, both have underground car parks. Marbella Marina charges around EUR 25 per day in summer; Puerto Banús charges EUR 30-40 and fills up by late morning. Arrive early or use a taxi.

Can I charter a licence-free day boat from Puerto Banús?

Licence-free day boats are rare in Puerto Banús because the marina prefers skipper-operated charters. Marbella Marina has a wider selection of these boats. If you want to drive yourself, choose Marbella.

Seasonal differences: how timing affects your choice

In summer (June to September), both ports are packed, but the crowds hit differently. Puerto Banús becomes a circus of superyachts, influencers, and EUR 20 cocktails. Marbella Marina is busy but retains a local feel, with more Spanish families and fewer tourists. For a charter in July, expect to book at least two weeks ahead in Puerto Banús; Marbella gives you more flexibility, especially for smaller boats like RIBs or fishing boats.

In winter (November to March), many boats in Puerto Banús are laid up or used for private events, so charter availability drops. Marbella Marina stays more active, with local fishermen and a handful of charter boats operating on demand. The weather is cooler (15-20 degrees C), but you can still cruise for dolphin spotting or a lunch at Estepona. From Puerto Banús, winter charters are mostly for corporate groups or special occasions, and prices drop by 20-30% compared to summer. For a spontaneous winter day out, Marbella is the safer bet.

Spring and autumn are the sweet spots. April, May, September, and October offer 22-28 degrees C, fewer crowds, and lower prices (10-20% off peak). Both ports are pleasant, but Puerto Banús feels less frantic, making the premium easier to stomach. If you want a relaxed charter with good weather, aim for May or September from either port.

Specific boat examples: what you can actually book

Let us get concrete. At Marbella Marina, you might find a 40 ft Azimut motor yacht for a half-day charter from around EUR 900. It seats 10 guests, has a sun pad and a small cabin, and includes a skipper. At Puerto Banús, the same model could be EUR 1,100, but it might come with a more experienced crew or a complimentary bottle of cava. For catamarans, a Lagoon 42 from Marbella might cost EUR 1,400 for a half-day; from Puerto Banús, a similar Lagoon 42 could be EUR 1,600, but with a larger flybridge and water toys included.

RIBs are a different story. A 30 ft RIB with twin 300 HP engines from Marbella might cost EUR 500 for two hours, perfect for a quick blast to Cala del Faro. From Puerto Banús, the same RIB could be EUR 650, and you often get a newer model with more horsepower. Fishing boats, like a 25 ft walkaround with rods and bait, are almost exclusive to Marbella, starting around EUR 400 for four hours. Puerto Banús rarely offers dedicated fishing charters; instead, you get luxury motor yachts with fishing gear as an add-on.

For licence-free day boats (under 15 HP, no skipper needed), Marbella Marina has several options starting from EUR 250 for four hours. These are ideal for couples or small families who want to explore the coast at their own pace. Puerto Banús has almost none, so if this is your plan, head to Marbella.

Hidden costs and tips: what to watch for

Fuel is usually included in the charter price on BoatHire24, but confirm this before booking. In Puerto Banús, some operators add a fuel surcharge for longer trips, especially if you go to the Strait of Gibraltar (which burns more fuel). In Marbella, fuel is more often bundled. Food and drink are typically extra at both ports, but Puerto Banús charters often push premium catering packages (EUR 50-100 per person for a seafood platter and champagne). Marbella charters are more likely to let you bring your own food and drinks, saving you money.

Tips for the skipper are customary (10-15% of the charter price) at both ports. In Puerto Banús, the expectation is higher because the service level is higher. Budget for this. Parking costs are higher in Puerto Banús (EUR 30-40 per day) and the car parks are often full by 10 am in summer. Marbella Marina has a larger car park and a cheaper rate (EUR 25). If you are staying nearby, consider walking or taking a taxi to avoid the hassle.

Another tip: check the wind forecast. Both ports are sheltered, but the sea state can differ. In a Levante wind (easterly), the coast east of Marbella can get choppy, while Puerto Banús is slightly more protected. In Poniente (westerly), the opposite is true. A good skipper will adjust the route, but if you are prone to seasickness, ask your charter operator about the conditions on the day.

Local attractions after the charter: extending your day

After a charter from Marbella Marina, you are steps away from the old town. Walk through the Orange Square, visit the 16th-century Ermita de Santiago church, or grab a plate of espetos (sardines grilled on a stick) at a beachfront chiringuito. The marina itself has a small fish market where you can buy fresh catch. From Puerto Banús, the post-charter options are glitzier: browse designer boutiques, have a cocktail at a portside bar, or book dinner at a Michelin-starred restaurant like Skina in Marbella (a 10-minute taxi ride). The contrast is deliberate: Marbella is about local culture, Puerto Banús about luxury.

If you want to combine a charter with a visit to Estepona, consider departing from Marbella and sailing west. You can anchor at Estepona marina, walk the old town's flower-covered streets, and then sail back. From Puerto Banús, the same trip is shorter by 10 minutes, but you miss the Marbella old town experience. For a full day out, start from Marbella, go to Estepona for lunch, and return via Cabopino for a swim. That route is harder from Puerto Banús because you backtrack.

For families, Marbella Marina has a playground and a small beach within the port. Puerto Banús has no beach; the nearest is San Pedro de Alcántara, a 5-minute drive. If you want to combine boat time with beach time, Marbella wins hands down.

Booking strategies: how to get the best deal

Book early for both ports, but especially Puerto Banús. In peak season, luxury charters are snapped up weeks in advance. For Marbella, you have more flexibility, but popular boats (like the 40 ft catamarans) still sell out. If you are flexible on boat type, you can often find last-minute deals on our search for Marbella, as some operators offer 10-20% discounts to fill empty slots. Puerto Banús operators rarely discount because demand is high.

Consider a full-day charter (8 hours) instead of half-day. The per-hour cost drops significantly: a full-day motor yacht from Marbella might cost EUR 1,500 versus EUR 900 for half-day, giving you double the time for 66% more money. From Puerto Banús, the same logic applies but the absolute numbers are higher. For groups of 8-12 people, a full-day catamaran from Marbella is often the best value, as you can split the cost and explore further (Nerja or Gibraltar).

Finally, use the departure port to your advantage. If you are staying in Marbella town, charter from Marbella Marina to save on taxi costs and time. If you are in Puerto Banús or nearby (San Pedro, Benahavís), charter from Puerto Banús for convenience. The sailing time difference is negligible, but the land logistics matter. For a stress-free day, choose the port closest to your accommodation.
