title: Marbella vs Benalmadena Boat Rental: Which is Best?
excerpt: Compare boat rental in Marbella vs Benalmadena. Discover which Costa del Sol port suits your charter style, budget, and vibe.
metaDescription: Marbella vs Benalmadena boat rental: compare marinas, boat types, prices, and local vibes. Find the best port for your Costa del Sol charter.
author: Mardo Soo
content:
The 30-second answer

If you want glitz, superyachts, and a party atmosphere, choose Marbella (Puerto Banús). If you prefer a more relaxed, family-friendly vibe with lower prices and easy access to dolphin-watching, go with Benalmadena. Both ports offer excellent boat rental options with licensed skippers, but your choice depends on your budget and preferred scene.

Puerto Banús vs Puerto Deportivo de Benalmádena: the marinas

Puerto Banús is the flashy heart of Marbella's boat scene. Think Ferrari-lined docks, champagne bars, and a crowd that likes to be seen. The marina itself is a spectacle: designer shops, high-end restaurants, and yachts that cost more than most houses. You'll find motor yachts from 40 to 100-plus feet, sailing yachts, and the occasional superyacht. Benalmadena's Puerto Deportivo is more laid-back. It's one of the largest marinas on the Costa del Sol, but it lacks the pretension of Banús. Here you'll see families, local fishermen, and a mix of charter boats. The promenade is lined with casual chiringuitos and tapas bars. Benalmadena also has a large marina with a dedicated fishing port section, so you can charter a fishing boat easily. The vibe is less 'look at me' and more 'let's enjoy the sea'. Both marinas have good facilities: fuel docks, chandleries, and parking. Banús parking is notoriously expensive and tight; Benalmadena is more spacious and cheaper. If you're arriving by car, factor that in.

Boat types and prices: what you get for your money

In Marbella, you're paying for the address. A 40-foot motor yacht for a day charter starts from around EUR 1,200 in low season, rising to EUR 2,500 in August. Catamarans are similar, with 40-foot models from EUR 1,500. Benalmadena is typically 20-30% cheaper. A comparable 40-foot motor yacht might be EUR 900-1,800. RIBs and speedboats are more abundant in Benalmadena, with prices from EUR 400 for a half-day. Licence-free day boats (under 15 hp) are also more common there, starting around EUR 250 for a few hours. Sailing yachts are available in both ports, but Benalmadena has a stronger sailing community, so you might find better deals on older models. Superyachts (over 80 feet) are almost exclusively in Puerto Banús; Benalmadena rarely sees them. Fishing boats are another differentiator. Benalmadena has several dedicated fishing charter operators offering half-day trips from EUR 350. Marbella has fewer, and they tend to be more expensive. For dolphin-watching, both ports are good, but Benalmadena's proximity to the Strait of Gibraltar migration routes means shorter travel time to the best spots.

Local attractions and day trip options

From Marbella, you can head east to Cabopino (a quiet nature reserve with a small marina) or west to Estepona (the charming old town with flower-filled streets). A popular route is a lunch stop at Cala del Faro, a small cove with a beachfront restaurant. You can also cruise towards the Strait of Gibraltar for dolphin sightings, though it's a longer trip (about 1.5 hours from port). From Benalmadena, you're closer to the Strait. A typical day trip might include dolphin-watching near the Strait, a stop at a secluded cove like Playa de la Vibora, and lunch at a chiringuito in Fuengirola or Mijas Costa. Benalmadena is also a 30-minute drive from the Nerja caves (not by boat, but worth a day trip if you're staying longer). Both ports offer sunset cruises, but the backdrop differs: Marbella's skyline is dominated by La Concha mountain, while Benalmadena has the iconic marina and the Benalmadena Pueblo (the old hilltop village). If you want to combine a boat trip with a visit to a historic town, Marbella's old town is walkable from the port; Benalmadena's old town is a steep climb but worth it for the views.

Which is better for families, groups, and parties?

For families with children, Benalmadena wins. The marina has a playground, a sealife centre, and the Tivoli World amusement park (though it's currently under renovation). The waters are calmer, and the charter operators are used to accommodating kids. Many boats have shaded decks and safety gear for small children. Marbella is more adult-oriented. The party scene in Puerto Banús is legendary: you can charter a yacht with a DJ, drinks, and a stop at a beach club like Ocean Club or Nikki Beach. Groups of friends looking for a lively day out will prefer Marbella. Benalmadena has its share of party boats, but they're tamer. For corporate events or special celebrations, both ports work. Marbella offers a more impressive backdrop for a memorable experience. Benalmadena offers better value for larger groups on a budget. If you're a solo traveller or couple looking for a romantic sunset sail, both are fine, but Benalmadena's quieter coves might suit you better. Note that all charters include a licensed skipper, so you don't need a licence for any boat type.

How to book and what to expect

Booking through BoatHire24 is straightforward. Use the search page to filter by port, boat type, and date. Both Marbella and Benalmadena have a wide selection. Expect to pay a deposit (usually 30-50%) at booking, with the balance due on the day. The skipper will meet you at the port 15 minutes before departure. You can bring your own food and drink on most charters, but some operators offer catering packages. Check the weather: the Costa del Sol is sunny most of the year, but wind can be strong in the afternoon, especially in summer. The skipper will decide if it's safe to go out. Fuel is usually included in the price for half-day and full-day charters, but confirm. Tipping is not mandatory but appreciated (10-15% is standard). Cancellation policies vary: some operators offer free cancellation up to 48 hours before, others charge a fee. Read the terms carefully. For more tips on boat rental in Spain, check our blog.

Common questions

Q: Is Marbella or Benalmadena better for a first-time boat renter?
A: Benalmadena is more relaxed and cheaper, making it ideal for beginners. The marina is less intimidating, and skippers are used to inexperienced groups. Marbella is fine too, but the higher prices and flashy atmosphere might feel overwhelming.

Q: Can I rent a boat without a licence in both ports?
A: Yes, all charters include a licensed skipper, so no licence is needed. Licence-free day boats (small boats under 15 hp) are available in both ports but more common in Benalmadena.

Q: Which port has better dolphin-watching trips?
A: Benalmadena is closer to the Strait of Gibraltar, so you'll spend less time getting to the dolphin zones. Both ports offer dolphin-watching, but Benalmadena is more efficient.

Q: Are there any hidden costs I should know about?
A: Check if fuel is included (most charters include it). Some operators charge extra for water toys (paddleboards, snorkel gear) or catering. Parking at Puerto Banús is expensive; Benalmadena is cheaper. Always confirm the total price before booking.

Q: What is the best time of year for boat rental?
A: May to October is peak season, with July and August being the hottest and busiest. June and September offer good weather with fewer crowds. Winter charters are possible but weather-dependent; many boats are laid up from November to March.

Q: Can I take a boat from Marbella to Benalmadena or vice versa?
A: Yes, it's a short trip (about 30-45 minutes by motor yacht). Some charters offer a one-way drop-off, but check with the operator. It's a great way to combine both ports in one day.

Q: Which port has more luxury superyachts?
A: Puerto Banús in Marbella is the superyacht capital of the Costa del Sol. Benalmadena has fewer large yachts. If you want to charter a superyacht (over 80 feet), Marbella is your only option.

Seasonal differences: when to book which port

June and September are the sweet spots for both ports, but the dynamics differ. In Marbella, July and August bring the peak crowd: Puerto Banús is packed, prices hit their maximum, and you'll need to book weeks in advance. The heat can be intense, often hitting 35 degrees C, but the sea breeze helps. Benalmadena is also busy in August but feels less claustrophobic because the marina is larger and the beaches are wider. In May and October, Marbella is quieter but still pleasant, with daytime temperatures around 22-26 degrees C. Benalmadena in October can be windy, especially in the afternoon, which might affect smaller RIBs. Winter charters (November to March) are possible in both ports but weather-dependent. Benalmadena has more year-round fishing charters because the Strait of Gibraltar is less affected by winter storms. Marbella's superyachts are often in the Caribbean during winter, so the selection drops. If you're booking for a special occasion like a birthday or anniversary, June offers the best balance of good weather and availability in both ports.

Navigating from each port: distances and sailing times

From Puerto Banús, the nearest decent anchorage is Cala del Faro, about 4 nautical miles west. It takes 20-30 minutes by motor yacht. Further west, Estepona is 10 NM (45 minutes). Eastwards, Cabopino is 5 NM (25 minutes), and Marbella Marina is just 2 NM (10 minutes). Benalmadena is 15 NM east of Puerto Banús, a 45-minute motor. From Benalmadena, the Strait of Gibraltar dolphin zones are about 12 NM south-west, a 40-minute run. Fuengirola is 4 NM west (15 minutes), and Mijas Costa has several coves within 3 NM. For a full-day trip from Benalmadena, you can reach Nerja (35 NM east) in about 2 hours, but that's a long day. A better option is to head to the Cala de Mijas or Playa de la Vibora, both within 20 minutes. If you want to combine a visit to Marbella's old town with a boat trip, departing from Puerto Banús means you're a 15-minute walk from the old town. Benalmadena's old town (Benalmadena Pueblo) is a 10-minute taxi ride uphill from the marina. For a lunch stop, both ports have beachfront chiringuitos within walking distance of the dock.

Practical tips for first-time renters in each port

Arrive at the port 30 minutes early, not 15. Parking in Puerto Banús is a nightmare: the main car park charges around EUR 30 for a day, and spaces fill by 10 AM. Use the free park-and-ride at the edge of Banús and walk 10 minutes. Benalmadena has a large free car park near the fishing port section, plus paid options closer to the main marina. Bring sunscreen, a hat, and a light jacket even in summer. The wind on the water can be 5 degrees C cooler than on land. Most boats have a small fridge, but bring your own ice if you want to keep drinks cold for a full day. Benalmadena charter operators are often more flexible with last-minute changes. Marbella operators are used to high expectations: if you want a specific brand of champagne or a particular playlist, ask in advance. For a half-day charter, Benalmadena is better value because you can get a 4-hour trip for EUR 400-600 on a RIB. In Marbella, half-day motor yacht charters start at EUR 800. Always confirm the maximum number of passengers: Spanish regulations allow 12 passengers on most charter boats, but some smaller RIBs only take 6-8.

Food and drink options on board and ashore

In Marbella, you can order a catering package from the charter operator: think sushi platters, paella, and cava. Prices range from EUR 30-60 per person. Or you can bring your own: stop at the Mercado de Marbella (central market) for fresh seafood and local wines. In Benalmadena, the marina has several supermarkets within 200 metres, so stocking up is easy. Many Benalmadena charters include a stop at a chiringuito for lunch. The best one is Chiringuito La Vibora, accessible only by boat, serving grilled fish and cold beer. In Marbella, the chiringuito at Cala del Faro is popular but expensive: expect EUR 40-50 per person for a meal. If you want a beach club experience, Marbella's Ocean Club and Nikki Beach are famous but require advance booking for a table. Benalmadena has beach clubs too, like the one at Playa de la Vibora, but they're more casual and cheaper. For a sunset drink, both ports have bars right on the marina. Puerto Banús has the famous Ocean Club for post-charter cocktails. Benalmadena has the less pretentious Bar Náutico with live music. Most charter operators allow you to bring your own alcohol, but some charge a corkage fee for glass bottles.

Environmental considerations and responsible chartering

The Costa del Sol's marine ecosystem is fragile, especially around the Strait of Gibraltar. Both ports have operators committed to responsible practices, but it's worth asking. In Benalmadena, several fishing charter operators use sustainable catch-and-release methods. For dolphin-watching, choose operators that follow the voluntary code of conduct: no chasing, no approaching within 60 metres, and limited time with pods. Marbella has fewer dedicated dolphin-watching operators, but the ones that exist are generally responsible. Anchoring in seagrass meadows (Posidonia oceanica) is illegal in Spain. Ask your skipper to anchor on sandy bottoms. Both ports have designated zones for anchoring. If you're renting a licence-free day boat, be extra careful: these boats are often used in shallow coves where seagrass grows. Benalmadena's marina has a recycling point for boat waste. In Puerto Banús, the fuel dock accepts bilge water for disposal. Consider bringing reusable containers for food and drink rather than single-use plastic. The Mediterranean is already polluted enough without adding more waste from a day trip.

Comparing the booking process and customer support

On BoatHire24, you can compare both ports side by side. The search page lets you filter by port, boat type, capacity, and price range. Marbella listings tend to have more photos and detailed descriptions because the operators are used to a discerning clientele. Benalmadena listings are often more straightforward but still include essential info. Customer support for Marbella charters is usually faster because the operators are larger and have dedicated staff. Benalmadena operators are often smaller family businesses, so response times can be slower, but they're more personal. When you book, you'll receive a confirmation with the skipper's contact details. In Marbella, the skipper might be a professional captain with years of experience; in Benalmadena, the skipper is often the boat owner who knows the local waters intimately. Both are qualified, but the style differs. If you have special requests (like a birthday cake or a specific route), communicate them at booking. Marbella operators are more likely to accommodate complex requests. Benalmadena operators are more flexible with spontaneous changes on the day. For more tips on the booking process, check our blog.

title: Marbella vs Estepona Boat Charter: Pros & Cons
excerpt: Deciding between a Marbella and Estepona boat charter? We break down the pros and cons of each departure port, from the glitz of Puerto Banús to the laid-back charm of Estepona. Find the best fit for your day on the water.
metaDescription: Compare Marbella vs Estepona boat charter: pros and cons of each port, boat types, costs, and local highlights. Choose your ideal Costa del Sol departure point.
author: Andra Kiirkivi
content:
The 30-second answer

If you want glitz, nightlife, and a guaranteed party vibe, charter from Marbella (especially Puerto Banús). If you prefer quieter waters, cheaper mooring fees, and easier access to the Strait of Gibraltar's dolphin colonies, start from Estepona. Both ports offer the same Mediterranean conditions, but your choice depends on whether you value celebrity-spotting or chilled-out sailing. BoatHire24 covers both, so you can compare directly without the sales pitch.

Marbella: the celebrity magnet

Marbella boat charter means Puerto Banús. That marina is a floating catwalk for superyachts, and the people-watching is top-tier. You'll see everything from 60-metre motor yachts to sleek Italian RIBs. The main advantage is the sheer choice: dozens of operators, from budget-friendly licence-free day boats to luxury catamarans with jet skis onboard. Departure is quick, usually within 30 minutes of arrival, and the crew know the coastline intimately. The downside? Crowds. In peak July and August, Puerto Banús is a scrum. You'll queue for fuel, for the check-in desk, and for a parking spot if you drive. Prices are higher too: expect to pay from around EUR 1,200 for a half-day on a 10-metre motor yacht, compared to EUR 900 from Estepona. If you're after a bachelor party or a boozy sunset cruise, Marbella wins. But if you value your eardrums and your wallet, read on.

Estepona: the understated alternative

Estepona boat charter is the quiet cousin who throws the best house parties. The marina here is smaller, less flashy, and far more relaxed. You'll find the same range of boats, motor yachts, catamarans, sailing yachts, RIBs, but at lower rates. A half-day on a 12-metre catamaran from Estepona starts around EUR 1,500, versus EUR 2,000+ from Puerto Banús. The real draw is the proximity to the Strait of Gibraltar. A 20-minute cruise southwest puts you in prime dolphin territory: common, striped, and even pilot whales in season. The water is clearer here too, thanks to less river runoff. Estepona's old town is a 10-minute walk from the marina, with tapas bars like La Escollera serving fresh catch. The trade-off is nightlife. Estepona has bars and a casino, but it's not Banús. If you want to dock for dinner and then hit a club, you'll need a taxi back to Marbella (30 minutes, around EUR 40).

Cost comparison: Marbella vs Estepona

Let's talk numbers. Prices vary by season, boat size, and extras, but the baseline is clear. Marbella commands a premium for its brand. A typical 10-metre motor yacht for a half-day (4 hours) in July: Marbella from EUR 1,200, Estepona from EUR 900. A 15-metre catamaran for a full day (8 hours): Marbella from EUR 3,500, Estepona from EUR 2,800. Fuel is usually extra, and Marbella's fuel dock charges about 10% more per litre. Mooring fees ? Marbella's Puerto Banús charges around EUR 100 for a 10-metre boat overnight; Estepona is EUR 60. If you're on a budget, Estepona stretches your euro further. Check our search page for real-time pricing on both ports.

Boat types and availability

Both ports offer the same categories: motor yachts, catamarans, sailing yachts, RIBs, fishing boats, licence-free day boats, and superyachts. The difference is scale. Marbella has more superyachts (over 24 metres) available for charter, often with helipads and onboard spas. Estepona has a higher proportion of sailing yachts and catamarans, which are ideal for dolphin-watching because they're quieter. Licence-free day boats (under 6 metres, no skipper required) are more common in Estepona, where the marina is less congested. If you want a fishing charter, both ports have dedicated boats, but Estepona's fleet is slightly larger due to the local fishing tradition. For a RIB speedboat, Marbella has more options with bigger engines (300+ HP) for watersports. Book via BoatHire24 to see the full inventory.

Scenery and routes

From Marbella, you can head east towards Cabopino and Cala del Faro, a secluded cove with a beach bar accessible only by boat. Or west towards the Río Verde estuary, where you can anchor for a swim. The backdrop is La Concha mountain, which looms over the coast. From Estepona, the classic route is southwest to the Strait of Gibraltar, where the Atlantic meets the Mediterranean. You'll pass the Punta Doncella lighthouse and the cliffs of El Saladillo. The water clarity is better here, and the dolphin sightings are almost guaranteed. If you have a full day, you can push to Gibraltar itself (about 30 NM from Estepona, 40 NM from Marbella). The views of the Rock are spectacular. For a shorter trip, Estepona's own beaches like Playa de la Rada are pleasant but busy. Marbella's Cala del Faro is more exclusive. Both routes offer sunset views, but Marbella's skyline is more dramatic.

Local colour and extras

Marbella's Puerto Banús has the Gucci store and the yachts that make Instagram jealous. You can dock, walk to the casino, or eat at a Michelin-starred restaurant like Skina. Estepona's old town is a maze of whitewashed streets with flower pots and a weekly market on Wednesdays. The marina has a decent selection of chiringuitos (beach bars) like El Mirlo. If you want a stop for lunch, Marbella has more high-end options; Estepona has better cheap seafood. Both ports offer jet ski rentals, but Marbella's are pricier. For a truly unique experience, charter a fishing boat from Estepona and try for bluefin tuna (seasonal, June to September). Marbella's fishing charters focus on seabass and bream. The choice boils down to your tolerance for crowds. Marbella is a stage; Estepona is a living room. Read more on our blog for detailed itineraries.

Practicalities: access and parking

Marbella's Puerto Banús is accessible by car, taxi, or bus from Málaga airport (45 minutes). Parking is a nightmare in summer: expect EUR 30 for the day in a nearby lot, or EUR 50 for the marina's own garage. Estepona is 30 minutes further from the airport (75 minutes by car), but parking is easier and cheaper (EUR 10 for the day). Both marinas have taxi ranks and bus stops. If you're flying in, Estepona is a bit more of a trek, but the savings on charter costs often offset the taxi fare. For a day trip, consider renting a car. If you're staying in Marbella, you're already there. Estepona requires a short drive. The traffic on the AP-7 motorway can be heavy in August, so factor that in. Both ports have full facilities: showers, toilets, restaurants, and fuel docks.

Which one should you choose?

If you're planning a party, a stag do, or a high-roller experience, Marbella is your port. The energy is infectious, the boats are flashier, and the nightlife is legendary. If you want a peaceful family day, dolphin watching, or a romantic sunset cruise without the crowds, Estepona wins. The water is clearer, the prices are lower, and the atmosphere is relaxed. For fishing enthusiasts, Estepona offers better access to the Strait's tuna grounds. For watersports, Marbella has more RIBs and jet skis. The final factor: your budget. Estepona gives you a bigger boat for the same money. Use our search tool to filter by port and compare. Either way, you're on the Costa del Sol, so you can't go wrong.

Common questions

Which port has cheaper boat charters?
Estepona is generally 20-30% cheaper than Marbella for the same boat size and duration. Mooring fees and fuel are also lower in Estepona.

Can I see dolphins from both ports?
Yes, but Estepona is closer to the Strait of Gibraltar where dolphin pods are more frequent. From Marbella, you need a longer cruise west.

Do I need a licence to rent a boat in either port?
No, because every charter on BoatHire24 includes a licensed skipper. Licence-free day boats are available in both ports if you want to drive yourself.

Is Marbella better for nightlife after a charter?
Yes, Puerto Banús has clubs like Pangea and Olivia Valère. Estepona has quieter bars and a casino, but it's not a party hub.

Which port is closer to Málaga airport?
Marbella (45 minutes by car) is closer than Estepona (75 minutes). But the extra drive saves you money on the charter.

Can I charter a superyacht from Estepona?
Yes, but the selection is smaller than in Marbella. For superyachts over 30 metres, Marbella is the better choice.

What's the best time of year for a boat charter?
May to October offers the best weather (25-30 degrees C). July and August are busiest and priciest. September is ideal: warm water, fewer crowds.

Dolphin watching: Estepona's secret weapon

If dolphins are your priority, Estepona is the clear winner. The Strait of Gibraltar is one of the world's best spots for cetacean sightings, with common dolphins, striped dolphins, and even pilot whales present year-round. From Estepona marina, you can reach the prime viewing areas in 20-30 minutes. From Marbella's Puerto Banús, you're looking at a 45-minute cruise west, eating into your charter time. The water depth drops sharply near the strait, creating upwellings that attract baitfish and the dolphins that chase them. On a typical 4-hour charter from Estepona, you'll see dolphins 80-90% of the time between April and October. The boats used are mostly catamarans and sailing yachts, which are quieter and don't spook the animals. Some operators even have hydrophones to listen to dolphin clicks underwater. Marbella charters can see dolphins too, but it's less reliable. You're better off booking a dedicated wildlife trip from Estepona if that's your main goal.

Fishing charters: which port lands the bigger catch

Fishing from Marbella vs Estepona is a tale of two fisheries. Marbella's coastal waters are shallower, around 20-40 metres, and the catch is mostly seabass, bream, and mackerel. It's fine for a relaxed day with a rod, but don't expect trophies. Estepona, by contrast, sits at the edge of the Strait of Gibraltar where the Atlantic meets the Mediterranean. The continental shelf drops to 800 metres within 5 nautical miles of the coast. That means bluefin tuna, swordfish, and even sharks are on the menu. A half-day fishing charter from Estepona costs from around EUR 400 for a 6-metre boat with a skipper, compared to EUR 500 from Marbella for the same setup. The season for bluefin tuna runs from June to September, and Estepona's fleet of fishing boats is roughly 30% larger than Marbella's. If you're serious about fishing, choose Estepona and bring your own gear or rent top-shelf tackle from the marina shop.

Weather and sea conditions: a practical breakdown

Both ports share the same Mediterranean climate, but local geography creates subtle differences. Marbella is sheltered by La Concha mountain, which blocks some of the westerly winds. That means calmer seas in the morning, but the afternoon Levante wind (easterly) can kick up chop from 2-3 knots to 15-20 knots by 3 PM. Estepona is more exposed to the west, so it gets the Poniente wind (westerly) more often, which is generally lighter. In summer, both ports average 25-30 degrees C air temperature and 22-26 degrees C water temperature. The key difference is the Strait of Gibraltar effect near Estepona: tidal currents can run at 3-4 knots, creating standing waves in the narrows. For a standard coastal cruise, this doesn't matter. But if you plan to cross to Gibraltar or head offshore, check the tide tables. Marbella's waters are more predictable for beginners. Estepona requires a skipper who knows the local currents. Every BoatHire24 charter includes a licensed skipper, so you're covered either way.

Seasonal pricing: when to book for the best deal

The cost of a Marbella vs Estepona boat charter varies dramatically by season. In May and June, Marbella prices are 10-15% higher than Estepona. By July and August, the gap widens to 25-30% as Marbella's demand spikes. For example, a 12-metre motor yacht in August: Marbella from EUR 2,200 for a half-day, Estepona from EUR 1,600. In September, the gap narrows again to 15-20% as the crowds thin. October is the sweet spot: both ports drop prices by 30-40% from peak season, and the water is still 22 degrees C. If you're flexible, book Estepona in September for the best balance of weather, dolphin activity, and cost. Marbella in October is also good, but you'll miss the nightlife buzz. For superyachts, Marbella's prices barely drop in shoulder season because the boats are in high demand for events. Estepona's superyacht fleet is smaller, so you might find a deal if you book 2-3 weeks in advance.

Day trips from each port: specific routes and distances

From Marbella, a classic 4-hour route goes east to Cabopino and Cala del Faro, a total round trip of about 15 nautical miles. You anchor at Cala del Faro for a swim and lunch at the beach bar. The water depth there is 5-10 metres, clear enough for snorkelling. A full-day route from Marbella pushes west to Estepona or even Gibraltar, but that's 40 NM round trip, leaving little time for stops. From Estepona, the best 4-hour route is southwest to Punta Doncella and the Strait viewing area, about 10 NM round trip. You'll see dolphins, then anchor at Playa del Cristo for a swim. A full-day from Estepona can reach Gibraltar (30 NM round trip) with time for lunch at Ocean Village marina. The views of the Rock are unmatched. For a longer trip, both ports can access the Nerja caves, but that's 50 NM from Marbella and 65 NM from Estepona, requiring an overnight charter. Stick to local routes for a day charter. Use the search tool to filter by duration and port.

Boat types for specific activities: matching the vessel to the goal

Your choice of boat depends on what you want to do. For dolphin watching from Estepona, a 12-15 metre catamaran is ideal: stable, quiet, and with plenty of deck space for kids. Prices from EUR 1,500 for a half-day. For a party cruise from Marbella, a 15-metre motor yacht with a sound system and onboard bar is the go-to, from EUR 2,500 for a half-day. For fishing from Estepona, a 6-8 metre RIB or dedicated fishing boat with outriggers is best, from EUR 400. For a romantic sunset from either port, a 10-metre sailing yacht is perfect, quiet and intimate, from EUR 800 from Estepona, EUR 1,000 from Marbella. For watersports like jet skiing or wakeboarding from Marbella, a 7-metre RIB with a 250 HP engine is standard, from EUR 600 for 2 hours. Licence-free day boats (under 6 metres, no skipper required) are available in both ports for around EUR 300 for a half-day, but Estepona has more options due to less marina congestion. Check the full inventory on BoatHire24.

Practical tips for first-time charterers in either port

If you're new to boat charters, a few things apply to both Marbella and Estepona. Arrive 15 minutes early to check in and meet the skipper. Bring sunscreen (SPF 50+), a hat, and a light jacket for the wind. Most charters include water and soft drinks, but check before you go. Food is usually extra or you can bring your own. In Marbella, the marina is huge; look for the meeting point on your booking confirmation. In Estepona, the marina is smaller and easier to navigate. Both have free Wi-Fi in the marina office. For parking, Estepona is easier and cheaper (EUR 10 per day versus EUR 30-50 in Marbella). If you're prone to seasickness, take a tablet an hour before departure, especially on Estepona charters heading into the strait where currents are stronger. Tipping the skipper is customary: 10-15% of the charter cost is standard. And always book in advance during July and August, especially for weekends. Last-minute bookings are possible but you'll pay a premium. Read our blog for a pre-charter checklist.
